Biosecurity Incursions—Report of Auditor-General into Ministry of Primary
Industry’s Preparedness and Responsiveness

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have also received a letter  from the Hon Damien O’Connor
seeking to debate under Standing Order 386 the report from the Controller and Auditor-
General on the effectiveness of the Ministry for Primary Industries in preparing for and
responding to biosecurity incu rsions in New Zealand. The release of the report is a
particular case of recent occurrence. As  an Auditor-General’s  report, there is no
ministerial responsibility for the report itself, but it de als with matters involving
ministerial responsibility. The report finds evidence that the Ministry for Primary
Industries is under-prepared for potential incursions of some  high-risk organisms, and
makes wide-ranging recommendations to improve preparedness.
Given the significance of the matter a nd the need for a high level of public
confidence in New Zealand’s biosecurity re sponse, I consider it important enough to
warrant the immediate attenti on of the House by way of an urgent debate. I call upon
the Hon Damien O’Connor to move that th e House take note of an urgent matter of
public importance.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labou r—West Coast - Tasman) : I move, That the
House take note of a matter of urgent public importance . Last week we received from
the Auditor-General a report that was perhap s one of the most al arming things to be
tabled in Parliament over the last 12 months. This report, in brief, said that we are not
prepared for an outbreak of foot-and-m outh in this country. There will be many
members, including the Speaker himself, I am sure—[Interruption]

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Members, please
show some courtesy.
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR : —who are aware of the significance of our primary
industries and of the constant threat to each and every one of those sectors through foot-
and-mouth. The Auditor-General’s overview sa id: “Our country is more dependent on
biosecurity than any other developed count ry. Biosecurity is fundamental to New
Zealand’s economic health and natural heri tage.” Well, no truer statement could be
written down, and no truer commitment to Ne w Zealand’s future could be made than
that from a Government that properly funds, properly resources, and shows commitment
to biosecurity.
What did National do when it came into pow er? Its very first Budget cut over $2
million from front-line services for biosecu rity, and ongoing cuts resulted in 96 front-
line staff being chopped from MAF Biosecu rity New Zealand. At that time the

items.speaker: Government came back saying
items.text: “Well, wh at did Labour do in Government?”. In
Government we doubled the amount of f unding for biosecurity from 1999 through to
2008—we doubled the commitment to biosecurity. We still knew that it was not perfect,
but we had doubled the funding, and we had formed Biosecurity New Zealand as a
separate entity within the Ministry of Ag riculture and Forestr y—a separate entity
focused on protecting New Zealan d from biosecurity risk. We had then instructed it to
undertake a strategic review and develop a strategic plan for biosecurity moving
forward. Labour in Government both recognised, acknowledged, and funded biosecurity
as the most important area—more important than military security. We doubled the
funding and we have done a lot in that area.  The National Government goes on about it,
but biosecurity, as the Auditor-General’s review has said, is one of the most
fundamental and important issues for our economy.
12 Mar 2013 Urgent Debates 8397
We still get 30 to 40 incursions—that is, unwanted pests and diseases—coming into
this country every single year. I note the ability of the prof essionals, and I would like to
acknowledge the people who have worked in  biosecurity. They do an outstanding job.
But in the last 4 years I have been contacte d by a large number who have left the job.
They simply cannot commit to their conscience. They cannot in all honesty say that they
can remain in the job and do it properly under the cuts that have been forced upon them
by the National Government and by the faults  that this Auditor-General’s report has
clearly identified.
So, firstly, in 2009 we had cuts to front-l ine services. The Aud itor-General’s report
did not actually address the border security issues; it actually looked behind the scenes
to where we were told by the Minister a nd have been told on numerous occasions—the
former Minister, in particular—that New Zealand’s biosecurity system is world class. It
is world class—the Minister has repeated it in this House numerous times and through
press releases. Well, if it is world class, it is simply not good enough. We have 30 to 40
incursions every year. The Auditor-General’s report said that the planning is not up to it
not only for the single biggest threat, which is foot-and-mouth, but also in all other areas
of biosecurity—strategic planning, trai ning, human relations, management, staff
training. You name it; there are huge, huge ga ps. The recommendations are very clear.
We have got in the Auditor-General’s report an identification of the lack of leadership.
This comes squarely back to the Governme nt, because if you do not have a Minister
who is prepared to lead in their portf olio area, you will not have a Government
department—not you, Mr Assistant Speaker R obertson; perhaps the Speaker, who was
formerly in the Chair, but not you. If you do not have the leadership, you do not have
the strategic vision, and you do not have the effectiveness of the department.
I will go through a few of the recommendations. The report said that we should make
“all biosecurity planning more realistic …”. There have been, from Biosecurity New
Zealand and going back probably more than 4 years, some ambitious targets. Those
targets were set on the basis of funding that was committed by the last Labour
Government. We doubled the funding, rememb er—the funding that was going to be
consistent to all areas of Bi osecurity New Zealand. It had ambitious targets. There was
no doubt about that; the Auditor-General said so. But the Auditor-Gen eral said that it
was unrealistic, particularly given the cons traints on resources that the incoming
National Government placed on MAF Biosecur ity New Zealand. It is no good making
false promises or assurances when you cannot deliver. That is what the Auditor-General
said.

items.speaker: The second recommendation is
items.text: “Complete response plans for high-risk organisms,
including foot and mouth disease, and review  them at regular intervals …”. We had the
fruit fly outbreak, a major scare in this c ountry—the single biggest threat to the
horticulture industry is the Queensland fruit fly. We had one fly identified in Auckland,
and this report said that the response plans we re not complete and that, in fact, had that
outbreak been real, had the number of flies been far more than the one, we were not in a
situation to handle that incursion properly.
Again, on the third one—clearly  identifying the foot-and-mouth disease—it said that
we simply have to “Prepare better …”. There was Exercise Taurus in 2012. In fact,
going back, prior to that, we had a suspect ed foot-and-mouth outbreak and there were
lessons learnt. Unfortunately, the lessons have not been implemented into better
processes for MAF Biosecurity New Zealand. In fact, I have to be up front and say, of
course, that we got rid of Biosecurit y New Zealand. In fact, now the National
Government, in getting rid of Biosecurity New Zealand, has put it back into a super-
ministry called the Ministry for Primary Indus tries, which deals with issues from trade
through to food safety, forestry, fishing, and biosecurity. It is  little wonder, then, that
8398 Urgent Debates 12 Mar 2013
the issues of biosecurity get hosed down. They will be suppressed or compromised by
the trade negotiators, a number of whom w ill be with the Prime Minister in South
America at the moment, who are promising to  open doors and increase the trade, which
we need, I understand—we al l understand—but not at th e expense of biosecurity
standards.
The staff capability, which was something we were very proud of under Biosecurity
New Zealand, has been compromised. Because of the constraints on resources and on
finance, the planning, the support, and the training for each and every area of
biosecurity have been compromised, and the Auditor-General has clearly identified that.
Can I say that we are today, tomorrow, f acing threats from incursions, and one in
particular that I would like to raise that we have not properly assessed because of the
constraint on resources is the one of palm kernel expeller. That is the supplementary
feed brought in from Malaysia  and from a couple of other Asian countries to feed
cows—supplementary feeding for the most pa rt, and, actually, in times of drought, it is
essential feeding, which I acknowledge. Ho wever, there has been a report done by
farmers who went to Malaysia and who aske d to go to a factory where this product was
made. It is a by-product of the palm oil i ndustry. They wrote a report that is quite
alarming. They sent that report to the Ministry for Primary Industries and we have yet to
hear a dickey-bird from the ministry. That re port said that palm kernel is coming into
this country. It is potentially exposed to animals, to vermin, that are themselves exposed
to foot-and-mouth endemic areas. We are fearfu l that we may allow into this country,
because of insufficient monitoring by an under-resourced, under-prepared group of
people—a not unskilled but unprepared, I gue ss, group of people who have not had the
support and sufficient training in the last  few years—foot-and-mouth through palm
kernel expeller. That would be a disastr ous situation. At a time when farmers are
looking for more supplementary feed, it is going to come in in greater volumes. We
want to know that the National Government  is going to resource the Ministry for
Primary Industries to ensure that we do not get foot-and-mouth in this country.
This is quite a substantive report. I applaud and acknowledge the independence of
the Auditor-General’s work. It is first-class.  It does not pull punc hes, but it is alarming.
If the Government does not act on the recommendations, it is like placing a bomb in the
middle of the room here and waiting for it to go off, because one thing is for sure:
without major improvements in both the res ourcing and the planning,  the training, and
the preparedness of our bios ecurity team, then we are going to face a major problem.
Psa is destroying the kiwifruit industry as we speak. Psa identified flaws in the system.
We were told that the Government was m oving to improve that system; the Auditor-
General says otherwise. The Auditor-General  has said our biosecurity system is not
world class. In fact, it is deficient for a country—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Whose is better?
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR: Oh, Nick Smith. Yeah, he is  over there. He has been
one of the Ministers who has sat on his hands, squeezed resources for this vital area, and
then he will go around the country and say: “Oh, I’m the Minister of Conservation.” It
is not only the primary sectors that are thre atened by biosecurity incursions, it is the
conservation estate, and the Minister should wake up to that fact . It is, in fact, all of our
natural heritage, it is our economy threat ened each and every day, and the Auditor-
General says that we are not prepared. We are not prepared as a country and unless Nick
Smith and his colleagues and his cronies ar e prepared to put in more money, more
focus, and more resources, he and his colleag ues will be responsible for the destruction
of our economy, because, if foot-and-mouth co mes in here, we will all be paupers, and
that is the truth of it.
12 Mar 2013 Urgent Debates 8399
I go back to one of the first statements made by the Auditor-General: “Our country is
more dependent on biosecurity than any other developed country. Biosecurity is
fundamental to New Zealand’s economic health  and natural heritage.” The Minister of
Conservation, who is sitting on his chuff over there, should listen to that. The natural
heritage that we use to draw tourists to th is country and that we are so proud of in our
“100% Pure New Zealand” image is dependent upon us keeping out unwanted pests and
diseases. I applaud the Auditor-General. I hope  that there will be a report in 2 years’
time when we come into Government that clearly identifies a drastic improvement
because the Government has for once decided to put resources into the right areas of
Government responsibility. I applaud this repor t, I table it, and I seek help from the
Government to take some action on it.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.role: Associate Mi nister for Primary Industries
items.text: I wish to
begin by laying out for the House my belie f regarding the words of the previous
speaker, Damien O’Connor. The previous sp eaker has set out today to undermine the
work of biosecurity, to lay down very cl early—I absolutely acknowledge this—his
concerns for biosecurity, but in  doing so he has, in fact , damaged our reputation for
biosecurity. Today I am going to outline the very balanced response—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Read the report.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: —the very balanced response th at this Government is taking
to that report.
The previous speaker said that if the G overnment does not act—well, I can assure
this House that the Government has alrea dy acted on some of the recommendations and
will, in fact, act on all of them. The Government welcomes the Auditor-General’s
report. We will carefully consider any a dvice and recommendations made that could
improve our biosecurity system, because we as a Government understand how
important biosecurity is to this nation.
The Ministry for Primary Industries has accepted the report and all seven
recommendations, though it may not have sounde d like that a little while ago, and they
are already being worked on. Biosecurity is our top priority, and the Government is
delivering long-lasting solutions for our bios ecurity and the primar y sector to boost
productivity. Three-quarters of  a billion dollars is spen t annually on biosecurity by
central government, regional councils, indus try, and private landowners. Government
spending on biosecurity is almost double what it was in 2000 under the previous
Government, and last year saw record numbers of biosecurity staff recruited.
I too am going to quote from the report, a nd I do so now: “MPI and its predecessor
organisations responsible for biosecurity ha ve been, by and larg e, successful at
responding to incursions, dealing with betw een 30 and 40 incursions a year.”—again,
overinflated by the previous speaker; he had it up to 50. “They have developed
generally high-trust relationships with part ners by working together on responses and
have improved biosecurity by sharing knowle dge and fostering innovative practice.”
This is from the Auditor-General’s report.  “No border control”—I continue to quote
from the report—“is 100% effective, so it is important that New Zealand is prepared to
deal with incursions effectively.” And this report is very helpful in that respect.
Overall, I maintain that New Zealand does have a world-class biosecurity system. As
a Government we are extremely conscious of how important it is to protect our borders,
and continuing to improve that system is a major priority. We are always looking to
review how we do things and improve systems. This report is part of that, and I contend
that the improvements are ongoing by all Governments and therefore I also contend that
the system is now far better than it was so me 4 or more years ago, because it is
continually improving.
8400 Urgent Debates 12 Mar 2013
We do not accept that our planning for foot-a nd-mouth is inadequate. This is an area
of major work for the Ministry for Primary Indus tries, as seen with Exercise Taurus last
year, which was, as those who read the report will know, observed by the Auditor-
General. This was a planning exercise to model an outbreak, and follow-up actions are
to be completed by June this year.
It is worth noting that this report looks at only one part of the biosecurity system—
that is, responding to pests and diseases wi thin New Zealand. Although we need to be
prepared to respond quickly and efficiently to  incursions, we also have strong systems
in place to prevent incursions from occurri ng in the first place. The report also shows
that the Ministry for Primary Industries has been successful at responding to incursions.
As I have already mentioned, significant changes to the biosecurity system had
already occurred before this report was rel eased and I want to assure the previous
speaker, because in fact he was concerned about that. Improvements already in progress
include updating plans for dealing with specifi c pests, better survei llance targeting, and
more regular exercises and simulations. For ex ample, work is under way to identify the
highest priority gaps in high- risk organism preparedness so that these can be addressed
in plans. This work will be completed by September this year and will then be simulated
and tested in the biosecurity exercise programme.
The report notes that preparedness for foot-and-mouth disease is improving. The
Ministry for Primary Industries and indus try are working together on action plans
covering areas such as refining scenario s for foot-and-mouth disease incursions,
developing a vaccination policy, establishing guid elines for disposal of carcasses, and
developing on-farm biosecurity plans. This work will result in shared ministry and
industry plans that will be completed by Sept ember this year and will include planning
on the areas specifically mentioned by the A uditor-General, such as carcass disposal,
vaccine plans, and deployments.
The Ministry for Primary Industries is de veloping a programme to deliver foot-and-
mouth disease testing and simulation exer cises over the next 5 years, and our
preparedness will be tested on an ongoing basis. In 2013 eight exercises will be
completed. The next whole-of-Government biosecu rity exercise will be held within the
next 2 years.
The Auditor-General’s repo rt notes that the Minist ry for Primary Industries
recognises the need for more planned reviews and testing of systems, work is under way
to identify the highest priority gaps in high-risk organism preparedness, and the ministry
is developing a business case to replace its existing bio-containment laboratory with a
replacement laboratory, up and running in 2018 if the business case is approved.
The Ministry for Primary Industries st atement of intent 2012-15 commits to
improving capability, including cr eating a strategy for people capability and leadership
training, to be supported by new information systems. The ministry also supports
making contracting simpler, faster, and more efficient for response partners, and this is
under review.
A review of the biosecurity response servic es contract began in early February 2013.
The project team looking into th is contract is due to make its first report back to the
ministry’s senior management in mid-Marc h this year, after taking advice from legal
and policy staff. The Ministry for Primary Industries is developing its management of
the three major systems in biosecurity, food safety, and primary production, following
our mergers, and will continue to develop its current governance arrangements, business
planning, and strategy setting in a way that supports management of the three systems.
The Ministry for Primary Industries St rategy 2030 and the recent Performance
Improvement Framework, or PIF review, iden tify the importance of setting results-
based performance expectations and buildin g our people capability. The ministry will
12 Mar 2013 Urgent Debates 8401
set clear and results-based pe rformance expectations and provide an accelerated focus
on building our people capability. In fact, last year the ministry employed 45 new
quarantine inspectors, and 11 more were recru ited in January this y ear. Last year seven
detector dog handlers were re cruited, and this year a furt her four. Last year 11 new
detector dogs graduated from the Mini stry for Primary Industries detector dog
programmes.
It is completely incorrect for the Oppos ition to claim that biosecurity funding has
been reduced. Vote Biosecurity has gone  from $181 million in 2007-08 to a forecast
$196 million for 2012-13. In that period—
Hon Damien O’Connor: No, no.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: Well, Mr O’Connor, it certainly  sounds like an increase to
anyone listening to those figures. In that  period, annual spendi ng on surveillance and
investigation increased by around 35 percen t, spending on core response capability
increased by around 13 percent, and spendi ng on preparedness and pest management
increased by around 5 percent. Retaining a worl d-class biosecurity system is critical to
delivering New Zealand’s economic success. Pe sts and diseases pose serious threats to
our primary producers, who rely on a good biosecurity status to support their
businesses. Our access to export markets is heavily dependent on our biosecurity status.
None of this is news to this Government. We know that trade a nd travel patterns are
changing rapidly. As New Zealand interacts with more international partners, tourism is
increasing and pressure is building for more streamlined travel. Around 175,000 items a
day come across our borders. Therefore it is very, very important that we take a risk-
based approach, not a blind-regulation appro ach, to assessing the risks to New Zealand.
As a result the Government’s three border agencies, the New Zealand Customs Service,
the New Zealand Immigration Service, and th e Ministry for Primary Industries are now
working more closely together to better coordinate border services.
Members need to be assured that the Mini stry for Primary Indus tries is constantly
developing its response, incl uding after the susp ected foot-and-mouth disease outbreak
on Waiheke Island. Let me just outline the chan ges since then: policy for the ministry’s
response to risk organisms and biosecurity  response knowledge base, the Biosecurity
Law Reform Act, progress towards implem enting Government-industry agreements, a
whole-of-Government biosecurity respons e guide, a biosecurity science strategy,
FarmsOnLine, and National Animal Identification and Tracing, or NAIT.
Building the national biosecurity cap ability network does not sound like a
Government sitting on its hands to me. We  now have a much stronger and more
effective border system than we did when we took over in 2008. The previous
Government was slow to react. Page 67 of  the Auditor-General’s report notes that
“Evidence shows that many recommendations  from the 2005 foot and mouth disease
simulation were not put into effect fully.” So it is empty words indeed to hear the
Opposition criticising this Government when  it has already undertaken to progress
many of the recommendations, and in fact accepted all of them, and will put progress
into place as soon as is practi cable. In fact this is a Gove rnment that is taking action on
this serious issue.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. I am pleased to be able
to stand to speak to the Aud itor-General’s report into the primary industry’s ability to
deal with biosecurity incursions. That wa s a very, very damning report on biosecurity
agencies over this last while. However, I w ould like to tell the Minister for Primary
Industries and those associated in Nationa l that we look forward to working on
biosecurity with them, becau se there needs to be significant improvement—and very,
very fast, at that. The Government needs to  front up. It needs to  show where it is
actually going to do new spendi ng on biosecurity, and it must be very quick about that
8402 Urgent Debates 12 Mar 2013
too. We have got a Budget coming, but we need some very strong signals, not just
working within the current Budget framework.
We completely agree with the Auditor-Gener al’s assertion that our country is more
dependent on biosecurity than any other de veloped country, and that biosecurity is
fundamental to New Zealand’s economic health  and its natural heritage. I have got a
few examples to speak of in a moment or two. However, the problem with it is that this
National Government is continuing to put inte rnational trade ahead of biosecurity time
and time and time again. We have seen that over the issue with the porcine disease—the
“pork age”, you might call it—where it wants to  bring in raw meat that will risk our
New Zealand industry. Why? It is just to protect major tr ade agreements. We know that
with honey, it wants to bring in honey from Au stralia, where there is disease we do not
have here. Why? Just for some trade agreements . It seems to think it is worth the risk to
sell off our biosecurity, our children’s futures—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: What about fire blight in Australia?

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: —our farming families’ futures for some short-term trade
of unsustainable products, which you seem to  be totally focused on, Mr Smith. I will
just carry on with what this Auditor-G eneral’s report comes up with. She focused
primarily on foot-and-mouth disease. What did it show? That we are totally unprepared,
and what did she add in there, or what do we know about this? Th at the cost to New
Zealand in 2 years, if that went ahead, would be $10 billion and 20,000 jobs. This is a
Government that reckons it is creating j obs; this is a Government that through
biosecurity alone is costing jobs.
We can go into some more such as Psa a nd Psyllid. We have got a number of them
there to consider.
The Auditor-General said that there was a risk that the inadequately resourced
surveillance strategy has damaged the minist ry’s reputation amongst stakeholders such
as local government. I would include the public, importers, and producers. Within New
Zealand we have issues of biosecurity about what is happening. It is not even just the
incursions. We have Chilean needle grass th at the Government looked the other way at
as it spreads further into Canterbury. We ha ve also got Kauri dieback up north, towards
which this Government has decided it is not going to do any Budget funding. It is not
going to go for any new funding on Kauri di eback, another part of New Zealand’s
natural heritage. Is this going to be the next M āui’s dolphin? It is not. There is no new
Budget money. It has said that. The Ministry fo r Primary Industries said it to the people
up north—the people who are having real concern about that.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: That’s not true.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: It is. Well, that is really  good, Dr Smith, and I am really
looking forward to seeing new Budget money on Kauri dieback. It will be fantastic,
because the research is not happening there. It is a Phytophora taxon Agathis  disease
that is really, really difficult to sort out , and the Government seems to be looking the
other way. There is no money for operations, ju st public relations st uff. We need better
from this Government around biosecurity.
Getting back to what is happening at the bo rder, we know that there are very, very
lax import standards or management ar ound containers. We know  that. Successive
Governments have been part of that, but this particular Government ongoing is allowing
for lay people to effectively be biosecurit y inspectors in warehouses of imported goods.
So goods come in—a business or a wholes aler or whatever that has imported a
container—and who inspects it? Somebody w ho has done something they can pretty
well do online to get the tick for being an inspector. That very same wholesaler has got
a bundle of customers waiting for the products in their shops or th eir businesses around
the country, for the products out of that co ntainer, and that layperson, that business
12 Mar 2013 Urgent Debates 8403
person, opens it up and a moth or something crawls out of it. A nd what happens? What
they are meant to do is get hold of the Mini stry for Primary Industries, which may, if it
feels it is important enough, come out there and fumigate it or do something. It may do
that, but that person who has opened up that co ntainer and seen that  insect, spider, or
whatever come out of there, has got a conflict of interest. They have customers waiting
for product, yet they are the one s who are meant to do somethi ng about it. That is a hell
of a lot of good faith in somebody who has a very, very big vested interest.
We need to change our systems. We need to be doing far, far more inspection at the
ports, and you cannot do it on current budgets. You have to lift the game for that. I want
to ask the Minister how much new spending he is going to do on biosecurity this year—
new spending, very clear spending, not robbi ng Peter to pay Paul, but new spending.
The other question is whether the Minister, or any of the Minist ers, including the one
barking from over there, can have confiden ce in the New Zealand biosecurity system
after this. Can they have confidence after th is Auditor-General’s report? Can they have
confidence considering Psyllid is costing hug e money? The Psa outbreak is potentially
costing the country $800 million over 15 years.  Add that to the Psyllid and we are
talking over a billion dollars there. That is  less than foot-and-mouth, but is that the
trade-off to flog off a bit of unsustainably  produced milk powder and logs through our
wharf? It is not value-added. It is fouli ng up our reputation, fou ling up our waterways,
and we sell off future generations’ in comes through poor biosecurity. There is
significant cost. It is not just the dollar value of that; it is what that does to communities.
We have seen what it has done in the kiwifruit industry, and we have seen what happens
in the primary production world every time.
We also have to think about what this flow-on is to the New Zealand community.
Psyllid comes in—we had fantastic control in our glasshouses using non-toxic methods
of control even for conventional growers. Bi o-controls were in there. What do they do
now? They pour on chemicals to kill psyllid in those hothouses. Thankfully, we are
looking at new bio-controls. Th ere is a big cost to the community when you get more
and more of a chemical cocktail being poured into the community’s stomachs.
There is another issue. The Minister has ju st had a briefing for incoming Ministers.
In there, there is something that I would like  to see the Minister work out. The Auditor-
General says through the report that the preparing for and res ponding to security
incursions is basically really flawed. Yet th e briefing paper by the Ministry for Primary

items.speaker: Industries to him says
items.text: “New Zealand ha s a biosecurity system that retains a
sufficient”—note, sufficient—“level of protection while encouraging economic
growth.” This is the same ministry, the Mini stry for Primary Industries. I am not saying
that people in biosecurity in the minist ry cannot do a good job as  individuals. I think
they are probably striving very hard. I would say their morale is way, way down
because of the lack of support from central  government for them. So we very much
support the report from the Auditor-General, and we will do our best to help the
Government do something about this. Thank you.

items.speaker: SHANE ARDERN
items.text: I totally agree with the
comments of the previous speaker, Steffan Browning, when he said that the
Government supports the report from the Aud itor-General, and that is about where my
agreement with the previous speaker’s contribution ends. We do support this report. The
Ministry for Primary Industries has accepted the report, and all se ven recommendations
that the Auditor-General has recommended are being implemented or are already
halfway through being implemented as we speak.
It is without doubt that biosecurity is the biggest threat to the New Zealand
economy—without doubt—and to the total social  infrastructure and the standard of
living that we have become accustomed to. So biosecurity is a No. 1 issue for this
8404 Urgent Debates 12 Mar 2013
Government. So let us correct some of the statements and introduce some facts into the
comments made by our previous speakers. Fi rst of all, people would be surprised to
hear that, under the previous Governme nt, there were something like 30 or 40
incursions annually and some of those incurred a major bi osecurity risk. For example,
something like 8 tonnes of raw meat was intercepted at our bor ders by biosecurity
officers, under the previous Government—8 tonnes of raw meat. We know about that
because the Ministry of Agriculture and Fore stry’s own audit told us that. Eight tonnes
of raw meat—and the Ministry of Agricult ure and Forestry itself admitted that
potentially it had not been 100 percent correct.
So what has happened since then? We have heard a lot of sugges tions about funding
cuts. Well, in fact, there has been a 35 percent increase in surveillance. There has been a
13 percent increase in core response capabilit y. There has been a 5 percent increase in
pest management and preparedness funding. In fact, the funding has gone from $181
million in the 2007-08 year to $196 million fo r the 2012-13 year. That does not sound
like a cut to me. In fact, that sounds like a substantial increase.
So this Government does take biosecuri ty very, very seriously. In fact, this
Government implemented major changes in re gard to the way we deal with container
devanning. Under the previous Government  there was a major concern about the
number of devanning sites. I heard the previ ous speaker describe some of the processes
in regard to devanning as being inadequate. He was right. During the terrorist attacks
overseas—9/11 being the one th at, I guess, gave the most focus—the Customs Service
was required to carry out far greater levels of  inspection than it ever had been before. In
that process it discovered the ability to use X-ray equipment that allowed a far greater
surveillance of imported containers.
So biosecurity was able then, I guess, to some extent piggyback on the back of that
and use that technology, which, of course, ha s meant a far higher le vel of surveillance.
When that was first recommended to the pr evious Government, it turned that option
down. This Government has implemented it. So it is interesting and probably a little bit
rich to hear our opponents say that this is not a Government that is interested in
biosecurity.
The Minister outlined a whole range of areas where the Government has beefed up
biosecurity. There are Government-industry agreements. The industries themselves hold
a substantial amount of intellectual property on biosecurity  and are able to contribute
and, where that is possible, there are agreements implemented. Under the national
identification scheme, animals are now far mo re traceable than they were in the foot-
and-mouth scare, or hoax, on Waiheke Island. There has been the introduction of far
greater surveillance when people come thr ough our borders, using dogs, using X-ray
equipment, and using a much wider range of  opportunities there, and there has been a
reconfiguration of how people come into  New Zealand. When they come through a
high-risk area, they have a much greater level of surveillance. When they do not, they
have a lower level of surveillance. To sugge st that this Governme nt is not investing
heavily in biosecurity or is not taking biosecurity seriously is very, very short-sighted
indeed and, in fact, is not correct.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I thank the Hon Damien O’Connor for bringing
this matter to the attention of the House. It is obvious that all parties in this House do
accept that biosecurity is of enormous importance to New Zealand and to our economy.
In this day and age where advanced tech nologies in manufacturing, information
technology, and so forth are touted as being the way of the future, it is still a fact that 75
percent of New Zealand’s econo my one way or another, di rectly or indirectly, is
dependent on agriculture, and for that reas on biosecurity is probably the single most
12 Mar 2013 Urgent Debates 8405
important line of defence that New Zeal and can have for our economy and for
everything else.
We have heard a lot about reinvestment in  biosecurity from this administration. We
have not heard a lot about the cuts that pr eceded that. We have had cuts to front-line
services over the last few years. We ha ve had a reduction in boots on the ground. We
have seen a diminishing of morale amongs t front-line biosecurity officers—people who
work for the Customs Service, and people who work for the Ministry for Primary
Industries. They are disillusioned by the lack  of resourcing and by the redirection of
resourcing in biosecurity, which is moving away from the traditional established
methods of inspection—methods that they, as professionals on the ground, have had
confidence in over the years. They are seeing those methods being replaced by a
reliance on technology, a reliance on intelligen ce, and a reliance, to some degree, on
untested theory.
The fact of the matter is th at we now have fewer boots on the ground than we did a
decade ago. We have seen the results of a relaxation of the strenuous efforts made
previously around biosecurity. We have seen it with the introducti on of the Psa virus
and its devastating effects on our kiwifruit industry. We have seen what happens when a
fruit fly gets in, and we have no way of knowing how that fruit fly got in.
I remember back in 1997 when I was a sales rep on the road in Central Otago and the
rabbit calicivirus was introduced to the S outh Island. Calicivirus was something that
many in the farming industry had been calling for as a method of controlling rabbits. It
was investigated, and eventual ly the Government said that the farmers could not have
the calicivirus. By that stag e, of course, it was out a nd spreading—it was about 4
months before the Ministry of Agriculture a nd Forestry told the farmers that they could
not have calicivirus—on the farms of Cent ral Otago and South Canterbury. I remember
calling at a farm—mind you, I will not reveal  the location—where the farmer’s wife
was out the back of the house with a blender. She was blending the internal organs of
some rabbits that had died of the virus, and they were creating biocide and painting
carrots with it and spreading them on the farm s. So back in those days, when there was
a great deal more investment made in ade quate biosecurity, it was still possible for a
virus, an organism like the calicivirus, to  be introduced deliber ately by people who had
an agenda to do so.
We are told that the calicivirus came  in via two methods—one, possibly through a
diplomatic bag, and the other in  a pilot’s bag—but the fact of  the matter remains that at
that time when the ministry was better res ourced and was better focused on controlling
those sorts of threats, that virus still managed to make its  way in and still managed to
spread and become established. I was told quite proudly by a staff member from the
Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry days th at they had a plan whereby they could put
90 people on the ground anywhere in New Z ealand within an hour and a half of an
incursion being announced. We could not do th at today. We simply do not have the
resources.
Today the door is wide open. The door is wide open through SmartGate, which
allows passengers carrying Australian and New Zealand passports  to enter without
being stopped, without being inspected. Th e door is wide open to containers and
machinery arriving in this c ountry without being inspecte d properly and without being
clean. There is dirty machinery arriving off ships in this country.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: They go through just passport control, not customs.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: Well, the Minister says that it is passport control and not
customs. It is all front line. It is all people on the front line. It is all ways of stopping and
inspecting goods and passengers as they come  across the border. We have to take a
holistic approach to this because we are an island nation. The only two ways that we can
8406 Urgent Debates 12 Mar 2013
be reached and approached are by sea a nd by air, so everything—people, freight—
arrives by sea and by air. It is all crossi ng the border. We are wide open through fast-
track visa arrangements for carriers, such as  the one that has just been announced with
China Southern Airlines for their freque nt flyers. We have no way of knowing who
these people are, what they may or may not be bringing in, a nd now we are going to
start letting them in the same as we are le tting in Australian a nd New Zealand passport
holders, without inspecting them.
So as the Hon Damien O’Connor says, we are now wide open to a foot-and-mouth
incursion. Claims of increased spending a nd increasing resourcing around biosecurity,
even if they are true, are irrelevant if they  are not targeted to the right areas. As I say,
we did not take account of previous cuts and we place too much reliance on intelligence.
We have a reduction in boots on the ground.
I put questions to the select committee earlier in the year about the sorts of resources
the Ministry for Primary Industries had to c ounter an incursion. The ministry said it had
its own resources, obviously, and the reso urces of other Government agencies,
including the army, to call on. Well, we all know that the army itself is undergoing cuts
and reductions. It is losing people, it is losing vehicles, and it is losing the ability to help
in situations like this.
Of course, we also face the possibility th at there could be deliberate incursions, and
other nations, companies perhaps, wanting to make a competitive advantage over New
Zealand where we have advantages, where they  could seek to destroy those advantages
by bringing in any kind of virus that could diminish New Zealand’s ability to have a
competitive edge. We have seen it work the other way round. We have seen legitimate
New Zealand intellectual property being removed from this country through illegitimate
means. For example, a few years ago some  Chinese officials were stopped taking New
Zealand apple budwood out of the country. So if it can work one way, it can work the
other.
No system is 100 percent effective—this we know. But even with all the protocols in
place, something can get through. Without protocols in place, something will get
through. Without protocols in place, and without proper effec tive inspections and
controls, it is not a case at all of if—it is a case of when. We will get foot-and-mouth,
through this system.
I recall, again a number of years ago when  I was working in the wine industry,
receiving a crate off a carrier of cast-ir on pipeline fittings. We were putting in an
irrigation system, and this crate of pipeline f ittings had come in from China. We put the
crate on the ground—this was on a vineyard near Wānaka, so we were out in the middle
of nowhere. We were nowhere near a port of entry, we were nowhere near an inspection
facility, and we were nowhere near anywhe re where we could get fumigation. As we
opened the crate, a spider ra n out. I happened to notice th e spider, and I happened to
know that the crate had come from China. I di d not know what sort of spider it was, but
I did know that it could be something danger ous. I happened to be in  the right place at
the right time to see that spider. I got on the phone to my boss, got hold of some
information on the kind of chemical and the ki nd of application that we should use to
control it, went into town, got the chem ical, applied it to the area, and hopefully,
fortunately, we prevented something more dr amatic from taking hold in that part of
New Zealand. But that was a matter of a fort unate accident, of me  being in the right
place at the righ t time. Without inspections and without proper fumigations and
facilities in place at our ports, we cannot guarantee that we will always be lucky.
The Auditor-General’s report summarises that the Ministry  for Primary Industries is
unprepared for potential incursions from some  high-risk organisms. It emphasises that
not enough priority is being given to planni ng. It emphasises that the plan for dealing
12 Mar 2013 Urgent Debates 8407
with foot-and-mouth is inadequate, staff ar e not using the new response system to its
full potential, some information systems do not yet link together, information is not
used as effectively and as efficiently as  it could be, and performance reporting also
needs to improve. It is a damning report.
New Zealand First has been calling for action on this for over a year. I have a copy of
a press release put out by myself at almost this time last year, saying that New Zealand
First is calling for an indepe ndent inquiry into inadequate  biosecurity procedures and
staffing levels. We are going over the same ground, over and over again. We could
stand here on this side of the House a nd berate the Government—and deservedly so—
for its direction or lack  of direction on biosecu rity, for the fact that  it is not prioritising
the spending that it is making in the correct direction.
I think a more constructive a pproach would be for us to as k, to plead, please, for the
Government to listen, to r ead the Auditor-General’s repor t properly, and to take on
board the messages that are contained within  that report. Please listen to calls from
across this side of the House. Please listen to Federated Farmers. Please spend the
money, spend it in the right place, put the boots back on the ground, and safeguard New
Zealand’s agriculture and the three-quarter s of our economy that depends on it. Thank
you.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Deputy Speaker. The
Auditor-General’s report on bios ecurity is a damning report on this Government, and it
reveals that New Zealand is at a major risk  of a major biosecurity breach. What that
means is that our p ā defences are weak, and they ar e weak because of the slash-and-
burn policies of this Government and the dism antling that it has done of our biosecurity
defences in the continuous restructurings that have occurred with the Ministry for
Primary Industries.
People at home might wa tch reality shows like Border Patrol, and they will see our
hard-working customs and biosecurity people. They always make the bust; no one or no
thing ever gets through. But that is not the real ity, because the reality is that they do not
always get their man, and that has been accentuated by the fact that this Government has
been cutting funding, slashing front-line sta ff, and failing to properly prepare for an
incursion.
I want to focus on that last point, because the Associate Minister for Primary
Industries in her speech quoted from the A uditor-General’s overview. She was putting
all the positive spin that she could on the f act that the Ministry for Primary Industries
does respond to incursions and its responses to incursions have taken precedence. Then
she went on to say: “No border control is 100% effective, so it is important that New
Zealand is prepared to deal with incursions  effectively.” Then she stopped. But if she
had carried on with that para graph, she would have read th at the Auditor-General said:
“However, it is my view th at MPI is under-prepared for po tential incursions for some
high-risk organisms. Responding to incursions  has taken precedence over preparing for
the potential arrival of other pests and dis eases. Not enough priority has been given to
planning. Many response partners who have worked with MPI and its predecessors
believe that stronger response cap ability is also needed.” Wh at that shows is selective
reading by the Minister.
The Auditor-General’s report is very clear th at the Ministry for Primary Industries is
underprepared and it is not putting enough prior ity into planning and working with the
various industry groups. That could not be highlighted more  than by the risk that has
been identified with our risk of an incursi on of foot-and-mouth disease. The ministry is
woefully underprepared for a foot-and-mouth incursion. The Auditor-General estimates
that a foot-and-mouth outbreak could cost the country $13 billion. That is a huge impact
on our economy, and that is why we must keep our p ā defences strong. But you cannot
8408 Urgent Debates 12 Mar 2013
do that—you cannot have your warriors defending your p ā—when you have fewer and
fewer warriors in place.
What have we seen with this Government? The numbers: we have had 91 biosecurity
officer positions cut between 2008 and 2012, since National has been in office. The
number of sniffer dogs—those little beagle dogs that go sniffing around the airports—
has dropped, particularly at Auckland Air port, where it is down to 13. Although the
Government may talk about “We’ve got a little technology introduction here. We’ve got
incremental progress happening here and there.”,  the fact of the matter is that if you do
not have front-line people manning these key positions—and we are a huge country—
we are very exposed. The farm gate is wide open in the breeze, and this Government is
just letting all potential incursions, diseas es, pests, and other nasties come in. They
could be invading our borders because of the woeful record of this Government.
I also want to go on and make some re marks around Psa, because the member who
spoke for the Government last talked about  whatever incursions  occurred during the
Labour Government, but I think we need only  mention three letters, “Psa”, and what
absolutely devastating damage that has done to  our kiwifruit industry. If we just look at
researchers from Lincoln University, this is really interesting—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: It is devastating our industr y. I did not realise I had a short
call. We commend this report and we urge the Government to take proper action and
give proper resourcing to our biosecurity systems. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: The next call goes to Mr King. I think, to remind the
House, the next two calls are 5-minute calls.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: I am sure that we will adhere to that.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: You will.

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: The Government welcomes this report, and it welcomes it from the
point of view that it finally  wakes people in New Zealan d up to just how important
agriculture and the primary industries are to the New Zealand economy. I would have to
say that when you look at the other side of the House, it is only when a report comes out
and states the obvious that they actually  wake up and you hear Damien O’Connor
speaking. He is the lone voice around agricult ure on that side of the House and he is
pleased to inform his colleagues of how important agriculture is.
We welcome this report from the Auditor- General because it really does highlight
the point that I am making, which is how do yo u fight this thing before it gets to your
border? Let us face it, when you hear New Z ealand First say that you have to have a
standing army here, you ha ve to use technology and y ou have to use everything
available to you. I am pleased to see that the Government is moving very quickly to
enact those activities. There is a lot of work being done by this Government, including
National Animal Identification and Tracing. We have done a lot of stuff on our side of
the border, but the real challenge is to be  able to manage the overwhelming amount of
material that is being brought into this c ountry, because we are developing a consumer
society. This is an export-led economy, and we welcome this report because biosecurity
is very, very important. We welcome the report, but we are also very, very impressed by
the moves the Government has taken to date in order to improve biosecurity
management with regards to that challenge, which will continually confront this country
and every Government going forward. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: I, like almost all previous speakers in
the House today, welcome this report. I think this is without a doubt the most important
issue facing New Zealand, whether we like it  or not, on any one da y in our history.
Agriculture, of course, is the primary industr y in this country. It produces 70c of every
dollar spent in this country, so we certain ly cannot afford to take risks with the
12 Mar 2013 Urgent Debates 8409
biosecurity around it. I think we have to unde rstand that, as we make changes and bring
ourselves up to date with th e dramatic opportunities that technology and things like that
allow us, we need to ensure that we keep our levels of biosecur ity up, and we need to
ensure that we use modern t echniques to enable those pe ople involved in that industry
to do that.
Also, we are a trading country. We rely h eavily on agriculture for our living, and we
need to have relationships with our trading pa rtners that enable them to see very clearly
what we are doing as a country, and that also enable them to  participate in any activity
that they wish to participate in with us within reason. We need to protect the integrity of
our product and the integrity of our borders.
On the weekend a number of us visited Ka piti Island. While visiting Kapiti Island,
we found the fraughtness of biosecurity, in th at a stoat had got to Kapiti Island some 4
years ago and bred there. There is no wa y of knowing how she got there, but she
certainly had a couple of kids while she was there. Those have since been trapped and
eradicated. Interestingly, they also ha d a photograph of a possum floating to Kapiti
Island on a log, and if that can happen between Kapiti Island and here with a possum,
imagine how difficult it is for us in this c ountry to control a borde r of the magnitude of
the one we have, with sea all around it.
So I have no problem supporting this report. I think it is a great report. I think if we
were to go looking for reports that, I guess, to ld us we were perfect, we would have no
need to request reports on this sort of stuff. I welcome these kinds of reports, and I think
they are great value for the Government, they  are great value for the country, and they
will add to our ability to improve our biosecurity systems. Thank you for this
opportunity, and that is me.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: We are back to 10-minute calls.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: I rise to take a call in the urgent
debate on the Auditor-General’s report on bios ecurity. Let us, firstly, remember that we
have interrupted the business of the House to hold an ur gent debate on a matter of
critical national importance. It is not OK for the sleepy Government members to sit over
there on the Treasury benches snoring their way to accepting a report that actually
makes fundamental criticisms of the Governme nt in three regards. Firstly, it says that
this country is highly vulnerable to a major incursion of a critical pest or disease such as
foot-and-mouth. It says that we are under-resourced, that we are underprepared, and that
the systems are underdeveloped. That is a toxic cocktail of risk that threatens our major
livelihood industries, the primary industries of this country.
It is notable that members all round this House, whether on the Government benches,
the cross benches, or the Opposition benches, are all agreed on the central importance of
biosecurity. That is, at leas t, a good starting point for th is debate. The Minister, Ms
Goodhew, however, said that Labour currently was undermining the work of biosecurity
by damaging our reputation by re citing the results of this report of an independent
Officer of Parliament. The Auditor-General is an independent, non-partisan officer of
this whole House. This is not  a Labour Party report, nor a Government report; this is an
independent performance audit by the highest audit authority of the land, and it behoves
every member to listen to it. It will do the Government no good to accuse Labour of
mudraking.
Secondly, the Minister said that the invest ment in biosecurity is almost double what
it was in 2000, and then she claimed the credit  for it. I found that  fascinating, because
my advice was that it was the previous Labour Government that had doubled the
investment. So I went to check, and I can co nfirm that here are the numbers. I must
stress to the House that these numbers are not deflated to constant dollars. These are the
actual dollars in years gone by and therefore understate the relativ e contribution of the
8410 Urgent Debates 12 Mar 2013
previous Government. When Labour took over last time, the previous Government was
spending only $90 million a year on biosecurity. Under Labour it doubled, by 2008, to
$181,088,000—again, without allowing for any of the effects of inflation. Then the
current National Government cut the spending in its first year to $179 million, cut it
again, in its second year, to $168,203,000, and latterly has increased it back to about
where Labour had it, of $192,190,000. So there was a doubling. It ju st happened under
the last Labour Government, not under the cu rrent National Government. The best that
could be said for the current Government is that it is flat-lini ng, and that might be a
general statement about this Government.
The Minister then said that, yes, a number of criticisms were made in this report—
that is an understatement; it is full of criticisms—and that the Ministry for Primary
Industries recognises the need for improve ment. Well, that is good. We commend the
ministry for being willing to  learn from the report. But wh at are the improvements that
are being made? The Minister said “Well, we’re developing a business case for new
systems and we are writing a strategy for people development and we are going to put
the whole thing under review.” Well, that is th e old adage of when there is no answer to
the problem, do another review. But the peop le of New Zealand deserve better than
that—they do—because these are critical issues.
The report makes a number of very damn ing conclusions. I can do no better than
quote from the overview written by the Audito r-General herself. Sh e says: “it is my
view that MPI is under-prepared for poten tial incursions from some high-risk
organisms. Responding to incursions has taken precedence over preparing for the
potential arrival of other pe sts and diseases. Not enough pr iority has been given to
planning. Many response partners who have worked with MPI and its predecessors
believe that stronger response capability is also needed.” That is, the Ministry for
Primary Industries is so busy rearranging the deckchairs in another megamerger like the
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employ ment—“Mobie”, the great white whale of
economic development—that it has not got ti me to plan ahead for the incursion that
might come next week, next month, or next  year. The Auditor-General goes on to say
that although some “improvements are be ing made”—credit where credit is due—“…
serious weaknesses remain. Plans for respond ing to potential incu rsions from some
high-risk organisms are not yet complete. … the plan for dealing with a foot and mouth
disease outbreak is inadequate.” Strong word s from the Auditor-General. She goes on:
“Workforce planning and capability development needs to be stronger, so that MPI has
the appropriate people, with the right skills, in the right place. Staff are not using the
new response system to its full potential  … Performance reporting also needs to
improve.” and, of course, it “has an opportun ity to achieve lasting improvements” if it
follows the plans that are set out.
What does all this mean in practice? If we turn to figure 3 in the report we see a
sorry, long list—pardon me—of incursions. I am choking up thinking about biosecurity;
what do we know? There are the gum leaf  skeletoniser moth, didymo—known to any
fisherman as a terrible pla gue on our waterways—the so uthern saltmarsh mosquito,
kauri dieback, Psa of our kiwi fruit industry, and juvenile oy ster mortality. When I was
put down for this debate, I was initiall y wondering why an urban member from
Auckland was to speak about biosecurity. [ Interruption] In fact, my electorate—thank
you, Ms Delahunty—has had firsthand experience of  these problems. I want to mention
three that are either current or immediately past real issues in the electorate of New
Lynn.
Let me start with what was probably the la rgest issue, which was the painted apple
moth, and which, let me say upfront, did occur during the time of the previous
Government. In the painted apple moth experience we recognised a very strong need for
12 Mar 2013 Urgent Debates 8411
community involvement and community educ ation. The moth was eradicated with a
programme of overflying and applying a bacter ial solution to the moths. But the issue
was that the community needed to be invol ved. It was learning by doing on the part of
the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry and Biosecurity New Zealand and its agents, so
that by the end of that programme they ha d become much more skilled in community
involvement than they were at the start.
The next incursion I want to mention is that of the Queensland fruit fly.
[Interruption] That means the sound has gone off,  has it? Is that you, Mr Deputy
Speaker, or is that a word from the Lord, perhaps?

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: David Shearer works in mysterious ways!

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CUNLIFFE
items.text: Maybe it is a word from the Government benches. I
think it is still working—is it? It is not a wo rd from “Cue Ball”. Let us work with that,
and we hope that the guys behind the dark  curtain will keep the machine running.
[Interruption] “Put another coin in the slot”, sa id the Minister of Commerce, showing
that his commercial orientation never fails him.
In regard to the Queensland fruit fly, one  fly was found in Avondale, in the heart of
my electorate. That might not sound like a big deal, but it required controls being put on
moving fruit and vegetables. Thirty biosecu rity officers descended on the Avondale
market, and residents were uninformed a bout the fruit fly lockdown across west
Auckland. That all sounds pretty dramatic, but what the Auditor-General found was that
in the case of that fruit fly outbreak the ministry’s ability to  respond was woefully
inadequate, and that had there been more th an one solitary fly—in fact, had there been
two live flies, a little boy fly and a little girl fly—we might have had lots and lots of
flies. Yes, the rural members over there understand the story of the birds and the bees—
they have got that, so far. Yes, the bird s and the bees would have struck and the
ministry would not have struck, because the ministry’s response sy stems, according to
the Auditor-General, were inadequate.
Finally, there is kauri dieback. This is a huge current issue across west Auckland and
in the far north. Kauri dieback is a major diseas e. It is a bacterial infection of the roots.
My colleague Phil Twyford has been campai gning on this issue very, very ably. The
problem is that Biosecurity New Zealand, now the Ministry for Primary Industries, does
not see it as a priority and has cut the f unding to control kauri dieback. I say that the
Government should be ashamed. It is bad enoug h to take biosecurity officers and dogs
out of airports. We should get the kauri dieback funding.

items.speaker: JAMI-LEE ROSS
items.text: I am sorry that this side of the House could
not hear the last couple of minutes from David Cunliffe, but, judging from the first few
minutes, we did not feel as though we had mi ssed very much. I did, however, hear him
talk about rearranging the d eckchairs. I thought that was quite interesting, coming from
David Cunliffe. I am sorry that the micr ophones do not work all the way up the back
there, but we could still see you, Mr Cunliffe.
I am going to speak just very briefly on th is particular topic. The Government does
welcome the report that the House has been debating for the last period of time. We will
carefully consider any advice and recomm endations made that could improve our
biosecurity. In fact, the Ministry for Primar y Industries has already accepted the report
and all seven recommendations. Already work has been undertaken on working through
those recommendations. Significant changes ha ve already been made and had taken
place even before the report was released. Improvement is in progress on updating plans
for dealing with specific pest s, better surveillance targeti ng, and more regular exercises
and simulations.
Overall, we believe that New Zealand doe s have a world-class biosecurity system.
As a Government, we are extremely consciou s of how important it is to protect our
8412 Urgent Debates 12 Mar 2013
borders, and continuing to improve the system is a major priority for this Government. I
think it is worth pointing out that Government spending on biosecurity, according to the
information that I have been given, is now  at almost double what it was in 2000, when
the last Labour Government started office.  Last year we saw a record number of
biosecurity staff recruited—over 40.
The Government does take this issue very seriously. The Government does take this
report very seriously. Work is already under way on it. We will continue to work on
improvements to the system for the benefit of all New Zealanders.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
