In Committee

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The House is in Committee on the
Appropriation (2011/12 Financia l Review) Bill. The financia l review debate is the
Committee stage of the Appropriation (2011/ 12 Financial Review) Bill. The time
allocated for this debate is 4 hours and compri ses two distinct elemen ts. The first is the
debate on the annual Financial Statements of the Government as reported on by the
Finance and Expenditure Committee. Once this has concluded, the Committee debates
individual financial reviews of depart ments, Offices of Parliament, and non-
departmental appropriations as reported on by the select committees. The debate on the
Government’s financial position may be a fa irly wide-ranging one, but the debates on
the individual financial reviews of depa rtments, Offices of Parliament, and non-
departmental appropriations should be rele vant to their perf ormance in the 2011-12
financial year and their current operations.
The compendium of financial reviews and non-departmental appropriations available
for debate is on the Table. A member other than the responsible Minister may have no
more than two calls on each financial review. At the conclusion of the debate, a single
question is put on the provision s of the bill. There is no amendment to, or debate on,
this question. The Chairperson then reports the bill to the House and it is set down for
third reading forthwith. There is no debate on the third reading.
Will members please turn to the report of the Finance and Expenditure Committee on
the annual Financial Statements  of the Government. The ques tion is that the report of
the Finance and Expenditure Committee on th e annual Financial Statements of the
Government for the year ended 30 June 2012 be noted. I note that this report also relates
to the Finance and Expenditure Committee’s financial review of Treasury, so the
performance in the 2011-12 financial year and current operations of Treasury may also
be debated.
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8413
Treasury and the Financial Statements of  the Government of New Zealand for the
year ended 30 June 2012

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: The Finance and Expenditure Committee report
details that this year net Crown debt is in creasing substantially, as it says, from $40
billion, 20.3 percent of GDP, to $50.7 billion, 24.8 percent of GDP. This shows that
Government debt is still rising sharply as  we go into the fourth—coming up fifth—year
of this National Government.
The Labour Party has not been critical of the fact that  the Government has been
running a deficit post the global financial cr isis. Indeed, one of the reasons why the
Government can do that relatively comfortabl y compared with other parts of the world
is that it inherited Government debt that was amongst the lowest in the developed world
from the outgoing Labour Government. Indeed, gross debt had been reduced from about
40 percent of GDP to 18 percent of GDP, and net debt was down to virtually zero.
What we do say, though, is th at the financial review of Treasury and of the Financial
Statements of the Government shows that the Government has not met the undertakings
it made to the electorate when it was elected in 2008, and I want to comment on a
couple of those. First of all, we had the pr omise of the Government that it was going to
rebalance the economy towards exports. It was going to grow exports from
approximately 30 percent of GDP to 40 per cent of GDP. National came to Government
when exports were virtually 30 percent of GDP, and they are still virtually 30 percent of
GDP, having gone up or down in any 1 year  by 1 or 2 percent but not having moved
from the underlying position of 30 percent of GDP. There goes a failure.
We also had the Government saying that it was going to close the wage gap with
Australia. We know that it has been refusing to agree to a ny sort of milestone by which
it can be judged on this, because its performance on that is even worse than it is on
exports. Not only has it not improved the posit ion; it has actually gone backwards, so
much so now that the gap between New Zealand wages for a median wage earner in
New Zealand and an Australian on the me dian wage is $180 per week using the
purchase price parity measure that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have
both previously said they prefer. For a medi an wage earner in Australia, adjusted for
New Zealand spending, the wage is $1,067 per week. For New Zealand it is now
$887—a gap of $180 per week. That  is an increase dur ing the term of this Government
of $60 per week—$60 per week worse, rather  than getting better . No wonder record
numbers of people have left for Australia. It has now reached the point that an
Australian working 4 days can earn the equi valent of what we earn in New Zealand,
whereas a New Zealander has to work 5 da ys. So there goes another symbol of the
failure of the economic policy of this Government.
I raise a point of order, Mr  Chairperson. Am I to use that microphone so I can be
heard externally? Because if it is just internally—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Yes—no, it is externally.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Externally? OK.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Unfortunately, we are still having problems
with that.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Right. Is this on? How do I tell?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: It should already be on—just try.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: It is going? Yes—OK. Thank you. In addition to other
problems that we have in the New Zealand economy, the fact that the economy has not
rebalanced towards export-led growth is ev ident not just from the failure to grow
exports as a percentage of GDP but from the perennial current account deficit. New
Zealand maintains a current account deficit that , according to the IMF this year, will be
the second-worst in the developed world, at  an astounding $10 bill ion. That $10 billion
8414 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
external deficit is funded either by selling more previously New Zealand - owned assets
to overseas buyers or by borrowing from ove rseas. As a consequence, New Zealand’s
balance sheet, if you like, as a country ge ts worse as we are hollowed out as an
economy owing more to overseas and with more of New Zealand’s assets being owned
by overseas people. Treasury and the Reserve Bank forecast this as continuing to
increase to about 6.7 percent of GDP in 2016.

items.speaker: The Government turns round and says
items.text: “Well, look, this is not as bad as it was during
the heady days of the 2000s.” It is true that in two of those years it got higher than that.
That was not a good result. The problem for the Government is that it promised to fix it,
yet it refused to pull the levers of power th at would enable it to do so. The lack of
economic policy from this Government to make a true difference can be simply
evidenced from the fact that its biggest ec onomic policy for this term is the sale of
minority interests—up to 49 percent—in State-owned enterprises.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I understand, members, that this
microphone in front of me is the only microphone that is working, and that the handheld
microphone is not actually working either. What I propose, members—[ Interruption]
Order, please. What I propose is if the member—although we can hear in here, it cannot
be heard externally, other than through this mike here. So I am going to invite members
to come forward and speak from here, and we will just turn this microphone round until
we get something—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: The Speaker’s Chair would be better.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, we are in the Committee stage, so we
cannot go up there. I am inviting another member to take the call.

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: It is great to be speaking on the
Government’s financial position, because there has been quite a lot of debate about that
today. I would particularly lik e to draw attention to th e cost of the asset sales
programme and the big impact that that  is having on the Government’s books.
According to Treasury, the cost will be abou t $441 million over 5 years. That is the net
cost, and that is the result of the fact that  the dividends, or profits , that the Government
earns on these assets are much greater than th e cost of debt, which is being replaced by
the sale of the assets. Treasur y estimates that the net cost of the Government asset sales
programme is $441 million. That  is a giant hole in the G overnment’s books. When you
add to that the $100 million that the Government is proposing to spend, at least initially,
on the asset sales programme, you end up w ith a $541 million hole in the Government
books as a result of the Government asset sales programme.

items.speaker: So the question to the Government is
items.text: with a half-billion-dollar hole in the
Government’s books as a result of the asset sa les programme, what is it going to cut? Is
it going to increase reve nue or is it going to borrow more in order to cover this giant
hole in the Government’s books? If your aim wa s to protect the Government’s finances,
then you would not go down this path, because this path, according to the Government’s
own figures, is going to cost at least $541 million.
On top of that we have the share giv eaway programme, which at the moment is
unquantified. If the Government persists in its share giveaway scheme, it could cost tens
of millions of dollars on top of that, depe nding on how large it would be. It could be
$100 million. We do not know, because the Gove rnment has not announced what the
programme looks like, and al so because the Government itself does not know what the
uptake of the share giveaway or the loyalty bonus scheme will be. The question for the
Government is why this is worth spending ha lf a billion dollars on. Why is it worth half
a billion dollars to go down this path?
This comes against the background of th e broader economic management of the
Government, which is very problematic. We have the current account deficit, which is 5
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8415
percent and rising. When the Minister of Fina nce first came into office he talked a lot
about rebalancing the New Zealand economy. By that he meant reducing the current
account deficit, amongst other things, yet now we  hear very little from the Government
about rebalancing the economy, because, essen tially, it has failed. We have a 5 percent
current account deficit, and it is growing and projected to increase further down the
track. That seems to me a fundamental failu re for the Government in terms of the
current account deficit.

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Can we turn it off?

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: The Government does not want  to hear about this. The
Government does not want to hear about this . It wants the sound syst em to be off, but
the reality is that when you look at the numb ers, the current account deficit is 5 percent
and growing and is guaranteed to get wo rse under the current economic settings. Of
course, on top of that we have very high rates of unemployment under this Government.
We have had the highest and second-highest  rates of unemployment since National was
last in Government—around 7 percent—and that  itself is, I think, a real indication and
really a fail mark in terms of the Governme nt’s economic strategy broader than just the
fiscal strategy. The Government has told us  that it has 300 ini tiatives and so forth
around its economic management—and good on it—but when it comes down to these
macroeconomic indicators, you would have to  say that 4 years in, you cannot blame the
last Government for it. Four years in, the Government itself has put itself in a big hole
and has created the big problem —not to mention what I thi nk is one of the underlying
problems, which is that the attempts with the Resource Management Act reforms and
others to degrade the environment will unde rmine the long-term performance of the
New Zealand economy. They will undermine the environmental capital on which we all
depend for the long-term sustainability of the New Zealand economy.
So it is not just the fiscal performance that  is in trouble. It is not just the broader
macroeconomic performance, which when you look at the current account deficit you
see is in trouble, or  the unemployment numbers; it is also the underlying environmental
or natural capital on which our economy de pends long term. And if  we continue to
degrade that natural capital, as National is proposing to do, then the long-term economic
picture becomes very difficult as well.
We have also been discussing the manufact uring inquiry and looking at what is
happening in the manufacturing sector, wh ich we in the Greens believe is very
important. We are very interested in the de velopment of the green manufacturing sector
in particular. We have seen the loss of 40,000 jobs over 4 years. This is a long-term
trend. It is not simply a result of what this Government has done. It is a long-term trend,
but under this Government it has continued to get worse. We think that what happens in
manufacturing is important because it is a hi gh-value sector and because it is critical
that if we are to rebalance our economy, th e manufacturing sector performs as well, not
just the primary sector.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am going to call Paul Goldsmith. The
member must use the handheld microphone.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: It is my pleasure to speak on this bill here, the
Appropriation (2011/12 Financial Review) Bill. We have heard many tales of woe from
the other side of the Chamber. I suppose one  of the puzzles I have is why, given the
problems that have been outlined by the tw o previous speakers, this Government, 4
years into its period of office, is retaining the levels of support th at it is. They are at
historic levels. You have to go back to Michael Joseph Savage, I think, back in the
1930s—dear fellow that he was—to see this so rt of support from the public 4 years into
a Government. You ask what the reason for that is. I am sure the Prime Minister’s—
8416 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the member. Can
you just hold the microphone up a little bit.

items.speaker: PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: How is that? Thank you, Mr Chairperson. The reason we
continue to have this high level of support is the Prime Minister’s leadership, which is a
big part of it. What I want to talk about here is the consistency and the clarity of purpose
that this Government has brought to its economic programme. We have talked about the
four priorities: first, getting the books back  in order. This Government is making very
good progress on that, as the figures  here outline. We have halv ed the deficit in the last
year and are on track to be back to surp lus by 2014-15, which is  no small achievement
in a very difficult time.
Secondly, we have been focusing on im proving public services. Again, during a
period of 3 or 4 years of tough Budgets w ithout significant improve ments, it is very
remarkable that all the surveys that have been taken in the public sector have shown that
the public has been seeing an improvement in services, notwithstanding the tight Budget
constraints.
Then we are looking at rebuilding Christchurch—everybody understands the
rationale for that—and, finally, building a more productive and competitive economy.
That has been the real challenge because gett ing books back into order on its own is not
helping us. You need also to have that grow th in productivity, which is the key to our
enterprise and success. So that has been a bout getting the incentives  right. It is about
rebalancing the tax system, which was done in the first Budget, about the welfare
reform programme, which continues to get incentives correctly responded to, and about
the Business Growth Agenda, which is the core of the Governme nt’s programme in
terms of building productivity. A ll this is working quite well when we look at the state
of the economy. Treasury forecast in Decembe r real GDP growth from 2.3 percent in
2012-13 to around 3 percent in 201 3-14, and there are signs that  growth has picked up
in recent months. For example, the volume of  building work undertaken has risen in the
December quarter after gaining 9.8 percent in the September quarter. Manufacturing
volumes are rising, notwithstanding all the heat  and light that we have heard from that
sector. So this Government continues. We  are not giving away any gimmicks, in
contrast to what is being offered from the other side.
And then we look across to what the Greens co ntinue to talk about, which is to make
it difficult to either close or stop most of the industries that w ill grow the economy, yet
they blather on about the green economy, as if somehow this is going to magically
replace all the jobs that they will stop. Then we talk about  quantitative easing. We hear
a lot of talk about pul ling various levers. I am not quite sure what those are, other than
the capital gains tax. I am quite sure there are plenty of respectable economists who will
argue for a capital gains tax, and plenty of ot her countries have it. If I could have any
confidence that Labour would not introduce that just as an extra, new tax on everything
else and have more and more taxes, then we  might be more open to talking about it, but
I am quite confident that it will be just more and more taxes—significant taxes—that
Labour is piling on, right at a time when we need to be rewarding innovation and
investment. A capital gains tax does not seem to be a good way to increase investment
in this country.
These figures that we have got here in the financial review are encouraging figures at
a difficult time globally. New Zealand is holdi ng its head up high and has a very clear
path forward for progress. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon JOHN BANKS
items.text: I am pleased to be working with the Minister
of Finance, and I am very happy that Dr Norman and his printing press are not around
the chairs of the purses of public expenditure.
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8417
What we are looking at today, of course, and considering is an excess in spending
and a structural deficit that the Government has had to deal with—a  structural deficit
that the Minister has had to  grapple with. The report shows that spending growth must
be held to 2 percent per annum to restore a fiscal surplus by 2014-15. Holding spending
growth at 2 percent is tough; for the last  decade, spending gr owth has averaged 8
percent a year. Spending growth in this economy has averaged 8 percent a year over the
last 10 years. It needs to be brought back to 2 percent a year. It does not make sense that
every day, every week, every month, and ev ery year we borrow from savings from
offshore to spend locally on programmes that we simply cannot sustain, that we have
never been able to afford, and that are not as good for investment, growth, and jobs.
We are still cleaning up, for instance, Labou r’s KiwiRail mess, with $6.6 billion in
value of the network being written off to date—$6.6 billi on in value of the network
being written off to date. We are still deal ing with that legacy. As someone who has
been in business for 50 years, all I can tell  you is that you get Dr Cullen as a buyer only
once in a lifetime, Minister—once in a lifetime.
So here is where the country needs to go. We need top-down control of expenditure,
like ACT’s spending cap measure. We need spending cap measures so that we do not
have to borrow every day, every week, and ev ery month from the savings of others to
fund expenditure programmes we simply cannot  afford. We need much more rigorous
programme-by-programme scrutiny. This Pa rliament needs to do line-by-line and
programme-by-programme scrutiny of every single piece of expenditure on its worth.
We need to do much better at asking que stions and asking whether programmes
satisfy the OECD’s five basic questions. The five basic questions that the OECD puts to
us, and that the Minister is prescribing to, are these. Does  the programme still serve a
clearly defined public purpose? Is it an appropriate role for the Government? Would we
establish the programme today if it did not alread y exist? Is it desirable to maintain it at
current levels? And can it be delivered more effectively or more efficiently right now?
That is the slide rule that the OECD put  across all expenditure programmes, and we
should be doing it today because it makes sense and they are timeless propositions.

items.speaker: This is the wrap-up
items.text: the fi nance and expenditure  report observes that we can look
forward to only moderate growth of 2 to 3 percent and continuing high unemployment.
Moderate growth and continuing high une mployment—and the other side of the
Parliament wants to continue to borrow, to  tax, and to spend. Th at is the proposition
coming from the other side of the Chamber: borrow, tax, and spend. If we want to grow
faster and get more investment and more em ployment, we have to reduce the burden on
the private sector, so we should pass the sl ide rule over all regul ation on the private
sector coming through this House. Is it good fo r or is it bad for investment, growth, and
jobs? If it is bad for them, do not do it; if it is good for them, we get on to it.
Investment, growth, and jobs—this means less wasteful or unnecessary spending,
lower taxes, and less red tape and regulation. Do you hear that from the other side of the
Chamber? How often have you heard it from the other side of the Chamber? Never. We
never hear it. So this means less wasteful  and unnecessary spendi ng, lower taxes, and
less red tape and regulation.
I am pleased to be in partnership with this Minister of Finance in this National-ACT -
led Government, which is committed to less government, lower taxes, more
opportunity, world-class education, jobs for everyone, and a growing economy that pays
its way, and where all regulation is tested in this House to see whether it is necessary. If
it is not necessary, we do not want to know  about it, because we are committed to a
programme of getting this count ry back into surplus and paying its way so that we do
not have to borrow from the savings of other citizens of other countries every day, every
week, and every month to make ends meet. I finish as I began—
8418 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I call the Hon Davi d Parker. I understand
that the Leader of the Opposition’s microphone is working, if you would prefer to take a
call on that.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Shall I try that?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: You can try that.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: The Leader of the Opposition for 5 minutes. Is that
working? It is not working. [ Interruption] Mr Chairperson, is that working? I think that
was meant to be. That short-lived promotion to the position of Leader of the Opposition
was obviously not my calling. It is always am using to follow John Banks in this House.
He stands up and lectures the Opposition on fiscal responsibility, when in the last 3
years of his mayoralty he tripled council de bt. He tripled the Auckland Council debt.
That is even excluding the extra debt that was taken on for the so-called super-city. He
tripled council debt. This is the man w ho cannot even count up his own electoral
expenses accurately, lecturing us in the Opposition on prudent fiscal management and
economic policy. This National Government is propped up by John Banks, and it must
be a very uncomfortable experience to be propped up by that man, low as his standards
are.
We have got high unemployment in New Zealand. We have had 180,000 people go
to Australia. We had the Government, when  these statistics came out, saying that it
cannot reconcile the unemploy ment benefit with what is happening in the economy on
other measures. So the Government says  that the household labour force survey
overestimates unemployment, because there are not that many people on the dole. Well,
the reason for that is that most working pe ople now need two incomes to survive. When
one of those people is made redundant, th ey are not entitled to the unemployment
benefit. That is one of the things that we  have heard in the manufacturing inquiry that
the National Party blocked through select co mmittee, but that Opposition parties have
held anyway, outside of the select committ ee process, with full public submissions. We
have heard time and again that people, when they lose their jobs in manufacturing, are
not entitled to the dole, because they have  one person in the relationship who is still
working, and so they are unemployed. If you wa nt to look at the true measure of how
much work there is in New Zealand, look at the total hours worked under the household
labour force survey. The total hours worked is down. There is less work in New Zealand
than there was last year. Four years into th is Government, despite the fact that it is
spending all these billions of dollars of reinsurance money that is coming in from
overseas, the number of hours of paid work  that is available in New Zealand has
decreased.
This Government is mismanaging so many things—whether it was the Crown
guarantee, which cost hundreds of millions of  dollars extra because the Minister of
Finance did not do any supervision of Tr easury, and Treasury did not check whether
there were increases in lending under those gua rantees, or whether it is Solid Energy,
where the Government is so hands-off that it ignored the problem until it became one of
gigantic proportions. In fact, the reason the Government did th at was that it did not suit
its election agenda. The Government received reports prior to the election showing that
Solid Energy was in trouble, but it pretended that was not the case because it wanted to
take to the election the promise to sell Stat e-owned enterprises, including Solid Energy,
and did not want to acknowledge that under its term in Government it had become a
dog. So the Government hid that until after the election.
The scarcity of decent economic policy can  be gauged from the number of people
going to Australia, the fact that incomes are flat, the fact that unemployment is high,
and the fact that our current account defic it is amongst the worst in the world, and not
getting better. The fact that the Government  has as its central plank of economic policy
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8419
for this 3 years the sale of State-owned enterprises, selling what already exists, does not
improve economic output one iota. The fact th at that is the central part of this
Government’s economic agenda for these 3 year s shows how bereft of ideas it is. In the
last few weeks what has it said? Oh, it w ill look to loan-to-valuation ratios—Labour
Party policy. It will look at tidying up Govern ment procurement. It is not going nearly
far enough, but it is going to do something there—Labour Party policy, time and again.
I bet in this Budget it is going to do someth ing about a warrant of fitness for homes—
Labour Party policy. This party on the National Party side has not—[ Interruption]
Sorry?

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: And a Green Party policy.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Labour and Greens. The Greens al so agree that that is very
sensible, yes. Yes, we will give some credit to the Greens for that. But the National
Party—the johnny-come-latelys to those ideas, the visionless party on the other side of
this Chamber—has got no decent policy to lif t us out of this problem. Exports are not
increasing and the current account deficit is getting worse.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: Kia ora t ātou. Tēnā koe, Mr Chairperson.
Kia ora t ātou e te Whare. This Government’s line about spending the money it makes
from the sale of State assets on new schools a nd hospitals is a myth that is very quickly
exposed by a simple reading of this financia l review of Treasury and the Government’s
Financial Statements for 2012, which shows a number of things. One, even though the
Minister of Finance talks up his Governme nt’s target of 170,000 new jobs, he has no
plan to create jobs except to point to a ma rket place that is dumping Kiwi workers and
shifting our manufacturing sect or overseas. Two, even though the Minister says not to
read too much into our skyrocketing unemployment figures, not only did external
agencies correctly predict our current leve l of employment when the Government could
not, but those same agencies also pred ict another 25,000 unemployed in the March
quarter.
Three, even though the Minister says he cannot understand why unemployment is up
but the number of people on unemployment benefits is down, he happily votes for
welfare reforms that are forcing people off benefits, out of thei r homes, and on to the
streets. Four, even though the Minister says he is optimistic about our future, the review
shows that Crown debt will go through the roof over the next 4 years and that,
according to the IMF, our external debt is the second-worst in the developed world and
will be worse than Greece’s by 2014.
Five, even though the Minister is talking up the sale of Mighty River Power, the
review itself says that th e Crown is unlikely to maximi se its return from a public
offering of shares in the current economic cl imate. Such is the climate in which this
Government is preparing to sell off assets  that we already own. When it says to us:
“Hey, guess what, folks! You know that house that our grandparents built? Well, we’re
going to sell the kitchen because we need some money to fix the toilet. But don’t worry,
we can rent the kitchen back for the next 1,000 years.”, can you see how dumb that
sounds? This is our house, but we have got to rent back our own kitchen for ever at a
rent that will keep going up every year for a kitchen that our grandparents built.
The fact is that this country is in an economic hole with the second-worst external
debt in the developed world and that moneys from the sale of State assets will be used
to repay that debt—not all of it; just some of it. And is that not a good idea, I hear you
say, in order to repay debt? Well, no, because  what happens when we have sold off the
power companies? The debt will still be th ere, and then what are we going to sell?
Schools—oh, too late. We have already priv atised education. Health? Well, we have
already privatised health services as well, much to the joy of the overseas private health
insurance companies making a killing off our pain and misery. And houses—State
8420 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
houses are already being flogged off as we speak today, as witnessed by the
communities of Glen Innes, Porirua, and Maraenui.
The fact is that the rape and pillage brigade has already gotten its grubby little hands
on most of the family jewels, so this G overnment is now trumpeting our Third World
status and our low wages in an attempt to sell our labour to the world. That is the
climate in which this Governme nt is planning to flog off our  assets. That is why Mana
stood with the New Zealand M āori Council, which won its case, to ensure M āori rights
to water were recognised and to delay the sale of Mighty River Power until today. That
is why Mana will support the council’s effort to clarify the extent of those rights when
the case comes back before the Waitangi Tribunal later this month. That is why Mana
supports Pouakani’s bid to stop the sale of State assets until their interests in the water
that drives Mighty River Power have been pr operly clarified and protected, and that is
why today Mana was proud to stand alongsid e Labour, the Greens, New Zealand First,
the unions, Grey Power, and the Union of Students’ Associations in receiving the
petition of nearly 400,000 people calling for a referendum on asset sales.
On matters of principle people have to take a stand, because despite widespread
disapproval from the public over the pending sale of Mighty River Power, despite every
respected economist questioning its financial viability, despite several court cases being
brought by Māori over water rights, and despite th e Government already admitting that
the shares will be sold cheaply and that it cannot guarantee that those shares will remain
in New Zealand hands, this Government still plans to sell Mighty River Power. Today I
stand alongside those hundreds of thousands of New Zealanders who signed the petition
and challenge the Government to put its clai m that it has support fo r asset sales to the
ultimate test. A straight referendum, one simple question: “Do you support”—

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First in
this debate, and again toda y we have witnessed anot her example of a clueless
Government that, basically, has run out of id eas. The purler that we have had today is
the latest imposition of fringe benefit tax on car-parks for companies in Auckland and
Wellington to raise something like $18 million in revenue. You really have to be
scraping the barrel when this Government, which says it is going to try to help business,
try to help grow the economy, and try to increase New Zealand’s business environment,
comes out with things like: “L et’s start charging them frin ge benefit tax to park their
cars, as well.” It sort of follows on from ot her miserable taxes, lik e the taxing last year
of schoolboys and schoolgirl s delivering their newspapers, and all sorts of other
miserable little taxes around th e edges that really are show ing that the Government has
run out of ideas, and run out of substantiv e ideas, to get this  economy really moving
again.
It is very interesting. I ha ve been one of the members of Parliament sitting on the
manufacturing inquiry over th e last 6 weeks, which has been held in Wellington,
Auckland, Christchurch, and, on Monday, Dunedin. It is very interes ting to hear from
some very significant manufacturers and expor ters in this country—iconic names like
HamitonJet; we all know HamiltonJet, you kn ow, one of the grea test manufacturing
companies that has come out of New Zeal and—and for them to be saying how much
they are really struggling and finding it diffi cult to compete in world markets with the
New Zealand dollar where it is today, up around US83c, US84c, or US85c. They are
saying that it is so difficult and that this Government is really not coming up with any
ideas. Not only is it not coming up with any idea s but also it is not prepared to listen to
the ideas that are being suggested by some of these very reputable companies. Ideas—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Give us one.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: Yes, I will. Thank you, Gerry, I will give you one. There
are ideas such as in the United States, where they were seeing a huge vacuum of
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8421
companies disappearing off to China to manufacture in China. In the United States they
have brought in a 40 percent write-down on new technology and equipment in the first
year. As a result of bringing in that new policy in the Unit ed States, they have seen a
regeneration of productive US companies that  actually are now findi ng that they are
more competitive with their plants in the United States as a result of having those write-
downs on new technology and equipment. They are actually gearing up and retooling in
the United States and are moving their production back onshore.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Name one.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: So there is one. There is one. Is it not interesting? When
you have a proper inquiry, when you do not stay up on the ninth floor or the eighth floor
or the seventh floor of the Beehive and i gnore the country but you actually go out and
listen to the companies and the manufacturer s, and you sit down a nd you listen to some
of their suggestions, it is quite amazing. Y ou also hear that manufacturing provides
stable, long-term, good employment with good wages—reliable wages that a family can
take home and bank, they can go to their ba nk manager and get a mortgage, and they
can have a house and work. Many  of these jobs that are be ing lost in manufacturing are
turning into precarious jobs such as part-time jobs—jobs that are not giving any
reliability—and time and time again we have  heard of downscaling and downsizing of
companies in New Zealand, retrenching, and la ying off staff. And those very staff who
supposedly do not go on to a benefit—as we he ard, if they have already got one partner
working, they are not counted as going on to a benefit, so they do not appear in the
statistics—often then go to precarious, part -time, semi - part-time work, which then
does not bring into the family sufficient income, which they have been used to.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: That’s not right.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: It is right. It is right. I am sorry, Mr Brownlee, but we
have heard that from many, many, many sour ces. And when you hear it from some
manufacturers in Auckland and you hear it from manufacturers in  Dunedin, who are
1,500 kilometres apart and who have no connec tion between the two of them, there is
obviously something going on there. It is going to be interesting that when the results of
this manufacturing inquiry come out they will point a direction for New Zealand that we
can uphold. And if the Governme nt is smart, it would actua lly embrace the findings of
that inquiry. It would say: “Yes, we can learn from this and we should not be that
arrogant”—

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I would be happy to respond to some
of the issues raised by members of the Committee. First of all, I simply outline the fact
that the accounts that we ar e looking at here show the benefit of the Government’s
continued focus over a 3-year period since it  has been in office on a considered and
consistent change in the economy. We ha ve had considerable headwinds in the
aftermath of the global financial crisis. That has made it difficult for the Government, as
well as households and businesses, to achieve  the aspirations that they have, but the
Government has stuck right through that pe riod to a straightfo rward plan, which we
have every confidence is bearing fruit now and will continue to do so.
There are any number of examples I could gi ve, but one example I will use is around
infrastructural investment, where despite difficult times for the Government’s books,
the Government committed early on to a range  of investments in transport, broadband,
and energy, and it stuck to that plan. The pr ojects are funded, they are under way, and
some of them are completed.  The industry and the country know that that process will
continue with some confidence.
Just to pick up a few of the comments made by the members of the Committee, I was
interested in the member from the far nor th being worried about the Government’s—in
his words—lack of interest in creating jobs. He is a member  who spends a great deal of
8422 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
his time in the far north making sure no jo bs are created—leadi ng the movement that
opposes, for instance, the exploita tion of minerals, oil, and ga s not just in the far north
but also off the East Coast of the North Island. The fact is that jobs flow from
investment. If you do not have investment , you do get jobs, and that means your 17-
year-old in Kaihohe has less prospect if there is less investment. It would be worthwhile
the member spending a bit of time just seeing how that linkage works. Wishing for jobs
does not create them.
We also heard from the member for New Zealand First about the so-called
manufacturing crisis. If there was a crisis of the sort that he was describing, then I could
understand the level of concern that the Oppos ition is showing. However, it is not the
case. Of course it is difficult for manufacturing, and not just manufacturing—it has been
difficult for everybody in an economy that  has had a significant recession with a
relatively moderate recovery from that recession. What the members should be learning,
I think, from that inquiry is  the resilience that so many manufacturers and exporters
have shown. If they had not been very resili ent, we would not have  the revenue that is
flowing through the accounts that we are discussing today.
If fact, manufacturing is growing moderately . In the last quarter the most recent
employment numbers show a drop-off in the total jobs in manufacturing, but what is
surprising through the last 4 or 5 years is  not how much manuf acturing has shrunk,
because it has not, but how well it has held up, given the difficulty of markets where
demand is shrinking, including now Australi a, and the headwind of a high exchange
rate. It does not mean that some are not sh edding jobs. They are. Some businesses are
going out. What is less  visible is the large number of manufacturers and exporters who
are actually expanding their investment and expanding their employment.
One of the contributions, as I said, that th ey have made is a contribution to fairly
steady growth in tax revenue. The Government has set out to reduce taxes on work,
investment, and savings. That  was done back in 2010 and th ese accounts are starting to
show the fruits of the improved incentives in  the economy. As we see, taxes continue to
grow, and in fact grow just sl ightly faster than we might have been expecting, and that
is why we remain on track to surplus.

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: It is a pleasure to stand to speak in this
debate and I want to commend the last speaker, the Minister  of Finance, Bill English,
and to thank him for the great job he has done on behalf of New Zealanders over the last
4 years. You see, there is a member opposite who has just stood up who was a member
of the Finance and Expenditure Committee. Actually, as far as most Labour members
are concerned, he was a quite hard-wor king and reasonable member of that
committee—he has since moved on to the Commerce Committee—and he is
occasionally heard to say in this House “the worst of this and the worst of that for 50
years”. Well, I have done a quite bit of research and when Bill English became our
Minister of Finance, we inherited some of  the worst economic conditions in 50 years.
[Interruption] That is right. There we go. So on the Opposition side of the Chamber not
only are they Hobbit-haters, th ey are global financial crisis  deniers as well. When we
came into Government the global financial cr isis hit and the Government books went in
the opposite direction. And what happened to  members opposite? Well, they said there
was no global financial crisis, nothing was wr ong, New Zealanders had made a mistake
and they would wake up soon, and then 3 years later we had another election—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: All the Labour Party’s fault, th e global financial crisis! Labour
caused the global financial crisis, of course. What a pathetic argument!

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: That is right, Mrs King, you are still on that side of the Chamber
after that last electi on—exactly. So let us have a look at what Treasury is saying about
the job that has been done by this Govern ment over the last 4 years in extremely
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8423
difficult circumstances for New Zealand a nd New Zealanders—and we must recognise
that—and let us then compare that with what  is happening in other parts of the world,
which the Labour Opposition seems to want to be so much like.
Well, the Treasury forecast in December that GDP would grow 2.3 percent for 2012-
13, and 3 percent for 2013-14. So many other co untries of the world would like that to
happen. Indeed, if we look around the world at the countries that have between 0
percent and 1 percent interest rate at th e moment, which are responsible for over 60
percent of the world’s production, many of  them are still in  recession and their
unemployment rate is so much higher th an ours. Members opposite have spoken about
unemployment at great length in this House and almost everywhere in the country. But
let us compare what is happening in New Zealand with ot her countries. The
unemployment rate in New Zeal and at the last survey stan ds at 6.9 percent down from
7.1 percent last year, and we al l accept that that is a high number. But let us compare it
with Europe, because we hear so much about  the policies of parts of Europe and that
New Zealand should emulate them and be a lot more like them. Well, in the 17
eurozone countries, the 17 countries that have the euro—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Do they count their statistics in the same way?

items.speaker: TODD McCLAY
items.text: It is a good question, but me mbers opposite count statistics
however they want to just so that they  can go up to the House and confuse New
Zealanders. But 11.9 percent is the average unemployment rate. Of the 27 countries in
the European Union their average unemploym ent rate is 10.8 percent. In the USA—we
heard earlier from New Zealand First abou t what is or is not happening around
manufacturing in the USA—7.7 percent is its unemployment rate, which is the same as
the United Kingdom. And in the two countries  in the rest of the world that the
Opposition wants us to be so much like—at least, one would come to that conclusion
when we hear the policies that it would be putting in place for this country if it was on
the Government benches—Greece has 27 percen t, and Spain has an unemployment rate
of 26 percent.
I again say to our Prime Minister, John Ke y, and to our Minister of Finance, Bill
English, thank goodness New Zealanders decided that they trusted the judgment of
these two men, that they saw through very difficult, difficult times that New Zealand
was going in the right direction, and th at certainly they wanted good economic
management at the same time.
So what does the Opposition say about this? Well, really, it is to oppose. I accept that
when you are in Opposition, at the front of th e title it says “oppose”, but everything this
Government has come up with to help  the New Zealand economy, to give New
Zealanders a better chance to grow business and industr y, and to create jobs, the
Opposition has opposed. The first would be to bu ild a convention centre in Auckland. It
is against that every step of the way. Jobs will be created. Peopl e will travel from all
around the world to come here, but the Opposi tion does not want it, at all. It opposed
the changes that were made to allow the Hobbit movies to be made in this country. It
did not want the movies to be made here. I am very proud they ar e made here by hard-
working New Zealanders. I am very proud this  Government was able to put in place a
regime that was fair and that brought to this  country those movies and the billions of
dollars that flow over time because of th at. The Opposition opposed our changes to the
Resource Management Act.

items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Chair. T ēnā koutou e te Whare.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Tēnā koutou e te Whare. I rise to speak on the financial
review of the Ministry of Tran sport. I just wanted to start with this incredible piece of
work that was released just before Christ mas that the Ministry of Transport co-funded
and collaborated on, which is the City Centre Future Access Study.
If members recall, last y ear when the National Land Tr ansport Programme for the
next 3 years, that is 2012-15, was announced, I asked the Minister of Transport in this
House what new public transport infrastruct ure projects were planned for Auckland. At
that time the Minister could not name a single public transport infrastructure project that
had not been committed under the last Labour Government. So electrification, station
upgrades, the new electric multiple units that have all been ordered for Auckland, which
are highly anticipated and will be very effec tive—all of that is infrastructure that was
committed under a previous Government. There have been no new infrastructure
projects.
At the time the Minister announced—becau se he was not able to name any
infrastructure projects that are planned any tim e in the next 10 years that will be funded
by this Government—this particular study, which was co-funded by the Ministry of
Transport. Of course, the terms of referen ce were signed off by the Minister himself.
This study, like the 2010 busines s case before it and all the very thorough work and
studies that the Auckland Regional Trans port Authority completed since 2006, stated
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8425
conclusively that the Auckland city rail link is  an essential piece of infrastructure. It is
the only way to meet the needs of a growing Auckland.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No, it isn’t.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: The transport needs of Auckland. It is the only way—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: No, it isn’t.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: —to keep people and goods moving in the Auckland
region and to avoid gridlock, such as we saw last week in Auckland, becoming the norm
every single day.
The Government continues to say no, as the Minister is saying right now, to this vital
piece of infrastructure, which the business  community knows that Auckland needs. The
Government will not even fund half—not ev en half—of this piece of essential
infrastructure, even though its  own studies show that it is the only way to avoid
congestion. So it is very ironic or perhaps wilfully ignor ant that the Government claims
that its motorways of madness, which will suck up the vast majority of transport
funding over the next 10 years, will some how reduce congestion or improve transport
efficiency, when its own studies show that they will do no such thing.
In the National Land Transport Programme,  which was announced last year by the
New Zealand Transport Agency, we see th at 87 percent of all the funds on new
transport projects is going on road projec ts, and a tiny portion is going on public
transport, walking, and cycling, even though th ose are the most cost-effective ways to
meet the growing demand. Of course, it is road users and the economy that benefit from
investment in public transport, walking, and cycling, because that is the best way to
reduce pressure on the roads. It is the most cost-effective way to move more people at
peak hour. More road users and the economy w ill benefit from investment in the city
rail link than will benefit from the $1 billion P ūhoi to Wellsford “Holiday Highway” or
the $600 million Kapiti Expressway. Very fe w road users will benefit from these
projects, which are sucking up the va st majority of new funding under this
Government’s policy.
The Government is going to borrow and put up fuel taxes to pay for its pet motorway
projects, motorways of madness, which will carry only a tiny proportion of daily vehicle
trips—4 percent. This is not a good use of  road users’ money. Many road users,
especially road freight, will benefit far more from projects that  give commuters the
opportunity to leave their cars at home, because  that is the most cost-effective way to
reduce peak congestion. Nowhere in the world do you see cities trying to reduce
congestion by building a motorway out of the city. That is ri diculous. It is ridiculous
and insane that the Government can claim that it is going to reduce congestion by
throwing billions at motorways out of cities.
I would just like to sum up by saying that the Government has to be pretty mired in
ideology to not seize the opportunity provided by  smart, green transport, because that is
a better approach for the economy, it is a better  approach for road us ers, it is a better
approach for consumers, and it is even better for the environment.
In the responses to financial review que stions, the New Zealand Transport Agency
very helpfully gave me this table, which s hows the benefit-cost ratio percentage split.
That is the benefit-cost ratio percentage of all the different infrastructure projects that
were conducted over the financial year  under review. One hundred percent of the
projects—

Given the communication problems within this  Chamber, I thought that the Chair had

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! How this works is that this is a 4-
hour debate, and each party is allocated a number of speaking positions. In your case,
you were given—and I understand that was an agreement with a party—one call. You
have exercised that right to the call, so you will have no other calls available to you in
this 4-hour debate. Should you wish to take another call, then you would need to seek a

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I just want to make a few
comments in relation to the somewhat narr ow comments made by the previous speaker,
Julie Anne Genter, and in particular the rath er nasty assertion that the Government is
not taking public transport seriously. The rea lity is that public transport is a very big
chunk of the spend, and we are going to contin ue that. The member might like to reflect
that although a previous  Government spent a lot of time promising projects, it did very
little to deliver them. It is the current Government that has actually funded them.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: The member may find that slightly amusing, which is
somewhat typical of how you get a particul ar persuasion in Ne w Zealand’s politics
behaving. The reality is that the transport network in New Zealand is a great deal bigger
and a great deal more complex than just sa ying: “Let’s put a tunne l from Britomart up
north of Albert Street for about 1.5 kilometres to create a bit of a loop.” There is, in fact,
very little evidence that ther e would be any effect from a project like that beyond
perhaps 1 or 2 years at the end of this deca de. So we do have to look at all of these
things in quite a broad perspective.
There is also, I am sure, quite a strong opini on in Auckland that the roads that have
been built there—over the last 10 years, I would like to co ncede—in particular things
like the Victoria Park project have made a difference to the way traffic moves through
that city.

items.speaker: Julie Anne Genter
items.text: It was gridlocked last week.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Well, the member says it was gridlocked last week.
Let me tell you, if a train became derailed in  a tunnel, it would be a great deal more
gridlocked than a car accident on a highway. Those are things that  cannot particularly
be helped. I guess if we are all on bicycles or horses or some other sort of past transport
mode like those, then we might not have such a degree of congestion, but then we
would not have the pace in our economy that people expect today.
There is a need for roading to be fair and appropriately applied across the country,
and we do have a programme that sees, of those seven roads of national significance,
two very important South Island roads. One of them, which is now open, is the
Christchurch Southern Motorway link, and th e other, of course, is the western ring
route, which is being put in as well. Furthe r south, it is going to be rather like the
Auckland rail loop, where you have actually got  declining patronage on the rail in
Auckland—declining patronage on the rail in Auckland—and th erefore there is a much
weaker case for even considering what might be done in the future.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: What about the cost benefits?
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8427

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: One member just suggested there that we look at some
of the cost-benefit ratios. We ll, this is where our opponents really get upset, because
some of those cost-benefit ratios are very, very good for those various projects that I
have just mentioned. The sad thing is that it would not matter how good they looked;
ideologically there is going to be opposition to them. The reality is that New Zealanders
like their cars. New Zealanders like to be on motorways. New Zealanders like to move
around with the freedom that automobiles give them. And New Zealanders pay for
those roads through their excise tax and through their road-user charges, and they
should have a right to expect that there is good planning around them. So I think that
this year has been a very good year for Ne w Zealand’s Ministry of Transport and the
transport agencies that sit underneath it, including all of those agencies that are engaged
in safety of various types, in making sure that consumer s who are using our networks
are doing so in a safe manner.
Finally, I want to say that no one should underestimate the huge commitment that
this Government has continued with KiwiRa il. The $750 million that has gone into that
company over the last couple of years to recapitalise it has been extremely important for
making sure that we get more freight on the rail, therefore taking some pressure off the
roads. Of course, there is going to need to be an ongoing capital commitment to that
company for some time to come. All in all, I think our transport network is in good
shape, but it needs constant improveme nt, constant investment, and constant
commitment to it.
Report noted.
Ministry of Economic Development

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: The Super 15 rugby season is
under way, and there is all kind of interest in  that, with the Hurri canes on their way to
their triumphant first win in  Super 15 rugby. One of the things that people may have
noticed is an occasional change in the rule s when it comes to rugby, and one of them is
around what happens when a maul collapses. I think the Government should take note
of the change in rules. Here is what John Key said in 2009: “we are continuing to put in
place our Jobs and Growth Plan. This is a ‘rol ling maul’ of initiatives aimed at retaining
and growing jobs and preparing the economy for future growth.” Well, the Government
has collapsed its own maul, and that is currently against the rules in Super Rugby, and it
is not what New Zealand needs, either. The rolling maul of initiatives of this
Government has fallen apart, and it is left with two economic plans:  sell assets and sell
laws. They are the two plans this Governme nt has got: sell off assets, and sell off the
laws of New Zealand. Gerry Brownlee is l ooking quizzically at me. The problem, Mr
Brownlee, is that an economic development pl an for National is a big night at Skycity.
That is an economic development plan for National, but it is not good enough for New
Zealand. Selling things off is not going to grow the economy and it is not going to grow
jobs.
If we look back over this year of achiev ement from this Government when it comes
to jobs, the achievement that we find is another 50,000 people going to Australia,
163,000 people unemployed, and an unemployment rate of 6.9 percent. But bear in
mind that that rate of 6.9 percent is there on ly because 33,000 people just left. They left
the labour force. They either left for Austra lia or they gave up looking for jobs. If we
actually include those people, the real unemp loyment rate is 8.4 percent, which is
actually the worst since the mid-1990s. So  the real unemployment rate under this
Government is as bad as it was in the mi ddle of the 1990s, and that is because this
Government has absolutely no plan for job growth.
8428 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
But this is not just the Labour Opposition sa ying this. This is businesses saying this,
and we saw it in a survey that Ernst and Young did that was published in the Sunday
Star-Times. There were several interesting elements to that that this Government needs
to take on board. The first of those was that nearly 80 percent of the businesses
surveyed said that job creation was a partnership between Government and business and
community—

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Gerry Brownlee says that that is right, but we see no sign
whatsoever from this Government of a partnership, of it rolling its sleeves up and
saying: “We’ll get involved and we’ll help grow jobs.” We do not see that. What we see
is hands-off Government, from this G overnment saying: “We’re not involved.”
[Interruption] Gerry Brownlee is continuing to interj ect from the chair. I will take a few
more seconds for that, thank you, Mr Assi stant Chairperson. Gerry Brownlee knows
that this Government could be more hands-on. It could get in and ta ke initiatives that
actually help grow jobs. It could support our export sector by doing something about
monetary policy. It could do something useful  in procurement, rather than the words
that we are hearing at the moment. But no, th is Government sits back and it is hands-
off, and that is what businesses said in this survey.
But the other thing was that those businesse s were asked to rate from one to 10 the
National Government’s record on job creati on, with one being very poor and 10 being
outstanding. Well, 70 percent of  the businesses rated the Government average to very
poor, below average, essentially—a fail mark, as the Sunday Star-Times called it, on job
creation. This is not just the Opposition. These are busin esses who want to get on and
employ people. They are struggling and they are looking for a Government that wants to
help them out, and it is not happening; it is hands-off.
The Government and Mr Joyce have been particularly excited. There has been a lot
of time spent this year on the Business Grow th Agenda—the six glossy documents that
have been presented to Ne w Zealanders as some kind of growth agenda. Well,
unfortunately, that did not go down very well with business either, because in the same
survey 70 percent of businesses ranked the Government five or below on that scale of
one to 10 for whether it could actually develop and implement a Business Growth
Agenda. So business has given up on this G overnment. Businesses have said that the
Government is not there to help them create jobs and it has not even got the capacity to
develop and execute a Business Growth Agenda. That is the loss of confidence that has
happened under this Government. That is the loss of confidence that has happened
because there is not a real plan for sustai nable economic growth. It is not a plan to
simply sell off assets and sell off laws so that a casino can have a few more pokies. That
is not actually an economic growth agenda.
An economic growth agenda would say that  it was a moral shame on this country to
have 90,000 15 to 24-year-olds not in employment, not in education, and not in training.
Once upon a time we had Governments and Nationa l Ministers who said that we cannot
afford to let generations fail. Yet that is exactly what they have done, and those numbers
go up, and they go up. For all the flash programmes and the Job Ops and the Youth
Guarantee programmes, when we actually go out into the community and we talk to
training providers and we talk to the polytech s, what we hear is: “There’s so much
bureaucracy. We don’t even know if we’re actually able to deliver what the Government
wants. It changes every week.” That is  not good enough. We have to have as an
absolute priority in this country that young people in New Zealand do not fall off a cliff
face at the end of secondary school, and that we actually actively involve ourselves in
making sure there are opportunities not for just one small group picked off at a time, but
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8429
to say that for all of those young people we w ill give them opportunities to get skills to
be able to get into employment. And that is missing from this Government.

items.speaker: Clare Curran
items.text: It’s called hope.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Clare Curran says to me it is called hope, and that is
exactly what is missing at the moment for young people in New Zealand, who see their
future in Australia, not here in New Zeal and, because this Government has not been
prepared to invest in skills and training and in giving them job opportunities.
In response to the Ernst and Young surv ey Phil O’Reilly was asked by the Sunday
Star-Times about what the Government should  do, and he said that what the
Government needs to do is help subsidise employers so that they  can take on young
people, so they can get skills and training.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: There’s a good idea.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: And that is a very, very good idea from Phil O’Reilly. I
knew he would have a good idea eventually, and he has had it, because that is the policy
that the Labour Party took to the election.  The National Party di d not want to know
about it. It did not want to go in there and say to busines ses that it will help out. I
remember when Labour announced that. We said that for 18 and 19-year-olds we would
take that money that has been paid fo r the dole and give it as a subsidy for
apprenticeships. I had employers in my electorate ringing me up and saying: “If you did
that, I’d take two today. I want to bri ng people on board. I’m struggling. I need the
Government to get in and help out.” This  is not the Government doing everything for
businesses. It is rolling up its sleeves and being a hands-on Government that gives them
a helping hand. That is what is missing from this Government’s approach at the
moment, and that is what the Labour Party will bring.
I want to just refer in terms of the ec onomic development ministry back to the
question of Skycity, because I do think it is important. If this Government has anything
to think about back over this year, it is the fact that it has mucked around in this space
so much that it got a warning from Treasur y that the probity of the process in the
Skycity deal was questionable, and yet it ignored it. Actually, the Minister in the chair,
is the one Minister in that Government who can at least look at the report of the
Auditor-General and say that he did someth ing, because when he came in, he looked at
it and he said: “This is an absolute disaster. Why is the Prime Minister’s chief of staff
all over this negotiation with Skycity?”. Bu t, unfortunately for Gerry Brownlee, the
damage was well and truly done. The S kycity convention centre sums up this
Government. It was a corrupted  process. This Government thinks that it can be hands-
on by corrupting the process, and that is what the report said.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: Rubbish.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is very clear, Mr Brow nlee. The Auditor-General said
that up until August 2009 everything was going OK in the negotiations about a
convention centre, and then along came the Prime Minister, who wrote: “Let’s cover off
the Skycity angle.” on his briefing paper, a nd from that moment on officials in the
Ministry of Economic Development and acro ss Government began behaving in ways
that were not appropriate, and the Auditor-General said that. They did that only because
they had had that direction from the Prime Minister. New Zealande rs are getting sick
and tired of the cronyism of this Governme nt and they want Government members to
focus on job initiatives, on rolling up their sleeves, supporting businesses to employ
people, giving people hope in New Zealan d, and giving people a future. This
Government needs to hear the lesson. Young people in New Zealand want those
opportunities, they want to stay here, and they want to work, but unless there is a
Government that is prepared to be a partner with business, then that will not happen.
8430 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
New Zealand is a country with great  ideas, great innovation, and great
entrepreneurial skills. It needs a Government th at is prepared to pul l the big levers like
monetary policy and the smaller levers lik e getting alongside a small business and
saying: “We’ll make sure you have an appren ticeship in place.” This Government has
failed on job creation—that is the view of business and it is the view of the Labour
Party—and it must do far better.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I
think one of the things that that speech misses is that no business can thrive unless there
is a dynamic in the economy that allows it  to grow those business opportunities. And
that is not about the Government standing up and pouring huge amounts of subsidy into
here, there, and everywhere—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: That’s not there; that’s the problem.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: —as the reverend over there would have us believe; it
is about a Government that looks at a wide r economic policy that is about ensuring that
the country has a base wealth. So let us start with the first point. Th is first point is the
exchange rate, which, we hear from the Gr een Party and the Labour Party, is too high
and we have got to knock it down somehow. The Green Party, along with the Labour
Party, wanted to get out the printing presses and start printing so much money that the
value of our exchange falls. That hurts every consumer in this country, because that is
about saying to New Zealanders “We are the deciding to make you poorer.”, and that is
not an acceptable thing at all. It also rips out from consumers the purchasing power that
they have with their wages. So real wages, not subsidised wages, is  what it has to be
about.
I will tell you something else. When it co mes to supporting business, the tax rates
that we have brought in do encourage busin ess and businesses to expand, to do more,
and to grow. There is also the issue of mark et access. An unrelenting desire to get New
Zealand into different markets so that we can  have export choices has been a hallmark
of this Government so far. When it co mes to employing people,  it is no good saying
“Here—look. Here’s a subsidy for this person. Take them into the business that you’ve
got operating here.”, when, in fact, that person may not have the incentive they need. So
getting people who want work—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Sorry to interrupt the member. The time
has come for me to leave the chair for the dinner break.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

system is operating fully, so perhaps I should—
