items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: It will not work. Thank you, Mr Chair. I shall perhaps
endeavour to continue, desp ite the absence of the micr ophone. I fear other members
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8431
may miss my contribution because my quiet and retiring voice may not travel across the
Chamber. But the members opposite already kn ow that I will say loudly and clearly to
them that I am disappointed with econom ic development progress, because this
Government has the worst record of any G overnment in New Zealand in the last 60
years.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: It has the worst economic development record in the last—

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: 60 years?

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: I should say 50 years. I must co rrect myself. It probably is 60
years, but I should not exaggerate. So we w ill stick with 50 years—the years are adding
up, but it certainly has a poor record over a long period of time. The Government’s
promise to deliver on a Building a Brighter Future plan that would create 170,000 new
jobs over 4 years sounded grea t, but the reality has proven to be something altogether
different. It is a hands-off Government, a nd I think that its hands-off approach to
creating jobs in this country is really, real ly, really showing through in the absence of
progress.
Nowhere is this approach better epitomis ed than when we look across to “Mobie”,
the Government’s new creation—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: The whale!

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: —the big white whale, which is an agglomeration of many
other ministries. The interesting thing about  the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment is that the Government is so ha nds-off that the ministry has no Minister in
charge. I do not know whether this is unprecedented—some more mature and
experienced members may wish to comment—but  I think it is very unusual to have a
Government ministry that has nobody in charge of it. That is  truly hands-off. That is
taking hands-off to a whole new level.
Perhaps that is a picture—something that we can look to in order to understand how
this Government is approaching the job cris is that we see developing in New Zealand.
We know that the unemployment rate, at 6.9 percent, is as bad as it has been. It is the
worst it has been for a very long time. It is getting back to levels we saw in the 1990s
when National was last in power. We know that 1,000 people a week have been leaving
for Australia. I guess that is, for the Govern ment, a positive thing, because it brings that
unemployment rate down. But it is not a pos itive thing for New Zealand’s future—40
percent of those people permanently leaving New Zealand for Australia every week are
young people. They are our future. They are the people who will increase our GDP and
who will grow our economy in the future , and I am afraid those young people are
fleeing from this country because there are no prospects here for them.
The wage gap, which National promised to close when it took office, has grown 50
percent—a full 50 percent the wage gap wi th Australia has grown. That is an
embarrassment, surely, to this Government, when it has said that it would close the
wage gap and stop the loved ones heading offshore.
So the economic development record of this Government is in tatters. Steven Joyce’s
Business Growth Agenda has proven to be nothing more than a year of spin. There have
been no substantial announcements in that Business Growth Agenda—an awful lot of
re-announcements of policy already in pl ace, much of it introduced by previous
Governments. We have seen wasted res ource, in my view, merely re-announcing old
plans and dabbling in the old meek idea here and there.
What is very clear is that that will not work, because if  we do not change anything,
nothing will change. If we carry on with the policies of the 1980s th at this Government
is so comfortable with, we will not have jobs created. We will see the ongoing pattern
that we have now of skilled people head ing offshore and more and more and more
8432 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
young people ending up on the scrap heap beca use they have not got any prospects.
Glossy brochures will not fi x that. We need a real plan for the economy, and that
involves doing bold things, such as pro-growth tax reform. Let us see some research and
development tax credits. Let us see some capital gains tax that neutralises the
investment signals so that we actually ge t some investment in our export markets—
those businesses that would produce for our  export markets. Let us see universal
KiwiSaver so that we actually start to get so me depth into our savings, so that there is
some resource to support our businesses. Let us se e some pro - New Zealand
procurement policies.
We saw this week Steven Joyce announcing, effectively, that he was going to
announce current policy—

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I am very pleased to stand and
speak on the financial review of the Mini stry of Economic Development, which,
actually, is a ministry that has now been fold ed into a new ministry called the Ministry
of Business, Innovation and Employment. The ministry was established back on 1 July
2012, and it brought together a number of the Government’s business-facing functions
under one agency. It aims to support New Zeal and businesses in orde r to create a more
prosperous economy.
Is it not great that Treasury forecasts in December showed a real GDP growth from
2.3 percent in 2012-13 to around 3 percent in  2013-14? So while all the prophets of
doom on the other side—normally David Cl ark is a happy member, but what a
depressing speech. Normally we are able to ve ry easily just rebuff such depression that
comes from the other side of the Chamber.  We can see that New Zealand is forging
ahead.
We know that this country re lies upon its export markets.  We know that that is the
real lifeblood of our economy. It is great to  see that our Prime Minister has been very
active in Latin America, visiting four nati ons that are exceedingl y big in their GDP,
with $4 trillion between them—Mexico, Colomb ia, Chile, and Brazil—to build closer
trading relationships with these nations, whic h is going to enable Ne w Zealanders to be
able to export and earn more overseas exchange. New Zealand Trade and Enterprise
reported to us that over the last financial year New Zealand business presence in Asia
and Australia showed the biggest growth, and grew substantially as well in South
America. So the Prime Minister going there leading a trade delegation is very much part
of the strategy that we are building in th is nation to be global traders with our
commodities.
Latin America’s middle class is growing ra pidly, and now represen ts 30 percent of
the population—the World Bank tells us that. This group has more disposable income
and is fuelling demand for better infrastructure and an improve d quality of life. That is
where New Zealand can provide commodities to  this market. New Zealand’s exports to
Latin America were worth $1.36 billion in 2011.  We believe that we can substantially
increase that. What that means is jobs  for New Zealanders, and greater overseas
exchange for this country that is going to lift the quality of life for New Zealanders here
but also is going to bring a quality of life for our trading partners.
Our dairy products are a significant e xport earner. New Zealand has major
investments in dairying and farm production in the region, pa rticularly in Chile, Brazil,
and Colombia. So this is a good-news story.  It is a good-news story of what New
Zealand is doing, and continues to do, led by this National Government, which is
forging relationships with our  overseas trading partners. All of this is building the
strength that we have in the international market place.
Around that area, innovation is  such an important area of  economic development. If
we are going to see a lift, i nnovation is one of those key areas where a lift can happen.
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8433
Productivity lift does not just happen because you are doing more of the same. A lot of
the time it is doing something new and doing things better. What the Government has
done is establish Callaghan Innovation, a ne w Crown entity charged with accelerating
commercialisation of science-based innovation in New Zealand firms, particularly in the
manufacturing and services sectors, whic h include food processing and beverages, by
better connecting those sectors with science, technology, and support that th ey need in
order to develop and commercialise their ideas.
It is great to see that that is happening—i ncreasingly so. We are seeing real signs of
growth. There are signs that the pace of gr owth has picked up in recent months. For
example, the volume of building work undert aken rose by 1.8 percent in the December
quarter, which was seasonally adjusted, afte r gaining 9.8 percent in the September
quarter. We know that the construction sect or can create tremendous uplift for the
economy, because there are so many different sectors and trades that are involved in this
particular area. Manufacturing volumes rose by 1.5 percent in the December quarter.
Looking ahead, employment growth is expected  to pick up due to the Canterbury
rebuild, improving business confidence. Altho ugh we are still sail ing into headwinds
internationally, New Zealand’s economy has beco me more resilient, more efficient, and
more productive. Thank you.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON

items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I raise a
point of order, Mr Chairperson. It appears that the microphone is not working.

items.text: I am very happy to do that.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: If it is working—it is not working.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: There is another debacle that is happening on the Government’s
very doorstep that is the Government’s own do ing and that is poised to explode in its
face. It is a debacle of economic developm ent—of the economic development that was
promised in 2008, when National won the el ection, when it became the Government. It
was going to be the step change in our economy—Steven Joyce’s ill-thought-out ultra-
fast broadband scheme, John Key’s grand ultra-fast broadband idea, Chorus’ inability to
deliver on the ultra-fast broadband scheme, and Crown Fibre Holdings’ negotiation of
the contract between the Crown and Chorus to build the $1.5 billion taxpayer scheme. It
has been botched. It is a giant stuff-up—it is a giant stuff-up and they know it.
Just before Christmas the Commerce Co mmission announced a draft decision and a
well-signalled review of the way that the wholesale price of copper broadband is
calculated to one based on the actual costs fo r the services to be provided. It was well
signalled. It dropped the whol esale price per line per month from $21 to almost $9. But
the problem for the Government is that peopl e are not taking up fi bre and they are not
moving across to fibre. As a re sult, Chorus held that its drop in income on its copper
network would undermine the company and that  it just could not keep on building the
Government’s fibre network. So how did this  happen? How did we get to this point?
How did Chorus not know that this was likely? The telecommunications companies did.
How did the Government not know? Now we  see the Government’s much-vaunted
broadband scheme coming unstuck, and the Government does not know what to do
8434 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
about it except to try to stick its finger in the dyke. It will do this by bypassing the
Commerce Commission. “Forget about them.”, it said. “They don’t matter. Let’s change
the law.”, said John Key. He said it twice before Christmas, and one of those times was
in this House.
Ross Patterson is the former Telecommunications Commissioner for the Commerce
Commission. He was respecte d and highly regarded ac ross the industry and in
Government circles. He has described the Government’s response as unprecedented. He
said: “It is a fundamental principle of our telecommunications regulatory regime that the
regulator is independent, and is left to carry out its statutory role without interference or
undue influence from the Government.” He sa id the Government had crossed that line.
Does that sound familiar? Think of the Skyc ity deals; think of the $43 million loans to
MediaWorks; think of the change of law to suit Warner Bros in making The Hobbit in
New Zealand; think of the conflicted role of Stephen McElrea, the Prime Minister’s
electorate chairman, on the board of New Zealand on Air; and think of the Prime
Minister’s knowledge of, and involvement in, the illegal surveillance of Kim Dotcom
by the Government Communications Security Bureau and the FBI. This Government
will do what it likes. It will abus e the law. It will abuse the contract processes. And if it
does not like the law, it will change it. It wi ll ignore it or it will change it, and then
pretend it cannot remember or it does not really matter.
Two years ago Steven Joyce forced through changes to the Telecommunications Act
to allow Chorus to be given $1 billion to roll out the bulk of its ultra-fast broadband
network. Labour opposed many of those changes and the bill in its entirety, because it
considered that the Government was using a law change to allo w it to favour one
business over another in awarding a huge taxpayer-funded contract. There were two
major bidders: Chorus, which was part of Telecom, and Vector, the Auckland-based
electricity lines company. Chorus won the job, as we predicted it would, not because it
was the best bidder but because the Governme nt had already decided that it would get
the job. Chorus knew the terms and conditions of its contract. It was well signalled at
the time that there would be a review of  the copper pricing system by the Commerce
Commission by 2014. It was well signalled that  copper prices would fall. And what
happened? We are now into the fifth year since this Government was elected. Just 3,806
households have been connected. Not one  major telecommunica tions company has
announced a retail package to attract people on to fibre.
Report noted.
Ministry of Justice

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: As the new chair of the Justice and
Electoral Committee, it is my pleasure to stand and have a call this evening on this
financial review. One of the hallmarks of any civilised society is a robust judicial
system—a justice system in which people can have confidence, that is not corrupt, that
is efficient, and that is one that dispense s fair and equitable ju stice that people are by
and large happy with. I am pleased to say that  here in New Zealand, of course, we have
a very good justice system and we have a ve ry good Minister of Justice. In the very
capable Judith Collins we have a Minister of Justice who has a big agenda ahead of her
for my committee and for this Parliament in the months ahead. We have one of the very
best performing justice systems in the world.  There is very little  corruption—in fact, I
would dare say minimal corruption—we ha ve a strong judiciary, and we have high
public confidence in our institutions. Of cour se, this is of huge advantage to us as
citizens of New Zealand. And the approach th at Minister Collins is taking in terms of
justice is working. Total reported crime has fallen by almost 6 percent.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How much?
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8435

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: Almost 6 percent—6 percent. Youth crime itself has fallen by
about 4 percent and reoffending by nearly 6 percent. That is something like 21,000
fewer crimes. We had 3,000 fewer violent crim es over the past year, and that means,
therefore, thousands and thous ands fewer victims. Members will be pleased to know
that the rate of homicide and related offences, such as attempted murder and
manslaughter, has dropped by a whopping 22 per cent. The rate of serious assaults
resulting in injury has dropped by 8 percent. So this Government’s plan for better public
services within tight financia l constraints is working very well. This is a Government
that has ambitious targets for justice. Re ducing the crime rate by 15 percent, violent
crime by 20 percent, youth crime by 5 percent, and the reoffending rate by 25 percent—
these are targets that are aspirational and ambitious.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Sorry to interrupt the member. Members
may have just entered the Chamber, but we are working under duress without
amplification inside the Chamber. We have broadcasts going outside, and I have asked
members to be conscious of the fact that our environment is not what we are used to and
to curtail their desire to incessantly put in interjections.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. Could you just confirm
which vote we are discussing? I felt the me mber was talking about Vote Police rather
than Vote Justice.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Ministry of Justice.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: I am speaking about the Minist ry of Justice and the very
capable and wonderful job that the Minister of Justice, the Hon Judith Collins, is doing.
You see, justice results are very important. Delivering better public services to New
Zealanders within tight financial constraints, as I said earlier, is the sort of thing that this
Government is all about.
Within the justice sector, we have va rious departments working more closely
together. So we do have police and correc tions working more closely with justice—
more closely than ever before—and that help s us achieve targets. That is a good thing,
in my view, and something that we will be encouraging on this side of the Chamber. For
instance, crime, when it is down, means th at our court numbers are down, our number
of sessions is down, and appearances in court are fewer. So we have a unique
opportunity—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: That was brief!

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: —a brief but unique opportunity—here we go again.
[Interruption] This is good—yes. So we have a unique opportunity—hello? Can you—
no, I will go back to this one. Any minute now , if I were Brendan Horan, I would burst
into song. I am going to resist that urge to burst into song. We have within justice an
opportunity to work differently, to focus more on the underlying causes of crime and, of
course, crime prevention. We have a unique opportunity to—[ Interruption] Down? Oh,
I was just getting in to the really good bit! We have  a unique opportunity to work
differently, to focus more on those underlyi ng causes of crime, to modernise and
improve our operating justice model, and to build, I suspect, a more customer-focused,
lower-cost, and more accessible justice system.
One of the areas that my select committee is  exploring at the moment is the Family
Court Proceedings Reform Bill, which is goi ng through at the moment. That is a very
good piece of legislation being put through at a time when we can reform the Family
Court in a way that focuses on the most se rious cases, while at the same time putting
children and vulnerable people first. It is this putting children and vulnerable people
first, rather than those with just relationship problems, that is a very important part.
Report noted.
8436 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
Ministry of Health

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: The ministry at the 2011-12
financial review made the claim that the health sector was well managed and, although
some OECD countries were forced to cut Government health spending, New Zealand
had slowed expenditure growth without need ing to reduce health services or cut the
numbers of clinical staff. That was what was written in the financial review.
So let us examine those claims that were ma de in the financial review. It is not easy
to get the information that I would like to share with you, because, unfortunately, we
have a Minister who has been very, very clev er at keeping information very quiet. I did
receive a letter that I thought might put it into perspec tive. This letter is from someone
who works in the health system , who wrote to me and said: “T here is a climate of fear,
bullying, and intimidation from the Minister  and the national health board personnel
that is destructive and into micro detail and management.” That was followed up by a
comment from the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists, who said recently that
the Minister had, in fact, intimidated a doc tor into not speaking. So we do have this
climate of fear that exists in the health system.
I think it is important that I read to you from this letter what this person said about
our health system. It reads: “The absolute focus on the Minister’s health targets and the
counting numbers is unwinding much of the improvements that have been made
previously. Most of the increase in electiv e services was the result of work done under
the Labour Government and was just starting to work. The health target comparisons by
DHBs are so totally meaningless they do not reflect anything to do with real care or
quality of outcome. This will only get worse as financial pressures build in the last
quarter of this financial year.” That co mes from somebody who works in the health
system.
So let us go over those things that were said in the financial review. It was said that
the health system is well managed. What did the Health Committee itself say in its
report to this House? It said this: “We were  concerned about the ministry’s capacity for
delivering projects and meeting output target s, as reflected in the 7.6 percent reduction
in operating costs, and the 21 project dela ys that occurred in 2011/12. We note that
almost half of these delays were because of staff vacancies and redundancies.”
So is our system working well and is it well managed? Well, if the way to manage it
is to delay up to 21 projects because there are staff vacancies and redundancies, it does
not seem to me to be a very good way to manage it, at all. Then you have a look—and I
know Dr Hutchison will be interested in this—at what some of those 21 projects are that
we were told at the select committee had been delayed.
Well, when I looked at this list, an  alarm bell went off for me, because,
unfortunately, I was the Mini ster of Health, in Februa ry 2000, who was required to
present the report on the unde r-reporting of cervical cance r rates from Gisborne. A
ministerial inquiry had been carried out because of failures in the cervical screening
programme. So one of my first duties as a new Minister was to present a damning report
on our cervical cancer screen ing programme in New Ze aland, where New Zealand
women had died. But what has been de layed in 2010-11 and 2011-12? These are the
projects: the National Cervical Screeni ng Programme monitoring data—why was it
delayed? Because there are vacancies not fi lled—the development, a review, and the
update of the policies and standards with in the national screening programme; the
monitoring and improvement of the quality of ethnic data on the National Cervical
Screening Programme register; and the high- grade analysis report on women with high-
grade lesions on the National Cervical Scre ening Programme. Those are examples of
some of the 21 projects that have been de layed in the financial year that is under
review—delayed, all of those delayed—because of vacancies because they have to save
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8437
money. Dr Hutchison, you will know that it is  not acceptable to put on hold important
monitoring and evaluation of a programme like the Cervical Screening Programme.
Have we not learnt from what  we did in the past? So when it comes to saying that the
Ministry of Health and the health sector are well managed, they not well managed when
those vital programmes are delayed because the vacancies have not been filled.
Then let us look at “no cuts  to services”. Well, that is blatantly untrue—blatantly
untrue—and anyone who lives in provincial Ne w Zealand in particular will know that
that is untrue. The ministry is required to  save $700 million over 5 years, covering the
financial area we are looking at. So I want to  give you just one little example of a cut in
health services. It comes from a little place called Westport. What has happened in
Westport? They have had no orthopaedic c linics at Buller Hospital for the last 6
months—none. Why? Because there is nobody to  send there. And did the Government
tell the people that the clinics had been cu t? No, it did not. The people of Westport did
not know that their orthopaedic  clinics had been cut. It was withheld from them, and
they found out only when the Westport News—the little newspaper down there—looked
to see what was happening. I could give you many examples. I am sure Minister
Goodhew knows quite a few of them, because quite a lot of them are actually in her area
of responsibility. She shakes he r head, but I am happy to shar e them with her at a later
date.
We also have from this Government what  I call smoke and mirrors. Let us have a
look at the claim that we have more doctors in our health system. That has been claimed
by the Prime Minister and that has been claimed by Tony Ryall. Well, what does the
Association of Salaried Medical Specialis ts say? Of course, members opposite are
scoffing at it. It is a union, I suppose.

items.speaker: Dr Paul Hutchison
items.text: That’s it.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: Of course, I suspect, Dr Hutchison, that you were once a
member of that very good union. It said, at this repeated claim by Minister Ryall that
there are 800 senior doctors, that the doctors  “erupted with disbelief and anger.” The
association said: “this 800 number has been  completely discredi ted and disproven by
using official DHB and government data.”  There are no extra 800 doctors in our
hospitals. That is absolutely wrong. In fact, we have 373 over the 3-year period.
“Hospital specialist numbers have increased but not fast enough to keep up with
increasing demands … Furthermore,” said the Association of Salaried Medical
Specialists, “in the three year period Mr Ke y referred to,”—as has Mr Ryall—“the rate
of hospital specialist increases fell by 25% fr om the three years immediately before his
government took office.” So there you have it. The claims that there are more doctors
and that the Government has not cut the numbers of clinical staff are not to be believed.
We also have the claims that the Governme nt has reduced costs. Well, let us have a
look at some of the costs it has reduced, because when you look at them, you will find
that it might have reduced costs in the mini stry but it has now extended costs into some
new organisations: Health Workforce Ne w Zealand—how many people are employed
there—the Health Quality and Safety Commi ssion, Health Benefits Ltd, and so on. So
when you start to look at the bodgie figures—OK, so they might  not be in the ministry
but they have been moved into other areas. Let us take the Minister’s own office. He has
got only the same number that we had when we there: eight ministerial staff. When we
were there they were paid a total of $349,000 in salaries. What ar e they paid  now, 4
years on? There are $746,000 in salaries in the Minister’s own office. So all this talk
about cutting costs does not apply to the people who work for him, but it certainly
applies to those who work in the home-care s ector, who have not seen increases in their
salaries.
8438 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
So I have to say that when I look at what the ministry said about the health sector and
what it claims were the things that were happening, and when you examine them in just
a little more detail, you will find they are based on smoke and mirrors, some bogus
figures, and fiddling and twiddling with thos e figures. You will hear much more about
the health sector over the next year or so, because at least pe ople know that we are
prepared to stand up for them in places like—

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: It is an absolute pleasure to talk
about the health service review in New Zeal and. Investment over the last year has come
to a record high of $14.1 billi on. I must say that this hea lth system has been better
managed in the last year than ever before, and it is getting better and better. Compared
with the regime under Labour, where over 9 years the Budget went from $6 billion to
$12 billion with no real increase in output, the last 4 years have been quite extraordinary
in their success and should be celebrated.
I want to tell you just for one moment about  the Bay of Plenty Di strict Health Board
financial review. I happened to look at a little paragraph about Te Kaha, a small,
isolated, rural community on the East Coast.  There it reported th at almost 100 percent
of women were having cervica l screening, almost 100 perc ent of women were covered
for breast screening, and almost 100 percent of  children aged 2 were fully immunised,
whereas 5 to 6 years ago that would have been less than 60 percent, if not 50 percent.
That record under National is something th at should be celebrated. One can then
extrapolate it to the record of National ri ght around New Zealand. Whereas 4 or 5 years
ago immunisation coverage was 67 percent under Labour, now it is over 93 percent and
going up. In terms of extra op erations, 35,000 more electives are done per year in New
Zealand than 4 years ago. That has got to be  celebrated. So when we hear Annette King
having the gall to suggest that our health sy stem is not well managed, she ought to look
at herself very carefully in the mirror. She was the very lady who culled up to 30,000
patients off the waiting list and sent them back  to the general practitioners to wallow.
Today, as I said before, there are 35,000—35,000—e xtra electives per year than there
were 4 years ago under that extremely inefficient regime.
I would like to point out that some of the new initiatives over the last year that have
been shored in are incredibly important for sustaining the affordability of our health
services in New Zealand, because right around the world sustaining health services has
become problematic, particularly under th e very, very difficult position after the
financial economic crisis. The initiatives have included cementing in the National
Health Board, which is a national purchasing agency, to ensure that every health dollar
counts. Secondly, Health Workforce New Zealand—and we heard Annette King saying
that the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists was querying the figures of Mr
Ryall and the Prime Minister. Well, the facts are that it is talking about only hospital
doctors, not about doctors in pr imary care. We learn from the Ministry of Health that
the greatest gains in health will come fr om health promotion, disease prevention, and
the integration of primary a nd secondary care. That is where we need the new doctors,
and that is where National has delivered 1,000 new doctors  and 2,000 more nurses, and
has reduced back-office staff by 1,000. That has got to be pretty good. That is the fact of
the matter, and I think Annette King has been very, very selective when she has used—

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: It gives me great pleasure
and pride to rise this evening in the Chamber to talk about the progress that has been
made under this National Government as we address the financial review debate. But I
want to begin by speaking briefly about the previous Opposition speaker, Annette King,
who conducted herself in a way that could be st be described as dealing in personal
attacks on the Minister of Hea lth. She signalled that she wo uld deal in personal attacks
and nameless gossip. Lastly, I think the best descriptor of that member’s claims—and
they have been going on now for a couple of weeks—is simply “wildly imaginative”.
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8439
I want to deal first with the claims sh e has made repeatedly about the Ashburton
Hospital facing cutbacks. This has really pa ined the people of mid-Canterbury, because
they are on edge. They have lost their theatres because of earthquake damage and they
are waiting for the date when these theatres will be rebuilt. The Minister himself has
signalled that they will be rebuilt—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: When? What date?

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: —repeatedly, and in print, I say to the member. The Minister
has signalled that, and the chief executive of th e district health board has said that it
pains him greatly to have to come out agai n and say in the newspaper: “There is no
doubt. Nothing is being cut. Nothing at all. ” The people of mid-Ca nterbury are saying:
“Well, clearly we cannot trust this Labour Party spokesperson, who is simply feeding us
wildly imaginative tales and worrying us abou t our health services.” Absolute bollocks,
it is—absolute bollocks.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Be honest. That’s not what they are saying at all.

items.speaker: Hon JO GOODHEW
items.text: I am finding it really difficu lt to not laugh out loud right
now.
So let us go back to what we saw under the previous Labour Government, and then
move on to the good news under this Nati onal Government. Waste and bureaucracy—
those 30,000 patients who were culled off the waiting lists.  Patients waited for up to 15
weeks for cancer radiation treatment. Many we re sent to Australia. Do we remember
those front-page headlines of those patients who went to Australia? I certainly do. One
story close to my heart was that funding fo r PlunketLine was cut, despite demand from
parents, but National reinstated it. And dur ing all those years the Labour Government
said that rheumatic fever was a priority. Yes, well, we do not really imagine that we saw
any evidence of action on that front.
Just to briefly go over some of the things  that have been achieved—because I think
that members of this Committee, particul arly Opposition members, should remember
that when we talk about numbers, we are not  talking about just figures on a piece of
paper; we are talking about human lives. We are talking about children, we are talking
about mums and dads and babies, and thes e are the very New Zealanders who are
gaining from the National Government’s pe rformance. E-health is an important one.
The Ministry of Health continues to facilitate e-health and we have got 14 district health
boards already transferring patient records electronically to new general practitioners.
But I want to talk about some of those numbers. Shorter waiting times in emergency
departments have risen from 80 percent in  2009 to 94 percent of patients being seen,
treated, or discharged from  hospitals in 6 hours by the end of 2011-12. In terms of
improving access to elective surgery, in 2007-08 there were 118,000 procedures
completed, and in 2011-12 there were a record 154,000. The numbers speak for
themselves. They are real people who had pr ocedures done on them. The percentage of
patients receiving radiation treatment within 4 weeks—100 percent achieved. Members,
that is a stunning achievement, because what that means is people getting treatment for
their cancers. Immunisation of  2-year-olds has risen from  82 percent in 2009-10, when
we started measuring the performance, to 93 percent in the 2011-12 year. It has gone so
well that we have changed the target to the earlier target date of 8 months, meaning
babies’ lives will be save d. Better diabetes and cardi ovascular services—by 2014, 90
percent of the eligible population will have had their cardiovascular risk assessed within
the last 5 years.
We are helping smokers to quit smoking. In 2007 only 18 percent of smokers in
hospitals were offered assistance to quit. By 2011-12, 84.6 percent—
Report noted.
8440 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
Ministry of Education

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I do not know how to turn it on. There
we go—the microphone is workin g. I tell you what, it may be karaoke night here at
Parliament, but there is no one singing fr om the Government’s  song sheet in the
education sector this even ing. Nobody in the education co mmunity is happy with this
National Government tonight, and the people wh o are most upset tonight are the people
who have had debt collectors set on them by Steven Joyce. To rub salt into the wounds,
having not been paid, having been overp aid and underpaid, and having had Steven
Joyce talking to them for maybe 6 week s now about how he was going to get the
problem solved, Steven Joyce’s idea of solv ing the problem has been to stick debt
collectors on to people who have been overpaid.
I am aware of at least one teacher in my  electorate who was overpaid by Novopay in
one fortnight and the fortnight later they were underpaid, and now they have debt
collectors chasing them for the overpayment . They rang me up and they said: “Am I
allowed to send debt collectors back the ot her way, for the underpayment that I got in
the following pay period?”. No, they are not. Are they allowed to send debt collectors to
Steven Joyce to find out where their Kiwi Saver payments have gone—the ones that
have been deducted from their pay cheques but never paid over to the KiwiSaver
providers? Are they allowed to send debt collectors to the Government for that?
Apparently not. What about the child support payments that the Government has taken
but has not paid over? Should they be sending debt collec tors to the Government for
those?

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: The heavies.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: The heavies. That is right. The National Government put heavies
on to people.
It is through no fault of th eir own—bear in mind that thes e people did not claim this
money. They did not take the money. The Government just gave it to them, and in some
cases did not even tell them that it had given it to them. It just put extra money in their
accounts. It was Christmas-time. It is ve ry convenient to put extra money into
someone’s account at Christmas-time. Some people did not even know they had been
overpaid, and suddenly the Government turn s round to them and says: “Oh, pay the
money back. Pay it back right now, and if  you do not pay it back  right now, we are
sending the debt collectors around.” What a disgraceful thing for this Government to do.
It is absolutely offensive that having made  this mistake, having overpaid people who in
good faith have gone out and spent that m oney not knowing they had been overpaid—
for the Government to now put debt collectors on to them is absolutely shameful.
I am not surprised that every member of the National Government in the Chamber is
hanging their head in shame right now and th at they have nothing to say about that,
because Steven Joyce, with 6 weeks in the job to fix Novopay—

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Not at all.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Oh, Maggie Barry is not allowed to comment on this. She was
not underpaid by Novopay, so according to Magg ie Barry’s standing orders she should
just sit there quietly, because she is not allowed to comment on this. But I tell you what.
Steven Joyce said he was going to fix the Novopay problems, and 6 weeks on he is
telling teachers that there are 3 months to  go before the Novopay problems are going to
be solved, and he is still putting the debt co llectors on to people. A competent Minister,
a Minister who was actually getting on top of th is, would have said to the Ministry of

items.speaker: Education
items.text: “Whatever you do, do not put debt co llectors on to people  until we actually
know what is going on—until we actually know whether they have been overpaid or
underpaid, or whether they owe us money, or whether we owe them money.” But, oh
no, that has not stopped Steven Joyce. He ha s still got the debt collectors going to
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8441
people to collect money that they have been overpaid, and that is an absolute disgrace.
But, of course, this Government has absolu te contempt for people working in education
and it has contempt for the New Zealand public.
It is not willing to tell the New Zealand public why Lesley Longstone got a $425,000
payout—oh, no. And when Jonathan Coleman wa s asked about that in question time
today, what was Jonathan Coleman’s response? “Well, how should I know?”. “How
should I know?”—that was his actual answer —“How should I know?”. That was from
the Minister of State Services, the guy who is responsible—the guy who actually signed
the pay cheque, effectively. When asked why it was that she got the $425,000 payout,
his answer was: “Well, how should I know?”. That shows an absolute contempt for the
New Zealand public.
It shows how arrogant this National Government has become. It thinks that it can pay
people large sums of money. It thinks that it can set debt collectors on to other people—
people who are not being paid at all. It can set the debt collectors on to them, but it is
not willing to justify why it is that it paid $425,000 to the outgoing Secretary of
Education, who, incidentally, had been act ually doing the job for only about a year.
That is a phenomenal amount of money. I think it was something like $1,600 a day over
the time that she had actually been in the job that she got paid out.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: How do you get lieu in notice when you’ve quit?

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Yeah, well, I tell you what. It w ould have been a lot cheaper if
Hekia Parata had gone, and something like 60 percent of New Zealanders, when polled
by Television One, said that Hekia Parata  should have been the one who had gone. I
absolutely agree with them on that—I absolutely agree with them on that.
There is no accountability in this Government. All of the decisions, all of the things
that it is blaming Lesley Longstone for, were  all Hekia Parata’s de cisions. It was Hekia
Parata who thought bigger class sizes were  a good idea. It was Hekia Parata who
initiated the school closures in  Christchurch. It was Hekia Parata who decided to close
Salisbury School.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: Look, the Government re alises that the Novopay
issues are hugely frustrating, and we wish to  thank the school sector and administrators
and other staff for their patience and hard work while we address the issues. The issues
are complex—we have not made any secret about that—and there is no quick fix, but
everything is being done to resolve the issues  as quickly as possible. As Steven Joyce
has said, if there was a button to be pushed that could fix it right away, we would have
pushed it. I am looking at you, Mr Hipkins. I am looking at you. OK, we are on watch
now, but, you know, if you want to look in your own mirror back then, with Mr Mallard
and yourself, you put it together in the first place.
The Government measures we put in place  to address the issu e of Novopay include
$5 million under a remediation plan cove ring work on bug fixes and boosting the
number of call centres and data processing sta ff. We have instigated a technical review
to look at the stability of the system and its data, and it is expected to be released in a
couple of weeks after it has gone to Cabine t. A ministerial inqui ry will look into all
aspects of the Novopay project, as it is doing now, from the outset to the present day,
and we are in discussions with the former payroll supplier, Datacom, on a backup plan.
But let us get on to something more gene ral, and that is our overall spend on
education. We are investing $9.6 billion in earl y childhood education and schooling in
2012-13—the most ever. We are wanting to achie ve our goal of getting five out of five
kids achieving, and we want that to happen sooner rather than later. It is all very well to
say that four out of five are doing well, but we are aiming for five out of five. So we are
setting targets for early childhood education and at secondary school level, and we have
8442 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
also set targets of national standards in between. So we  are holding ourselves to
account.
We want to see 98 percent of all school entrants having part icipated in early
childhood education by 2016, and 85 percent of all 18-year-olds having achieved
National Certificate of Educational Achievem ent level 2, or an equivalent education
qualification, by 2017. We are investing $1.4 b illion in early childhood education, the
most ever, of which $47 million is targeted towards priority kids, and we are trying to
engage the kids in M āori and Pasifika communities and in low socio-economic areas
who are currently missing out. It is all very  well to talk about a 95 percent average
overall nationally, but we know that M āori and Pasifika particip ation is significantly
less than that. At the moment around about 70 pe rcent of kids are able to read and write
and do maths at or above their year level, but, overall, boys are trailing girls, and M āori
and Pasifika are trailing everyone.
Having said that, I want to pay credit to  some outstanding teachers in Manurewa.
Manurewa is a vibrant and dive rse community—33 to 34 percent M āori and Pasifika,
20 percent Asian. At decile 2 Redoubt Nort h Primary School with the outstanding work
that Jane Milner and her management team  are doing, their student s are leaving school
with a reading age at, on average, 2 years above their chronological age. That is an
outstanding result. The teachers at Manur ewa High School—in 2011 over 90 percent of
the students in year 13 had level 2 qualific ations. That is an outstanding effort. The
Education Review Office report of Manur ewa Intermediate School—Iain Taylor, the
principal, talked of a principal providing dyna mic, inspirational, professional leadership
for the school, staff, and community. It is a high-trust Education Review Office report.
The school will not be seen again until 4 to 5 years’ time.
Principals like Judd McLauchlan and Shir ley Maihi are doing an outstanding job in
our schools. But what is happening nationa lly? This is not happening all over the
country. We look at our PISA results for 2009. In reading, New Zealand got seventh—
seventh in the world. PISA stands for th e Programme for Inte rnational Students
Assessment and is run by the OECD. If we disaggregate the results, P ākehā are at level
two—second in the world—Asians are seventh, M āori are 34th equal, between Slovenia
and Slovakia, and Pasifika are 44 th, just above Mexico. This is not acceptable, and we
are instituting strategies to improve this. We were last equal—

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I do not know wher e the countries
“Selenia” and “Solakia” are. I suspect there we re some educational failings on that side
of the Chamber at some point.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Charter schools.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: A charter school—that is what  you get from charter schools.
Hekia Parata must go. Either she should be  sacked by the Prime Minister or—what I
would prefer her to do, actua lly—she should take a dignified exit and admit to her
mistakes and step down, because she has cl early failed and failed and failed as a
Minister. It is awful to see it happening to a perfectly nice, perfectly smart woman, but
it is worse to see the impacts on our kids. It does not matter what you might think about
Hekia Parata, at the end of the day it is our kids who suffer from her failures.
The financial review for 2011-12 that was undertaken by the Education and Science
Committee actually sets out those failures in qui te a lot of detail. In fact, the committee
looked at only those failures and wrote a great deal about them. Novopay, the
Christchurch schools restructuring, the class sizes debacle, charter schools—all of these
are set out because those failures were so significant that the Education and Science
Committee highlighted them as particular ar eas of concern, and those are certainly the
areas of concern to the New Zealand public.
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8443
It has already been said, of course, that  the majority of Ne w Zealanders do not
believe that Hekia Parata is competent e nough to be the Minister of Education, and I
agree. We must make sure that we protect  our kids from incompetent Ministers who
have such authority over their lives not onl y now as children in the education system
and over their school but, more important, over how their life trajectory will roll out—
their capacity and their ability to do well in their future.
We need to look, I think, at charter schools,  and that is my particular focus for my
contribution this evening. Charter schools are certainly the best way for the Government
to suck money out of the public school system and hand it on to private hands. Along
with the sale of our public assets, it is just another form of privatisation of public assets,
but it is the privatisa tion of our most critical children ’s institutions—their schools, the
places where they spend most of their time, th e institutions that are the most dedicated
to their well-being and to their future.
The charter schools debate really is a debate about the poor versus the rest, and about
why it is that this National Government is so committed to providing substandard
alternative schools to our most vulnerable learners.
To say that charter schools offer poor pare nts a comparable choice is an insult. John
Banks has always maintained that charte r schools will be an alternative and not
compulsory in any local community, but let us just think about what that means in
practical terms. This means that the ACT Pa rty board, which will decide where charter
schools go, will be running two schools in areas. So where the Government would never
normally build a second school in an area wh ere there is already sufficient capacity or
overcapacity, the ACT Party board responsible  for choosing the ch arter schools will be
doing exactly that, and that ha s very serious financial impl ications, particularly when
you look at the application documents for char ter schools that were released last week.
They stated that these charter schools, th ese private schools, should be funded on the
same basis as brand new State schools—eff ectively, sucking money out of the public
system to establish schools where there is already capacity or overcapacity.
Let us just have another think about wh at that means for Christchurch, for the
Christchurch community, and others around  the country who have had vibrant,
successful schools set for closure so that mone y can be sucked out of them only to be
funnelled into private schools where there is already overcapac ity. Teachers—rich
people do not send their kids to private school s because the teachers are untrained and
unregistered, yet these are the kinds of school s and teachers who will be in front of our
most vulnerable learners under the charter schools model, according to the ACT Party
board.
Why should poorer kids be subject to th is experiment? That  has been the big
question that has certainly been raised in the select committee looking at the legislation.
Where is the evidence th at this will work for these ki ds? In fact, if you look at the
evidence, there is none. The evidence shows that these schools will harm our kids and
certainly not help them. Not only that, but these schools will have 3 years to experiment
on our kids.

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: I am very pleased to speak
in this debate on the Appropriation (2011/12 Financial Review) Bi ll. Can I start by
saying that what our Government is focuse d on in education is actually results and
learning opportunities for children, but also we have demonstrated in our education
budget that we are prepared to invest in th e children of New Zealand. You can see that
with the fact that we are spending $9.6 billion—more than any other Government across
the world from the OECD perspective. Y ou can see that when you look at how much
money we are spending in terms of early ch ildhood education: $1.4 billion, which is the
second-highest in the OECD. What is very cl ear is that when you look at our
8444 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
Government we have absolutely improved funding across four Budgets, and we have
absolutely shown that we can demonstrate we can fund education—more than any other
country in the world in terms of OECD countries.
The second thing I would like to say is that when you actually look at outcomes in
accountability—because we heard tonigh t from Chris Hipkins the word
“accountability”—I want to make it clear that these are the things that actually matter in
terms of accountability. We as a Government  have an early childhood education target,
which is 12,000 more children enrolled. We are making good progress with that: an
additional 2,300 children enro lling last year and a fu rther 2,661 places being made
available. These are the account abilities that New Zealanders really care about—that is,
kids, particularly disadvantaged kids, in  early childhood education. When it comes to
national standards data, we ha ve a target of 85 percent of  18-year-olds having achieved
National Certificate of Educational Achiev ement (NCEA) level 2 or an equivalent
qualification. We hear often from the O pposition about disadvantaged children in New
Zealand. Well, under our Government, M āori and Pacific Island achievement rates for
NCEA level 2 are up. So what you can see on this side of the Chamber is the funding
and the accountability—actual targets, bringing to account both schools and also the
education sector, and saying that if we do not  have targets and if we do not have the
investment, then those children will not ge t the learning opportunities. And when you
look at our record it is very clear.
Tonight we have heard about  infrastructure issues. I am a Minister who is
responsible for property, school transport, and digital literacy, and what I want to say is
that we do have challenges in lifting our school system into the 21 st century. Any
Government at this stage, in my view, w ould have those challenges. We are working
through the Novopay issues. We recognise wh at that means for many teachers around
the country—but to say that we are doing nothing, when we have just put 100 staff into
the clearance unit, and when we have put $5 million in!
Also today in Parliament we heard about other issues that the Opposition is focused
on. Again, we are focused on outcomes and ensuring that we fund our education system.
But we heard about the issue of Lesley Longs tone, and I just want to raise that with
Chris Hipkins, who has been particularly intere sted in that issue. I want to take him
back and remind him of when he was Vi ctoria University of Wellington Students
Association president and what he said back then about a $420,000 package to get rid of
a former vice-chancellor. I quote from the New Zealand Herald in 2000: “Victoria
University Students’ Association president Ch ris Hipkins said … wh ile he did not like
the idea of paying people money to go awa y, it was money well spent.” So all I would
say on this side of the Chamber is that memb ers who are standing up on  that side of the
Chamber and want to raise issues like this ne ed to go back and remember their previous
positions.
We are focused as a Government on educa tion funding. We have actually got results
in terms of what we are spending. We are focused on outcomes in terms of early
childhood education. And what we have from the Opposition is a whole lot of issues
that do not focus on how you raise achie vement for young people in New Zealand,
because the Opposition opposes national stan dards. It has actually also opposed
partnership schools. What I want to say to members across the Chamber is that we have
choice in early childhood educat ion—the private sector is involved in the delivery of
early childhood education centres. I was recentl y in Botany, where I got to see a private
early childhood centre on school grounds. The adva ntage of that is that we get to see
children—and this was supported by the teach ers in that school—r ight throughout their
journey. The private sector is involved in tertiary educatio n and it is involved in early
childhood education, so the fact that we ar e offering some commun ities a bit of choice
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8445
is a great thing, because parents deserve choice  in education. So I think there is a very
clear difference on this side of the Chamber in education between a Government—

items.speaker: TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. Kia ora
tātou katoa. I would like to focus my k ōrero, if I can in my call, on the very last
paragraph of the 2011-12 financial review of the Ministry of  Education—the one that is
entitled “Achieving educational success as M āori”. It is probably timely to do so, given
that there was plenty of international atten tion given to this issue by the United Nations
Committee on the Elimination of R acial Discrimination during its 82 nd session in
Geneva.
On 21 and 22 February this year the Government’s performance in implementing the
international Convention on the Elimination of  All Forms of Racial Discrimination was
considered. One of the key recommendations  from the committee was that “the State
party consider strengthening its special measur es to increase the level of educational
attainment of M āori and Pasifika children, in particular by focusing its measures at
addressing the root causes of absenteeism and the high dropout rates in schools.”
We know that M āori students make up about 22 percent of the total school
population, and that is a very significan t reason on its own, let alone the Treaty
argument that I could suggest, for the protection of  all of our taonga, with one of them
being tamariki, the upholding of article 3 relating to citizenship rights, and the
requirement of article 1 for an effective and responsible Government.
So it is pleasing to see in New Zealand’s report to the United Nations that support
from family and wh ānau can influence educational achievement. Wh ānau are more
likely to feel alienated from the mainstr eam schooling system and are less likely to
engage with educators, due to their own negative educati onal experiences of schooling,
so engaging wh ānau and parents in ways that support children’s learning is definitely a
priority, as I understand it, for the Government, and the M āori Party absolutely supports
that.
The Government report also recognises the persistence of inequalities that face Māori
and Pasifika in education, as spoken to by th e Hon Nikki Kaye, and that it is essential
for the future of New Zealand that these inequalities be addressed. That, I hope, is going
to be the focus in the next couple of years left in this term.
So with all that good intent there are some things that we need to address. It is pretty
disheartening that a few pages on from the refe rence that I made earlier we read that 74
percent of European student s leave school with National Certificate of Educational
Achievement level 2 or above, and less than half of Māori students—47.8 percent, to be
precise—enjoy that same status. Under those circumstances we have got a lot of work to
do still, and a lot of things are still to come. There are still concerning trends with regard
to absenteeism, including the above-average rates of truancy, absenteeism, and early
departure from the school system, very often without any qualifications at all.
I want to come back to the financial review  in which the ministry told the Education
and Science Committee that its approach requires schools to engage with wh ānau in
ways that are culturally appropriate by adopti ng the culture of the learner and reflecting
it back to the school. It is also committed, so says the report, to helping boards of
trustees in schools in implementing that vision.
Under those circumstances we need to know then how effec tively and actively
Tātaiako, the guidelines on cultural competen cy, is being implemented. This is a
programme that was developed thr ough the relationship between the M āori Party and
the National Party. It has plenty going for it. It was developed over a year ago, and yet
we still need to have the full implementation of that particular programme.
To highlight the whole involvement of whānau within the education system I want to
bring to the attention of the Committee one particular kura called Te Pihipihinga
8446 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
Kākano Mai i Rangiātea Kura Kaupapa Māori. It is located in New Plymouth. It was the
kura that my wife and I were associated with  when it first started. It celebrated 20 years
last year. Like many other kura, what came a bout was that the first 2 years of that kura
were very much, in fact, without Govern ment funding. It did not have any. The wh ānau
fund-raised to keep the school going. I remember folding newspapers, the Taranaki
Daily News  in New Plymouth, and getting those re ady to be dispersed, to try to get
money to pay our teachers.
I think that shows just how much dedication wh ānau are prepared to give towards
providing total immersion educa tion for their tamariki. We must continue to attempt to
mobilise whānau, and not to make them work just simply to keep the kura alive. But, in
fact, at the end of the day it is about improving Māori education.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): Thank you very much. I will just
project my voice. Why not? Let us just talk out  loud. It was great to hear what we have
heard from the M āori Party, and I think it will be very  pleased to hear the work that is
happening around the partnership schools, whic h is going to allow our families to
engage. I raise a point of order, Mr Chairperson. Do I need the microphone?

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Yes. You are not going out over the networks.
SIMON O’CONNOR : We will have to start again. Thank you, Mr Chair. To the
World Wide Web listening in, I am now online. I think the M āori Party will be pleased,
and this Committee should be too, because w ith partnership schools we have heard in
select committee meeting after select committee meeting wh ānau, family from Pasifika
communities and M āori communities saying: “We want this.” That puts the left in a
terrible, terrible bind. To someone like me, it is quite funny to wa tch, but they said,
person after person, whānau after whānau, that they want this opportunity. I think that is
really important to hear.
One of the things about education is the importance of having a broad education, so I
actually want to turn the attention back to the tertiary sector. I noted that the Listener
recently picked up on a number of us, including the Minister, who were at the O-Weeks.
The National Party was certainly out in force in the O-Weeks, supporting our young
people, who have been signing up hundred s of people who are committed to that
brighter future, which National is interested in. One of the things that I have found, as
someone who goes through the tertiary sector quite frequently and not just in O-Weeks,
is the optimism we have in our young people.  Arguably some of that can be accounted
for by the successes that this National Government has had.
So I want to pick up and continue—broa den, if you will—what the Minister was
outlining earlier around successes in education, to talk about the successes in the tertiary
sector. Between 2008 and 2011 course completion rates in New Zealand increased from
76 percent to 82 percent, and qualification completion rates from 64 percent to 71
percent. These are undeniable facts and realit ies. This has been the commitment of the
National Government from 2008, and we have s een an increase in completion rates. We
have seen an increase in qualification rates—measurable success in the tertiary sector.
We have seen with student loan repayments  that these have increased by 11 percent.
The initiatives that this Government has put in are breeding success—tangible,
measurable success. The scientific method, if you will: you can test it,  you can show it,
you can prove it, and that is what the National Party is doing.
We have seen that the cost to the New Zealand taxpayer, to the Crown, has come
down. It used to be 47c, before this Government took power, for every $1 lent. That was
the cost of the student loan scheme. Now it is down to 39c—tangible, real, visible facts
around what this Government has achiev ed. We know now too there are 1,000 more
engineering places in our universities and our institutes of technology in 2013. We are
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8447
on track to make sure we are produci ng an extra 500—that is 500—engineering
graduates by 2017. This is incredibly important.
I had the great privilege last week of going out to an amazing New Zealand company
called Altitude Aerospace Interiors, which is le ading the way in interi or design. It is an
excellent, excellent company—hey, I can turn right around with this microphone; this is
great—doing amazing work with aircraft engi neering designs. The company is crying
out for further engineering graduates from this country, and it wants them. It knows that
graduates from the likes of the University of  Auckland are fantastic graduates, as they
are from other institutions throughout New Zealand. This Government has heard that
cry and is putting money where its mouth is.
I have had a lot of—again, I have mentione d it in this Chamber before—friends and
others in my electorate talking around student allowa nces and so forth, around the
changes there. We have seen the spending on student allowances. Context is important.
In any discussion like this we can pick up on absolute particulars and exceptions and try
to argue from it, but the context is important. Our expenditure has increased
significantly. In 2007 and 2008 the Crown spent about $385 million in student
allowances. In the last year that was $620 million. Whether we like it or not, this is
simply not sustainable. So this Government has worked to promote an allowance system
that focuses on giving that opportunity to those in low-income families in early years of
study, and I think, rightly, that these are things we can be proud of.
Report noted.
Ministry of Pacific Island Affairs

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I rise and I will wait for the microphone. I am proud
to take a call here on behalf of the Government to talk about the Ministry of Pacific
Island Affairs. I am somewhat disappoint ed, though, that other members of other
parties, such as the Labour Party spokesperson for Pacific Island affairs, are not taking a
call. Mr Kris Faafoi is not taking the call.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: How do you know?

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: That indicates to us quite clea rly they are saving their calls for
other things that they deem as being important. But for this Government we deem the
Ministry of Pacific Island Affairs and our Pasifika community to be of absolute
importance, hence the reason why we ar e taking a call. Miss Moroney, if you are
interested, if it is important to you, take a call. The Ministry  of Pacific Island Affairs is
the premier adviser on policies and interven tions to promote the social and economic
well-being of our Pacific pe oples of New Zealand. It is  around policy advice. It is
monitoring, communication, and engagement.
Our Pasifika communities are sick and tir ed of being labelled impoverished and
underprivileged. A good example of that is that some 4 weeks ago over in Porirua—that
is right, in the Mana area of Mr Faafoi —there were some young people talking about
Pasifika success in education. This is what they said. An 18-year-old Samoan girl stood
up and said this: “I am sick of being called underpr ivileged. I am sick of being called
impoverished.” This is what she said: “I am privileged because my parents support me.
They encourage me. They allow me to go into education, and this year I am at Victoria
University. If I get a B averag e, I will then be able to obt ain my scholarship to head
over to Scotland to Dame Kiri Te Kanawa’s college over there and to be a world-class
opera singer.” There were two young twins who turned up. They go to St Patrick’s

items.speaker: College. This is what they said
items.text: “We’re si ck of being called underprivileged. We as
Pasifika are successful, and th is is what we’re doing in ed ucation: dream, believe, and
achieve.” They are currently the Australasian 100 and 200-metre champions.
8448 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
This Government is about promoting success, not continua lly putting down our
Pasifika communities. I went to consultati ons of the Child Poverty Action Group with
Dr Airini. Dr Airini said th at in Napier and in Hawke’ s Bay the Pasifika community
said this: ‘Stop those people saying that we’re impoverished. Stop them using us as their
poverty statistics. Why? Because we are su ccessful. Why? Because we know we are
succeeding.” We are starting to see this under th is Government. So here is some of the
vision of successful Pasifika that is coming through.
The annual report of the Ministry of Pacific Island Affairs says that the ministry was
“in much better shape to catalyse positive change.”—positive change—for a very small
ministry punching above its weight. Why? B ecause for Pasifika communities, we know
that is what we are about, despite the fact th at the ministry has b een without the benefit
of any increase in funding or staffing for seve ral years. And may I say this—and it is to
the shame of the former Labour Government. The Minister of Pacific Island Affairs and
its portfolio was established in 1984. In fact, Richard Prebble was the first Minister. The
ministry began in 1990. From that time on, ne ver has that portfolio been out of Cabinet
except under a Labour Government. So how important is the Pasifika community to that
party? I tell you what—it is not important, because no one has taken a call. Maybe Mr
Faafoi, who has just entered the Chamber, may take a call to talk about what success
you have had. But this is what we are doin g—this is what we are doing. Education,
youth skills, and employment are very im portant. Our young Pasifika community is
important to us.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: What about the unemployment rate for Pasifika?

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Mr Faafoi will always talk about the unemployment rate, but
what he does not talk about is the alternatives—what we are doing and the difference
that we are making. [Interruption] Yes, they are excited now. Why? They may just take
a call. If it is important, take a call. If it is important, stand up and take a call. Tell us
what you have been doing. This Governme nt is making a difference through the
Ministry of Pacific Island Affairs.
In regard to housing we are seeing im proving economic well-being and living
standards with housing alternatives through the Ministry of Pacific Island Affairs. What
is it? It is the Tongan churches and th e Tongan communities up in Auckland getting
$4.3 million for alternatives to social housi ng. Why? Because what this Government
wants is for our Pasifika communities to  have opportunities to develop their own
solutions. That is the difference that this  Government is making to our Pasifika
communities. Stop labelling them as und erprivileged. Stop labelling them as
impoverished. You do no service to our commun ities. It is time to stop. If you have got
any alternative, then give us the soluti ons that make a difference. Under this
Government, we have increased early chil dhood education partic ipation. U nder this
Government, we are addressing all the social health issues, such as rheumatic fever.
That is what this Government is doing.
Report noted.
Ministry of Social Development

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: It is my pleasure to have an opportunity to speak
briefly to the Ministry of Social Developmen t financial review. I just have to say that
social development is picking up the hard end of the rhetoric that we heard from that
side of the Chamber just now. I have to sa y to that member who just took his seat,
Alfred Ngaro, that to block your ears, close your eyes, and pretend that everything is
fine is to do a complete disservice to th e community that that member purports to
represent. So while that member wa s sitting there and saying “Don’t call us
underprivileged.”, he was bloc king his ears to the fact th at there is 16 percent
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8449
unemployment among the Pasifika community right now. He was claiming that the
Government has done something on behalf of  Pasifika people whilst at the same time
ignoring the decline of Pasifika languages in  this country; whils t at the same time
allowing our early childhood education system to be deprived of basic materials for
Pasifika languages. That, apparently, is what a Government th at supports Pasifika
people does. Well, I would like to see what a Government that does not support Pasifika
people does.
No one is arguing that we s hould sit here and not have as piration on be half of our
Pasifika community. Of course we should, but aspiration starts with opportunity, I
would say to that member—and where is the opportunity for that community right now?
Where is the opportunity for that young woman to get the future that she wants when
social mobility under this Government is as s hocking as it has ever been in the history
of New Zealand? The gap between rich and poor in this country is wider than it has ever
been. You tell me how the Pasifika community, the M āori community, or any
community under those circumstances has the ability to move—the social mobility—
that New Zealand prides itself on when gaps like that exist. We have all the research
and the evidence in the world to back up what we are saying on this side of the
Chamber—that if you want to support commu nities and social cohesion, one of the
things you need to be mindful of is the growing gap between the rich and the poor.
That side of the Chamber might be quite co ntent for the Don Elders of this world to
sit at home earning a bucketload of money for doing absolutely nothing while solo
parents in this country struggle on $293 a week, raising child ren. That might be
absolutely fine on that side of the Chamber,  but on this side of the Chamber we have a
little more aspiration for the people of New Zealand. It matters to us that that gap exists,
because of what it means to the community. If we want to look at what is happening
within social development we should start with inequality. We should start with the
plight of the unemployed and that 16 percen t of the Pasifika community who cannot get
work. We should start with the increasing cost  of living, and the fact that the material
deprivation in this country under that Government has gone fr om 15 percent to 21
percent. That is not just a st atistic; those are the people who cannot afford to go to the
doctor, cannot afford to send their kids on school trips so that they can get the same
opportunities as everyone else, a nd cannot pick up their prescr iptions. It is meaningful
stuff; it is not just rhetoric. It is the stuff that matters to whether or not families can get
ahead and do what that side of the Comm ittee claims it wants families to do, but in
reality it just cannot—not under this Government.
It is also about what is going on for the kids  in this country. As much as we stand up
in this House and say that everything is fine —well, at least they do on that side of the
House—the statistics say something else . The 270,000 kids living in poverty do not
have a choice to stand up and make all the cl aims that that side of the House seems
willing to sit back on. They are the ones who are going to suffer if we do not invest in
the early years. They are the ones who not  only suffer the health effects of poverty
down the track but suffer the edu cational effects as well. If this Government wanted to
make a difference to those kids, it would be addressi ng child poverty. Government
members can talk about targets as much as th ey like. They talk about them in education
until the cows come home, but will they set a target on poverty? Will they set a target
on poverty? They will not even agree to measure it. They will not even agree on what a
measure is, even though the international comm unity is pretty clear on it, and that is
because they have no intention of closing that gap. They have no intention of addressing
child poverty in this country, and until they do, as far as I am concerned, they have no
intention of fulfilling the potential of the poor est kids in this country—because that is
8450 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
what it will take. You can talk about parent al responsibility all you like but until those
families have the tools they need, they will not succeed.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is a privilege and an
honour to speak in this debate on the fina ncial review of the Ministry of Social
Development. Before I talk about the subs tantive achievements th at this Government
has done in this portfolio area, I just want to say to the member who just spoke, Jacinda
Ardern, that if that member thinks that turning up to Pasifika Festival on a Saturday
afternoon gives her an insight into Pasifika children and the vulnerabilities that they
have and their families have, then she is mist aken. She is mistaken if she thinks that
turning up to the Grey Lynn fes tival gives her some sort of  insight into how Pasifika
people are living in this country.
It was a disgrace to hear that memb er talk about how Labour members are
aspirational, and yet they deny the fact that National Certificate of Educational
Achievement levels 1, 2, and 3 for Pasifika  people have improved over the last 12
months. They deny the fact th at pass rates for Pasifika people inside our tertiary
education institutions are going up. They deny the fact that the number of people
employed in this country of Pasifika des cent has gone up under th is Government. So
they might want to deny those facts, but certainly I will not.
It is not about rich and poor, but I will tell you what it is about. It is about the
Ministry of Social Development. I want to  thank the Minister, the Hon Paula Bennett,
for the work, the bold leadership, and the hard  work that she has put in to bring about
the reforms in this country. We all know about the investment approach. We know
about budgeting services and the investment that we are putting up front into vulnerable
families, parenting services, wraparound services, budgeting services—those are the
things that matter to people who are in need.
We know about our other welfare reforms in  terms of social obligations: the re-
categorisation of unemployment benefit as well as work te sting and testing for those
who are on drugs and want to work. But I want to talk about the 9,300 staff of the
Ministry of Social Development who are out  there, many of them on the front line,
dealing with vulnerable families and ch ildren—1.6 million people whom they are
servicing every day. It is massive. In terms of its scope, this ministry deals with the care
and protection of vulnerable children. It deals with in come support, superannuation
services, and funding for comm unity service providers. This  Government believes that
pushing our services out into the community, just as the M āori Party does through
