Whānau Ora—[Interruption] Louisa Wall knows this because she is a supporter of these
types of services, community services that actually interact with our wh ānau and our
families out in the community. Those are the sorts of services that our communities are
demanding.
This budget is one-third of the total Government spending across the whole
Government portfolio. It is $21 billion a year, so this is not to be underestimated in
terms of its importance. One of the things th at I think has worked is certainly Future
Focus, which was introduced in  2010 as a precursor to thos e reforms that I have just
spoken about. What it did was that it allowe d unemployment beneficiaries to reapply if
they remained on the benefit for over 12 months. It also provided for domestic purposes
benefit recipients with children over 6 to look for part-time work. That is a particularly
important reform, because what we are seeing is that when solo parents see their kids
going out into school, they are able to get part-time work. They are able to get part-time
jobs. It is good for them, it is good for their kids, it is good for our communities, and it
is good for our economy.
What has happened under these reforms is that we have saved taxpayers $74 million
since these reforms were put in place. That is  $74 million. That is nothing to be sniffled
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8451
at. That will be applied to services that  are needed in our co mmunities. What it has
meant is that 21,400 people have left the une mployment benefit as  a result of this
policy, and half of those did not actually comp lete the reapplication form that was part
of our reforms.
I support the reforms that we have done ove r the last 4 years in Government. They
have made a huge difference to the people in our communities. They have serviced a lot
of families that have been in need during th is global financial crisis. It has meant that
they are able to go out and get jobs—

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Mr Chair—can you hear me ? Oh, now it is working.
Fantastic. I would like to firs t of all start off by congratulat ing the Minister for Social
Development, the Hon Paula Bennett, on the i mmense amount of work that she does in
this very, very difficult and challenging area. This particular portfolio—as my colleague
Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, who is the chair of the Social Services Committee, has
mentioned—through the Ministry of Social  Development administers around $21
billion a year. It is the larges t of the Government’s spending. It is actually a third of all
Government expenditure and provides services to more than 1.6 million people. The
range of work that is actually carried out by the ministry is really huge and varied, from
the care and protection of vul nerable children to student allowances and fees, so the
workload is actually quite humongous.
I want to talk a little bit about the Government’s Children’s Action Plan, because I
know that everyone around this Chamber car es about our vulnerable children. Our
children mean so much to us. This Govern ment’s Children’s Action Plan is such a
positive initiative that targets support and services to our most vulnerable children
through more than 30 new initiatives introduc ed in the White Paper for Vulnerable
Children. These initiatives are the result of months of research, discussions, and policy
development. There were, roughly, around 10,000 submissions sent in on the Green
Paper for Vulnerable Children. I went to some of these meetings, and there were lots of
heated and vibrant discussions around the green paper, as  well as consultation with key
experts in health, justice, education, and so cial services, and what international best
practices show keeps children safe from ha rm. As part of a Government team that
actually went right around the country to talk about the White Paper for Vulnerable
Children, I was very heartened by talking to the people in the districts, actually, because
every time I met people talking about the white paper, they were passionate. They were
very positive about doing some thing. I guess it is because they  are sickened by the fact
that, you know, we have not done so well in terms of neglected ch ildren. Some of the
children have been so abused in this country, and we should be ashamed. This
Government is doing something about it.
It is time for fundamental change, and this Government is doing that through the
Children’s Action Plan. The white paper a nd the Children’s Ac tion Plan go beyond
politics. They are not only for the generation of children who are growing up now. They
are for the generations of children to come. The Children’s Action Plan will be the basis
of the most significant advancement in child protection that this country has seen. It
gives us clear, easy direction on how our child protection system will be reformed and
on the new measures that will be implemented over the next 10 years.
Many people are concerned about children but  are reluctant to call Child, Youth and
Family about their concerns. The new Child Protect line will be the first point of contact
to call to ensure the right response. The Vu lnerable Kids Information System will be set
up to hold information on children in one place, so that relevant professionals who work
with children will be able to access all the information from  one place. Would it not be
fantastic if teachers who deal with childre n and notice that children are being abused
can actually pick up information and realise that that child has been to hospital with
8452 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
broken bones, has been abused, and has been beaten, and that people can take action as
a result of this shared information? It is great to see the new children’s teams, which are
going to be created right acro ss Government agencies, working together with regional
directors to coordinate locally the responses to individual lives. This regional ownership
of the teams is a crucial element in this tria l, because the evidence is that local solutions
work best to meet local needs.
We are responsible for the welfare and well-being of our children. The Government’s
Children’s Action Plan will mean tough new restrictions for abusers through child abuse
prevention orders that will allow judges to stop child abusers from—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order! Is the member
seeking another call? No. Well, sit down then, if you are finished.
Report noted.
Ministry of Defence

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: What the review of the Defence Force at
the Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Committee showed was that the last year, under
the stewardship of Minister Jonathan Co leman, was the worst year in the modern
history of the New Zealand Defence Force. There is plummeting morale. The morale in
the Defence Force crashed from 58 per cent, when Minister Coleman and his
Government took over, to 35 percent—the lowe st morale rate in the history of the
survey of the Defence Force, under Minister  Coleman. And then there was the question
of attrition, which soared to 21 percent. That is more than one in five of our most skilled
and our most experienced members of the De fence Force quitting in 1 year. And then
look at the numbers of the Defence For ce. They crashed by over 1,000 in 1 year.
Minister Coleman—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Just to remind the member, we are
actually not on the New Zealand Defence Force. We are on the ministry—[Interruption]
Order! We are on the Ministry of Defence. The next appropriation is the Defence Force.
So if the member—[ Interruption] Order! I am on my feet . We are focusing on the
Ministry of Defence, so if you want to fo cus on that—otherwise you will have to wait.
What you are talking about is the New Zealand Defence Force.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Well, Mr Chairperson, the Ministry of Defence has responsibility
for policy governing the Defence Force, and I am  sure that the Mini stry of Defence is
utterly shattered that the po licy that it set out cannot be carried out by the New Zealand
Defence Force, because it is no longer cap able of doing so. The Minister of Defence
pretends that there is capability to carry out  the policy of the Ministry of Defence. That
is denied by the Auditor-General. The Audito r-General says that there has been damage
done to the Defence Force, and there is reduced capability. Minister, how can you say
that there is no reduced capability wh en the Auditor-General contradicts you
absolutely? The Ministry of Defence relies on having a Defence Fo rce to carry out the
policy. Yet in a recent court of inquiry into the death of Corporal Douglas Hughes that
court of inquiry found that the Defence Fo rce was unable to simultaneously carry out
the tasks required of it by the New Zeal and Government—it could not sustain the
Rugby World Cup at the same time as sending a force on deployment to Afghanistan. In
fact, the Minister should explain why it was that that force went there with 40 percent
less training than was required. The warrant officer said that—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Jonathan Coleman
items.text: I raise a point of  order, Mr Chairperson. I would just
like to reiterate your point for the second time in less than 5 minutes that Mr Goff is on
the wrong vote.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! I will determine that.
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8453

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: The Minister did pathetically at question time and he will not do
any better now. What the Minister needs to understand is that there is no point in having
a Ministry of Defence unless it has got the capability to carry out the policies that are set
out there. What that report showed was that  we were putting our people at risk by not
adequately preparing them for the deployment. When a warrant officer of the New
Zealand Army says our people are not prepar ed but it has no choice but to send them,
that is an indictment on the New Zealand Government. The main responsibility of any
Government deploying people overseas in pur suit of Defence Force and Ministry of
Defence policy is to keep our people safe . How can you keep people safe when you cut
their training? You cut their training, for example, in terms of management of stress and
identification of stress.
Is it any wonder that the family of Co rporal Douglas Hughes said that this
Government should hold an inquest, because there were things sadly lacking in the
preparation of our people before they went in to a zone where their lives were at risk?
The New Zealand Ministry of Defence has to have a Defence Force that is capable of
carrying out its policy. It does not have that when the attrition in the Defence Force is so
great that 1,000 people leave, and we cannot ev en put our ships to s ea. The Ministry of
Defence acquired new ships for the Defence Force. Brand new inshore patrol vessels,
acquired by the Ministry of Defe nce, sit idle at the wharf in the Minister of Defence’s
electorate because they cannot be put to sea,  because they do not have the personnel to
sail them. How humiliating that we have to  go to the Australian Defence Force to
borrow Australian sailors to put our ships at sea. Minister, you have failed the New
Zealand Defence Force and the Ministry of Defence. You have no right to hold that
position. You should resign.
Report noted.
New Zealand Defence Force

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I want to begin—and I
want to do it, actually, on Mr Goff’s behalf  as well, because I know he would intend
this to be done—by paying trib ute to our service people in the New Zealand Defence
Force. They have served very, very brav ely over many, many year s, and who are just
coming out of three very stressful and dangerous deployment s in Afghanistan—
Afghanistan, where 10 New Zealand Defence Force personnel gave their lives—East
Timor, and the Solomon Islands, where our people have served w ith distinction. My
first priority as Minister of Defence is to support our people overseas. They face
extremely dangerous circumstances, and I think the start of any speech on defence
should be to graciously acknowledge the risks that our people face in the name of the
New Zealand public.
I just need to say, Mr Goff, that that speech was an absolute unpatriotic disgrace—an
unpatriotic disgrace. When I go around New Z ealand Defence Force bases, what they
say to me is that they are absolutely fed up with traitors like Phil Goff talking down the
morale of the New Zealand Defence Force. Mr Goff—the one thing I know about him is
he will constantly misrepresent the facts. I have been in Parliament for 7 years. My
experience of that man, when he was a Minister and now as the Opposition defence
spokesman, is that he will constantly misreprese nt the facts. I think it is a total disgrace
that rather than actually taking the opportunity  to praise our people, he went on to trash
our Defence Force. Actually, Mr Goff asked whether morale has ever been lower. I can
say that it has, Mr Goff—it was lower when  you were Minister of Defence. I can say
today that four out of five New Zealand De fence Force personnel rate their morale as
very good or better—four out of five. I can say that if you had 80 percent of people in
8454 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
the Labour Party rating their morale as very good or better, you would be, frankly,
totally shocked.
So what I can say, Mr Goff, is we need people, New Zealanders from across the
House—and I am sure there will be many pe ople in the Labour Pa rty who will agree—
who will back our people, and who will sa y our Defence Force people are doing a good
job. It is no good for Mr Goff to constantly harangue me with meaningless interjections,
with drivel. As Charles Chauvel said, Mr Goff is the enemy within. He is the enemy
within the Labour Party and, frankly, he is  the enemy within for the New Zealand
Defence Force, because he does not back ou r troops. I was just li stening to this man
actually using the court of inquiry into a brave New Zealand soldier who died in
Afghanistan to make a political point. That , Mr Goff, is a complete disgrace because
you have broken a suppression order—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Stop the hypocrisy and answer the question.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I invite you to go out into the foyer and say that
again, because I do not think you would have the balls to  do it. I do not think you
would, because Mr Goff is all talk but no ac tion. He has been here tonight lying and
misrepresenting—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Minister, there is a Standing Order
that says that you cannot say that a member is lying. I know this is a robust debate, but I
will just ask the Minister to be very careful about that, and also some of the language.

items.speaker: Jami-Lee Ross
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Ch airperson. There are also Standing
Orders about a constant barrage of interjections.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, I will be the judge of that.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Anyway, I think we have had enough on that
particular topic.
What I do want to say is that when you look at the savings progr amme that we have
instituted across the New Zealand Defence For ce, it is not something that is unique to
New Zealand. If you go overseas and you talk to  the French, you talk to the British, or
you talk to the Americans, defence force refo rm is the response to  the global financial
crisis. It is an absolute fact. The New Zealand Defence Force has the best reform
programme across the New Zealand Public Service. Last year—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Come on—the highest attrition rate across the Public Service.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: —across defence we saved $140 million, and
that is quite remarkable. Mr Goff speaks about attrition. Well, I can say—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Yeah, if you speak of not paying the Defence Force a pay rise for 4½
years.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Well, if you would list en for a moment: the
attrition rate today is 17 percent. It was 19 percent in 2001 under Labour. That is a fact.
Army attrition is less than it was in 2005, when Phil Goff was Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: That’s not true. That’s a lie.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Air force attrition is less than half of the 24
percent reached in February 2002.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! I have just br ought the Minister to
account for using the word “lie”, and the same  applies on this side. Now it is even, so
we are starting off again. Sixteen seconds remain for the Minister.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: In summary, I back our personnel. They do an
excellent job. I call on Labour to back them as well. Our people need support. They take
massive risks. We have lost 10 people in  Afghanistan. Phil Goff needs to man up, stop
trashing the Defence Force, and back our people.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: It is a great pleasure to speak on the
financial review of the New Zealand Defen ce Force. Indeed, I must say that I was
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8455
appalled to hear that old neck-bulging, sh roud-waving revisitation from Phil Goff that
we got once again, which demonstrates his ab solute lack of integrity. But I too would
like to join my colleague the Hon Jonathan Coleman—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! I know this is a pretty robust debate,
but you cannot say that a member does not have integrity.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Tell the truth, Paul.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: I withdraw that. He might—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! I am going to ask the member to
stand and withdraw and apologise for that comment. You cannot say: “Tell the truth.”

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: I withdraw and apologise.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: I withdraw that comment about him not having any—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, no. No comment about my ruling.
Now you had better withdraw that comment.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: Of course, Mr Chairman. I withdraw.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Let us get on with it.

items.speaker: Dr PAUL HUTCHISON
items.text: I too would like to join th e Hon Jonathan Coleman in
paying tribute to our defence forces and th e incredible work they do, not only in the
active field, in which they have had many very important missions over the last few
years, but also in the field of peacekeeping, in the field of aid throughout the Pacific,
and, of course, in the field of civil service, where they have shown incredible dedication
and commitment down in Christchurch over the last few years.
We heard from Phil Goff that he considered there were problems of morale. That
does seem a little rich when we look back to what happened under his watch, when he
gutted the air combat wing in New Zealand and then said, just prior to the 2005
election, with Dr Cullen that  he would be able to sell  off that whole wing at a
reasonable price, and nothing happened. Not one thing happened, until finally the
National Government has recently been able to sell off those planes.
But the other issue that I think is really important to point out, if we are talking about
management, is that of the light armoured vehicles that were purchased under Phil Goff
to the tune of $100 million or more, and very many of them were absolutely irrelevant
and redundant and have not been used to this day. Th at is the sort of  management that
former Minister Phil Goff had over those 9 disgraceful years.
I would agree with Minister Coleman when he says that the saving and investment
programme has shown some very positive results.  In fact, the very fact that we had to
undergo a white paper in defence was due to the abysmal mismanagement under the 9
long years of Labour. But it has had some very positive results. The New Zealand
Defence Force has achieved savings of more  than $150 million over the last year, with
an aim of $350 million to $450 million over th e next few years. But every dollar saved
has been reinvested back into front-line capabilities. And despite the tight fiscal
constraints, these savings have funded a significant pay increase right throughout the
forces, and that has been extremely well received.
To go on to morale and attrition, as I said before, the changes needed were as a result
of the mismanagement of Labour over many y ears. We had the attrition rate back in
2001 that the Minister mentioned. But what we do know is that over each one of the last
three quarters morale has improved. Four in every five of our peopl e indicate they do
not have an issue with their morale, and nearly four in ev ery five of our people express
satisfaction with their job. Morale was not measured until 2003, so it certainly does not
cover the air combat capability review that occurred under the Labour Government. It is
absolutely relevant to note that those who feel committed to the Defence Force
outstrip—
Report noted.

New Zealand Police

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: The Minister of Poli ce, Anne Tolley, is
committed to New Zealanders being able to feel safe in their homes and feel safe in
their communities. National is also committed to providing better public services, so
this Government has set Public Service target s in the fight against crime. We want to
reduce overall crime rates by 15 percent, we want to reduce violent crime by 20 percent,
and we want to reduce youth crime by 5 pe rcent by 2017. In order to achieve these
targets the police are getting the tools they need to spend more time on crime prevention
and less time on paperwork.
Police now have new ways of working, with the Prevention First and Policing
Excellence programmes. Prevention First is the operating strategy for the New Zealand
Police that puts prevention at the forefront of the organisation and puts victims at the
centre. The strategy focuses on targeted  policy aimed at reducing reoffending and
reducing victimisation. Gone are the days when  a couple of cops w ould drive out of the
cop station and toss a coin to d ecide whether to turn left or to turn right to proceed with
their night’s work. Prevention First requires police to work with community services
and with community networks to protect vulne rable people, to act with urgency against
priority and prolific offenders, and to use innovative and practical solutions to manage
crime hot spots wherever they occur.
Last year several of us saw for ourselves  the actions of Coun ties Manukau police in
managing gangs in neighbourhoods where the shopping centre was besieged by a gang
in this street and another gang in this street  and yet another gang in  another street, with
community members and kids wanting to acces s the local dairy having to first negotiate
those warring gangs. Counties Manukau police,  with their Prevention First strategy,
take that issue very seriously. Together w ith the local community and networks, they
have now made that particular corner of Auckland safe again for those people who live
there and make that neighbourhood their hom e. We also saw Counties Manukau police
do a tin can collection so that they could de liver food to local kids because it was the
school holidays and the police knew that hungry kids were kids who tended to get into
trouble. That approach is part of Policing Ex cellence, a series of initiatives that will
enable the Police Commissioner to better manage crime and offending within New
Zealand.
Front-line police patrols have risen by 70 pe rcent in the last year. That is more
officers on the beat being deployed more stra tegically in areas at times when police
know there is a greater risk of crime taking place. Police are now trialling the use of
smartphones and tablets so that they can  access, input, and share information
immediately, without having to travel back to  the station to access databases or to write
reports. That not only provides for efficiency  within the New Zealand Police but also
enhances the safety for our New Zealand Police as they are able to quickly and
efficiently access information that they may need about an alleged offender whom they
are dealing with out on the stre et. So the police will be able to provide a better, more
efficient, and more visible service to the public.
Offenders, I might suggest, are now on no tice. There are 600 more police on the
front line, focused on having the right people in  the right place and at the right time to
prevent crime. Thanks to the work of the Minister, the Police Commissioner, and
serving officers, we now have the lowest crime rate in 30 years, and we are on track to
achieving those Public Service targets. In th e past 2 fiscal years we have seen crime
rates drop by 5.6 percent and 7 percent respectively. Thank you.

Department of Corrections

items.speaker: MARK MITCHELL
items.text: It is an honour to get up and speak in
support of the Department of Corrections. I would like to just briefly touch on two
areas. Tonight in the Chamber we have spoken a fair bit about youth and education, so I
would like to talk about the programme that  is being implemented by Minister Tolley,
and, if I get time, I would also like to touch on Serco. The mix of public and private
sectors working together is, I think, going to be a very successful model for New
Zealand, for the Department of Corrections, fo r the prisoners, and, of course, for our
taxpayers, because we are going to see a great mix of ideas and exchange of information
between a very good private sector compan y and a very good and efficient Public
Service.
Corrections Minister Anne Tolley has officially opened a young offenders unit at the
Hawke’s Bay Regional Prison that will delive r a much more structured approach to
dealing with young prisoners. The under-20-year-olds will be re quired to take part in a
daily routine that includes education, vocational training, a nd a rehabilitative
programme. We do not want these young teenager s to get used to a life of crime and to
continue creating victims in the years ahead. While they are being punished for
committing crimes, we can give them the opport unity to turn their lives round, so that
when they are released they are better  equipped to contribut e to society, enter
employment, and be much less likely to re offend. We will also be saving the taxpayer
$96,000 a year for every offender who does not re turn to prison. This is no easy task, as
young prisoners are often aggressive, destructiv e, and antisocial, but if we can address
these issues while they are under 20 and still impressionable, while giving them
education and skills training, then we can make a real difference and, ultimately, we can
make our communities safer.
The 30-bed refurbished unit replaces the pr evious youth unit, which was closed in
2011. The department has now strengthened it s links with Child, Youth and Family,
youth justice, and police youth aid to bette r tackle youth offending. Under this
Government and under Minister Tolley and Mi nister Collins we are seeing a model that
is being rolled out throughout the country where there is much better cooperation and
communication between the different agencies that are touching and having to deal with
these offenders. This youth offenders unit ha s a major contribution to make in reaching
that goal, alongside our other important targets of a reduction of the total recorded crime
rate of 15 percent, a reduction in the record ed violent crime rate of 20 percent, and a
reduction in the youth crime rate of 5 percent.
Two thousand prisoners are to be enrolled  in an education programme leading to
National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA) qualifications over the next 2
years as a result of a new partnership that has been formed between the Department of
Corrections and The Open Polytechnic. The pa rtnership will help the department reach
its Better Public Services target of a reduction in reoffending of 25 percent, with 18,500
fewer victims of crime each year by the ye ar 2017. Offenders will receive 2 hours of
coaching a week on top of 8 hours of distance learning as part of the Get Ahead with
NCEA programme, and will be able to study for an Open Polytechnic certification in
career and self-development, a national certificate in employment skills, and a
certificate in work and life skills, and NCEA  levels 1 and 2 will become available to
them.
We know that a lack of education is a major driver of crime. Education and
qualifications are powerful tools in helping st eer offenders away from criminal activity,
which leads to fewer victims of crime and, ul timately, safer communities. The reality is
8458 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
that around 90 percent of prisoners canno t read or write pr operly—90 percent of
prisoners cannot read or write properly. Most will be released back into our
communities, but while they are inside prison  they are the ultimate captive audience. If
we can give them access to an education while inside the wire, or just after release into
the community, they can learn literacy an d numeracy skills and earn qualifications,
which will help them to hold down jobs and make a positive contribution to society,
instead of returning to crime.
Report noted.
Vote Climate Change

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: This year’s financial review, I think, reveals as
little about the Government’s budgetary policy on the issue of climate change as they
did in previous years. The stated purpos e of the Appropriation (2011/12 Financial
Review) Bill is “to confirm financial matte rs relating to the 2011/12 financial year;”.
The bill retroactively confirms expenditure incurred by the Government for that year.
We are about to approve expenditure alrea dy incurred in excess of the appropriation
then existing or even without appropriation, so it is important that such confirmation be
laid before the House with accuracy and tran sparency. After all, as the bill explains in
the explanatory note, “It is a basic const itutional principle that the Government can
spend public money … only in accordance with  [parliamentary legisl ation] and in an
otherwise lawful manner.” Ye t public funds pertaining to climate change are spread
across a number of Government departments— the Ministry for Primary Industries, the
Ministry for the Environment, the Minist ry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and
Treasury—so transparency tends to suffer.
The Vote Climate Change non-department al output classes shown in the Local
Government and Environment Committee report are twofold. Allocation of New
Zealand Units shows net surplus of $1.2 m illion, and issue of New Zealand assigned
amount units under the Permanent Forest Sink  Initiative showed net surpluses of $7.6
million. Why is this? Because the demand fo r New Zealand Units declined following
the weakening of the emissions trading sc heme by this Government in 2009. The final
gutting of the emissions trading scheme was in late 2012, after the period under review,
but we can all see the effect on New Zealand’s climate policy from the 2009 actions.
The fact is that New Zealand has never had a genuine climate policy. We have
lurched around since the 1990s between tradi ng and taxation. We have never developed
a pathway for a quantitative cap up to 2050 or a series of 5-yearly Budgets. We gift free
allocations without auctioning. We allow in cheapened international credits that force
down the domestic price to absurdly lo w levels. We consciously witness the
dysfunctional outcome of a climate policy in the name of the purity of the free market,
yet we drop that ideological purity when it suits us, such  as imposing a price cap and
choosing sectors and corporat ions for special favourable treatment, except forestry,
which has been left twisting in the wind.
Meanwhile, the scientific findings on climate change, plus the continuing growth in
global emissions, make it clear that we are moving from a dangerous to a “cataclysmic”
future, as the World Bank puts it, on current em ission trends. It is no t just Australia or
Russia or Pakistan with their fires and their floods. It is not only the Philippines, Samoa,
and the United States with their hurricanes . Climate Change has hit New Zealand. We
have extreme drought now. The New Zealand drought, like any other extreme event, is
part of a pattern of weather events consistent with climat e change, yet this Government
displays an endearing politic al reticence over use of the term “climate change”. The
Acting Prime Minister in the House this afte rnoon spoke airily of long-term change in
weather patterns—it will not pay to frighten the voters ! He speaks as if we are
12 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8459
confronting a natural phenomenon and the change will be over a long term, so New
Zealanders, not least the farmers, will be able  to adapt. This is consistent with the
Government’s refusal to adjust New Zealand’ s emissions trading scheme settings to the
level required for behavioural change. That  is why the financial review of 2011-12
reveals a drop in activity pertaining to the issuance of New Zealand Units.
The Acting Prime Minister, wittingly or  otherwise, conveye d a breathtaking
indifference to intellectual hone sty and political in tegrity this afternoon. He affirmed
governmental support for farmers in distress from extreme weather in the short term,
but in the long term the farming community must adapt, as it has in the past. He then
lumped in households and businesses, just to round the point off. In this he refuses to
acknowledge that the changes in weather occurring around us ar e unprecedented in
scale and that the occurrence of climate change is, to cite the scientists, incontrovertible,
yet Mr English wishes to assuage the voters by saying that all they have to do is adapt.
Report noted.
Ministry for the Environment

items.speaker: Hon MARYAN STREET
items.text: The financial review of the Ministry for the
Environment for the 2011-12 year  contains, in the report of the Local Government and
Environment Committee, a reference to work that the ministry was doing at the time. I
have to say, to begin with, that I thin k this ministry is both under-resourced and
undervalued. But it seems to me that it is just as appropriate to talk about the work that
it was doing that has come to light in the last 10 days or so, because it is apparent that
when it comes to the environment the only thing that National is protecting is its own
agenda. There is this complete failure to recognise and understand that the economy and
the environment are not two rival forces to be balanced against each other, but are in
fact two sides of the same coin and are interdependent.
But National’s development agenda has seen us weaken air-quality standards, rush
through some flawed exclusive economic zone  legislation, and fa il to sign up to a
second commitment of the Kyoto Protocol, among a host of other failures. Most
recently we have seen the release of  a discussion document on the Resource
Management Act. There is going to be a lo t more that needs to be said about the
proposals and the discussion document before th at matter is over. Then, most recently,
we saw the National Government releas e proposals on freshwater quality and
management. These proposals were meant to reflect some of the 4 years of work that the
Ministry for the Environment has been doing in conjunction with the Land and Water
Forum. Well, that forum in particular, and now the Ministry for the Environment, has to
become involved in the Minister’s application of those reports.
What I am concerned about is that we ar e getting contradictory messages from the
Government, and I do not know how the Ministry for the Environment is to implement
contradictory policies. First of all, in the Resource Management  Act discussion paper
the Minister for the Environment, Amy Adams, is pushing for more ministerial
control—less power vested in the Envir onment Court—over local decisions, which are
more likely to affect individual people w ho want to build a deck on their house than
anything else. But in the latest proposal s for the quality and management of our
waterways, the Minister is pushing for local councils to make the decisions over
waterways that are, in fact, national treasur es. They are not simply the province of the
people who live beside them, but they are, in  fact, taonga, they are treasures, they are
facilities that all New Zealanders hold dear. So on the one hand the Minister has got the
reach of Government wrong in the Resour ce Management Act proposals and wants to
override local councils, and in the second proposal she has got it wrong again, by
wanting to leave decisions on quality and mana gement of waterways to local councils
8460 Financial Review Debate 12 Mar 2013
without any cognisance of the nationwide significance and the need for national
environmental standards applying in respect of these waterways.
So we are really pressed to understand how  it is possible for the Ministry for the
Environment to enact two contradictory directions from the Minister for the
Environment. The only conclusi on we are left to draw is th at the Minister’s agenda is
simply a narrowly focused development agenda—beyond all else, a narrowly focused
development agenda—that does not take into  account the larger significance of the
environment. For all of the blue-green prot estations, it is entirely clear from this
contradiction that there is only a small num ber of people who are going to benefit from
these proposals, and they are the ones this Government traditionally supports.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: The Ministry for the Environment spent nearly $51
million in 2011-12, and a major appropriation w ithin that allocation, and a major work
stream for a number of the ministry’s sta ff, is a programme called improving resource
management. The ministry may have receive d a very good rating from the Office of the
Auditor-General on its financial informati on systems and controls, but the suite of
changes that this ministry has been direct ed to make to the Resource Management Act
by the National Government is receiving a thumbs down and a very poor rating from
anyone who cares about our lands, our waters, our coasts, and our air and from anyone
who understands that a healthy environment is the basis of economic success. It is a key
plank of the National Government’s pro-deve lopment, anti-environment agenda that it
has directed the ministry to dismantle the concept of sustainable management that has
been in the Resource Management Act for 20  years; to strip out five of the key
environmental criteria in Part 2, the core of the Act; and to put in provisions that would
see economic effects emphasised over environm ental ones, so that the playing field is
tilted very much in favour of development,  regardless of how destructive or poorly
planned that development is.
When the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment released her submission
on the Resource Management Reform Bill, which is before this House, she said that it
would “unbalance” the Resource Management Act. She criticised the ministry’s policy
work on the bill and the plans to increase th e influence of economic concerns. She said:
“There is a sense in the changes that the environment is considered the enemy of
economic progress”. That is certainly someth ing we have seen in the discussion paper
that was released last month, and that the ministry is now taking around the country in a
very rapid roadshow. Groups like the Enviro nmental Defence Society have called the
proposals in the discussion document “deeply tr oubling”. So what did the Minister do?
She moved to shut down the discussion almo st immediately by describing groups such
as the Environmental Defence Society a nd the Royal Forest and Bird Protection
Society, and their criticisms, as being “out of touch” and being “scaremongers”, when it
is those groups that provide a thin green line to protect our environment with their
work—

12 Mar 2013 Obituaries 8375 
TUESDAY, 12 MARCH 2013 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
OBITUARIES 
Geoffrey Bernard Braybrooke QSO 
Mr SPEAKER: Honourable members, I regret to inform the House of the death on 8 
March 2013 of Geoffrey Bernard Braybrooke  QSO, who represented the Napier 
electorate from 1981 to 2002. From 1999 to 2002 he served as Deputy Speaker. I desire 
on behalf of this House to express our sense of the loss we have sustained and our 
sympathy for the relatives of the late former  member. I now ask members to stand with 
me and observe a period of silence as a mark of respect for his memory.  
Honourable members stood as a mark of respect. 
MOTIONS 
Human Rights, Fiji—Treatment of Detainees 
Hon PHIL GOFF (Labour—Mt Roskill) : I seek leave of the House to move 
without notice and without debate a motion concerning the beating and the torture of 
detainees in Fiji. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
appears to be none. 
Hon PHIL GOFF : I move, That this House condemn the beating and torture of 
detainees in Fiji evidenced in a recent video recording of the event, and call upon the 
interim Government of Fiji to publicly condemn  the use of torture, to hold to account 
those responsible, and to uphold, as standards of  best practice, the requirements of the 
United Nations Convention against Torture and the International Covenant on Civil 
and Political Rights. 
Motion agreed to. 
Iran Hostage Crisis, 1979—Fictional Representation of Role of New Zealand 
Diplomats 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First) : I seek leave of the House to 
move a non-controversial motion without notice and without debate to correct the grave 
misrepresentation of the courageous and co mmendable role of New Zealand diplomats 
in the 1979 Tehran hostage crisis in the movie Argo.  
Mr SPEAKER: Leave is sought for that course of  action. Is there any objection to 
that? There appears to be none. 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS: I move, That this House acknowledge with gratitude 
the efforts of former New Zealand diplom ats Chris Beeby and Richard Sewell in 
assisting American hostages in Tehran duri ng the hostage crisis  in 1979, and express 
its regret that the director of the movie Argo saw fit to mislead the world about what 
actually happened during that crisis whe n, in reality, our courageous diplomats’ 
inspirational actions were of significant he lp to the American hostages and deserve the 
factual and historical record to be corrected. 
Motion agreed to. 
8376 Motions 12 Mar 2013 
Black Sox—2013 Men’s World Softball Championships Victory 
TE URUROA FLAVELL (M āori Party—Waiariki): I seek leave of the House to 
move a motion without notice and without de bate in relation to the recent World 
Softball Championships and the success of the Black Sox.  
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
appears to be none. 
TE URUROA FLAVELL: Kia ora t ātou. I move, That this House congratulate the 
six-time World Softball Championships - winning Black Sox on their record-breaking 4-
1 win against Venezuela over the weekend, in  the final of the Men’s World Softball 
Championships 2013. 
Motion agreed to. 
RESIGNATIONS 
Charles Chauvel, New Zealand Labour 
Mr SPEAKER: I wish to advise the House that I have received a letter from Charles 
Chauvel resigning his seat in the House with effect on Monday, 11 March 2013. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
State-owned Assets, Sales—Public Support, Purpose, and Cost 
1. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his statement that “I think we got a mandate” for asset sales at the last election, 
given a majority of New Zealanders voted for parties that opposed his Government’s 
asset sales policy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Acting Prime Minister) : Yes, and the Prime Minister 
stands by his full statement where he said : “An election campaign is all about the 
contest of ideas. One of the most hotly de bated issues was the mixed ownership model 
and the contrast between that and increasi ng New Zealand’s debt. And in Government 
we lifted our party vote.” In respect of major ities, there is one majo rity that matters in 
Government and that is the majority in this House. 
Dr Russel Norman : Is he comfortable for that majo rity to rely on the discredited 
vote of John Banks? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The Government is comfortable with a majority based on the 
duly elected members of the Parliament. I know that the Green s do not respect the 
parliamentary majority or the election result, but the rest of New Zealand does. 
Dr Russel Norman : How can he claim a mandate to sell our assets when the 
majority of New Zealanders voted at the last  election for parties opposed to asset sales, 
and the vast majority of Ne w Zealanders continue to oppose asset sales in every poll on 
the issue? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : As has been said in this House many times before, the 
National Government laid out in detail at th e start of 2011 its programme for the partial 
sell-down of Government companies. That  was debated vigorousl y, including by that 
member, right through election year. In fact, the dominant issue of the election 
campaign was asset sales. Every New Zealan der had the opportunity to decide what 
weight to give that issue in their vote. Th e result of the vote was a majority in this 
House for a Government that had pledged to  carry out that plan, and now we are doing 
what we said we would do. 
12 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8377 
Louise Upston: How many New Zealanders have pre- registered to apply for shares 
in the first partial share float in the G overnment’s share programme, and over what 
period has that been achieved? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : As of early this afternoon the number of New Zealanders 
who have pre-registered to apply for shar es in Mighty River Power has reached more 
than 290,000—more than 290,000—signatures, whic h is in 1 week a bit short of the 
number achieved in a year with paid par liamentary staff bailing up schoolchildren for 
the petition that is now put before the House. 
Dr Russel Norman: Does the Prime Minister deny that 51 percent of the votes cast 
at the last election were cast in favour of parties opposed to asset sales? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: No, the Prime Minister asserts that the result of the election 
was that a party that laid out its plans in detail and allowed 10 or 11 months of intensive 
debate, including a whole election campaign based around asset sales, was duly elected 
as the Government of New Zealand, and in a contest of mandates—his dodgy petition or 
the voice of the people—we go for the voice of the people. 
Dr Russel Norman : Given his acknowledgment that asset sales require a mandate 
from the public, will his Government pledge not to sell any assets until that mandate can 
be unequivocally and directly tested in the coming referendum? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: No, the Government will stick to its plans. That member just 
needs to accept that with a w hole year to debate this issue with New Zealanders and 
allow them to make up their own minds and express that thr ough the ballot box, he 
happened to lose the argument , because people took this issue not on its own but in the 
whole of economic management, of their aspi rations for New Zeala nders, and of their 
fear of debt in a global financial crisis . He simply lost the argument, and the 
Government is going to continue with its plans. 
Louise Upston: If the Government did not reorga nise taxpayers’ assets through the 
share offer programme, what alternative a pproaches would it have to pay for new 
assets? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The member is quite right that it is reorganising the assets. 
We will sell shares and, in return for t hose shares, obtain cash—actually, somewhere 
between $5 billion and $7 billion cash. If we did not do that, we would have to borrow 
the money from volatile global financial mark ets, pushing up New Zealand’s debt, or, 
of course, we could pay for new assets by printing money, which, I think, is what 
Opposition parties are advocating. 
Dr Russel Norman : Is it not the case that Treasury  in its Budget Policy Statement 
stated that the net cost to the taxpayer of the asset sales programme was $441 million 
over 5 years, and on top of that there is another $100 million cost in running the asset 
sale programme, so the total cost to the taxpayer of his petty little policy is over half a 
billion dollars? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : As we have pointed out before in the House in respect of 
those estimates, first, there are a number of different ways of measuring the impact over 
4 years. Some of them show the Government a bit ahead and some of them show it a bit 
behind. But all those measures are based on an assumption that these businesses would 
continue to make the profits they have made  and pay the dividends they have paid. As 
we have learnt from Solid Energy, those a ssumptions can be blown away by the reality 
of the market and commercial pressures. So  the Government is re ducing its exposure to 
risky commercial businesses, a nd is deploying the money it ge ts from that into long-
term social assets. 
Dr Russel Norman: Does the Prime Minister have so  little respect for the people of 
New Zealand that he will casually dismiss the 393,000 Kiwis who have signed the Keep 
8378 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Mar 2013 
Our Assets petition as children, tourists, and dodgy, and continue with this disrespectful 
attitude once the petition has been certified as legitimate by the Clerk of the House? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Government had sufficient confidence in New 
Zealanders to lay out its plans in detail. I recall at the time Opposition parties saying 
that the Government would certainly lose the election because it had laid out its plans 
for asset sales. New Zealanders had the full opportunity to debate the issue, and then 
there was an election. In  respect of the petition process,  the petition pro cess belongs to 
Parliament, and of course that process w ill be respected. Parliament has a petition 
process and people can express their point of view, but, as the member knows, 
Parliament has also said those referenda are not binding. 
Dr Russel Norman: Does he agree with Bill Englis h that National would like to sell 
Kiwibank “eventually, but not now”, in the words of Bill Englis h, and does this not 
show that National’s asset sales agenda does not end here—it wants to privatise more? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: I can confirm that, no, the Prime Minister did not agree with 
that statement by Bill English, and he made it pretty plain at the time. The 
Government’s asset sales programme has been set out in detail. We have started a series 
of floats of the companies that have been listed by the Government, and when those are 
completed the programme will be finished. 
Dr Russel Norman : Does he agree that the question in the petition, in the 
referendum, which is “Do you support the Government selling up to 49% of Meridian 
Energy, Mighty River Power, Genesis Power,  Solid Energy and Air New Zealand?”, 
accurately and neutrally states the policy choice facing New Zealanders? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: Yes. In so far as it addresses the sale of those companies, it 
does, in exactly the same way that the Government set out accurately and in precisely 
those terms its plans at the beginning of election year 2011. New Zealanders had the 
opportunity not just to consider  it as a single-issue vehicle for Opposition parties but to 
consider it as part of th e overall management of the economy through some pretty 
difficult times. On balance, they voted sufficiently for a group of parties that were able 
to come together to form a majority Government. In a democracy that is the true test of 
a mandate, and we passed it. 
Drought Conditions—Economic Impact and Government Response 
2. MIKE SABIN (National—Northland) to the Minister of Finance: What impact 
is the current drought likely to have on the economy? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance) : Well, clearly, th e longer the drought 
goes on and the more widespread it becomes,  the greater the impact will be. We are 
beginning to see a decline in milk production— in fact, a sharp decline in some areas—
and farmers are considering slaughtering capital stock, which will result in lower future 
production and reduced revenue for farmers. This may flow through to a negative effect 
on GDP compared with our most recent forecas ts. However, there are some factors that 
may offset that, such as the increase in pr ices, particularly for dairy products, and the 
fact that up until the drought began we had a str ong production season for milk 
production. Thirdly, the production in  the South Island will con tinue to partially offset 
decreases in the north. So we know the dr ought will peg back growth in the economy, 
but it is not yet clear by how much. 
Mike Sabin: What help is the Government offe ring farmers who are affected by the 
drought? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: In this context the Government is mindful that many parts of 
the economy and many households and businesses have had to adapt their 
circumstances because we have had harder ti mes, and the same will apply to farmers. 
There is some Government assistance, howev er. Once drought has been declared, extra 
12 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8379 
funding is made available to coordinate th e local rural support trust, which provide 
primarily moral rather than financial s upport; the Inland Revenue Department has the 
capacity to extend flexibility to farmers on a case by case basis to assist them with 
smoothing their tax payments; and in extrem e cases rural assistance payments are 
available at the equivalent rate to the une mployment benefit. This is a package of 
measures actually put together by the previ ous Government for dealing with floods and 
droughts, and we believe that it is appropriate in the circumstances. 
Hon David Parker : Does the Government still intend to be back in surplus in the 
2014-15 year? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: Yes. 
Mike Sabin : How can the Government support farmers if there are long-term 
changes in weather patterns? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : It certainly cannot do it thr ough financial means that are 
aimed to support those in extreme hardship for a short period of time. In the long run, 
farmers would have to adapt to changes in weather patterns, as they have before. New 
Zealand has been through cycles of wet summers and dry summers over the last three or 
four decades. Where the most direct Govern ment assistance comes in is through its 
funding of research and development and through the Primary Growth Partnership, 
which looks into improved production and into better drought management. 
Mike Sabin: How does the drought affect the Government’s plan to return to surplus 
in 2014-15? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : It remains the Government’s target to return to surplus in 
2014-15. There is no doubt, thou gh, that a drought is likely to have some negative 
impact and make that task a bit harder. Trea sury will be incorporating its view of the 
future impact of the drought into forecasts as we go into the Budget, and the 
Government will take that into account in making its spending decisions. 
State Owned Enterprises, Minister—Confidence 
3. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
have confidence in the Minister for State Owned Enterprises? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Acting Prime Minister) : Yes, he is a hard-working and 
competent Minister. 
David Shearer: When did his Minister for State Owned Enterprises first inform him 
that the falling coal prices were having a serious effect on Solid Energy and that the 
company was in financial difficulty? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : The Minister for State Owned Enterprises would have been 
involved in the initiation of the scoping st udy into Solid Energy, along with the other 
State-owned enterprises, at the beginning of  2011, just after he became the Minister for 
State Owned Enterprises. He would have received that re port, which highlighted some 
concerns about Solid Energy, at the same time as the Prime Minister did during 2011.  
David Shearer : Why did the Government show a book value of $3.5 billion for 
Solid Energy in November 2010, when earlie r it had been independently valued by 
Macquarie and Forsyth Barr at $1.7 billion and $1.6 billion, respectively? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The valuation of the company, as I understand it, was finally 
determined by the board, and that was the board ’s valuation. As it has turned out, that 
was based on assumptions about both the coal price and the company’s investments into 
alternative energy—assumptions that did not eventuate. 
David Shearer: Did either of the shareholding Ministers advise him on the scoping 
report received 3 weeks before the 2011 el ection, which highlighted Solid Energy’s 
financial problems; if so, why was that information not made public? 
8380 Questions for Oral Answer 12 Mar 2013 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The Minister would certainly have brought that report to the 
attention of the Prime Minister—in fact, it had been discussed throughout 2011, well 
before there was any drop in the coal price.  The scoping studies were not made public 
because they were commercially confidential documents. I might say, at the time, the 
Opposition was criticising the Government on th e basis that it was going to be ripping 
these places apart by applying commercial principles; now it is saying that we were not 
commercial enough. 
David Shearer : Why was the Government continui ng to pretend publicly that all 
was rosy at Solid Energy while preparing it for sale, when Ministers knew it was 
actually in financial trouble?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Because that is not correct. Th e sequence of events is that 
the scoping study highlighted a number of areas  of concern with So lid Energy, later in 
2012 those concerns turned in to pretty obvious vulnerabilities when the coal price 
dropped significantly, and then Solid Energy lost 25 percent of its export market. The 
Government was working with the board on these issues well before there was any 
question of Solid Energy’s financial viability.  
David Shearer : Why was the Government battling the Solid Energy board for 18 
months to stop it selling part of Solid Energy overseas, as the Prime Minister said just a 
few hours ago, when that is ex actly what the Government is planning to do when it 
floats it on the Australian Securities Exchange?  
Hon BILL ENGLISH : What the Government was doing was contesting with the 
board its opinions and views about the direct ion of the company, its opinions about the 
future track for the coal price, and its opi nions about the success of the alternative 
energy investments that it was pushed into by the previous Labour Government. 
Children, State Care—Gateway Assessments and Children in Care Package 
4. Hon PHIL HEATLEY (National—Whangarei)  to the Minister for Social 
Development: What results have the Government’s Gateway Assessments for children 
in care had to date? 
Hon PAULA BENNETT (Minister for Social Development) : Under Budget 2011 
we established gateway assessments for ch ildren who are in State care. Gateway 
assesses the child’s health, mental health, a nd educational needs, and we are picking up 
issues not ever before diagnosed. Almo st 1,700 children in care have now been 
assessed, with an average of more than three needs per child picked up. The most 
frequent health needs identified so far are 51 percent had emoti onal, behavioural, or 
mental health needs, 26 percent had dental  issues, 15 percent ha d developmental delay, 
14 percent had skin problems, and 13 percent had speech and language problems.  
Hon Phil Heatley : What examples have there been that show gateway assessments 
are making a difference?  
Hon PAULA BENNETT : There are many examples of how this investment in our 
most vulnerable children is making a differenc e, but one is that five children have 
received heart surgery following gateway asse ssments that picked up heart defects, and 
they are now receiving ongoing treatment. That was not picked up before these 
assessments were done. Another example is a child who was found with untreated club 
foot, and they received orthopaedic surgery and, 12 months later, are now able to walk. 
Children in care have had it tough enough, be fore you add unidentified developmental 
delay, mental health, and health problems to a toxic background of abuse and neglect. 
We are doing something tangible to improve those odds.  
Hon Phil Heatley : How is the Children in Care package ensuring better outcomes 
for these children?  
12 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8381 
Hon PAULA BENNETT : This is not about just fi nding and fixing problems; it is 
also about getting ahead of them. As pa rt of the package we funded some early 
childhood education places for 18-month-olds  to 3-year-olds. Around 230 children in 
care are receiving early childhood education as a result of this initiative, improving their 
chances and addressing developmental and learning delays, and also—importantly, I 
think—giving those people the chance that they need to have a bit of a break as well.  
Solid Energy—Minister’s Role and Former Chief Executive’s Contract 
5. Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE (Labour)  to the Minister for State Owned 
Enterprises: Does he stand by his statement “There was no change to Dr Elder’s pay or 
entitlements. Therefore, there was no effect on what his contractual arrangements would 
be during the changes to his employment”; if so, why? 
Hon TONY RYALL (Minister fo r State Owned Enterprises) : Within context, 
yes, because that is the advice I have received from both Mr Palmer and Mr Ford. 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove : Why does he continue to clai m that Dr Elder got nothing 
from the contract extension signed by th e outgoing chair on 31 August 2012 when the 
so-called transitional arrangements, where Dr Elder is being paid to stay at home for 2 
months, are nothing more than a rebranded golden handshake? 
Hon TONY RYALL: Because the advice that I have received from Mr Palmer and 
Mr Ford—which I have given to that memb er on at least, I think, four or five 
occasions—is that there were no changes to Dr  Elder’s pay and entitlements as a result 
of the contract being updated at the end of August. 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove: On what date did he first become aware that Dr Elder was 
being paid to stay at home as part of the so-called “tra nsitional arrangements” he had 
with Solid Energy? 
Hon TONY RYALL : I think it would have been at around about the time of the 
announcement of Dr Elder’s reti rement that Mr Ford would have informed me that Dr 
Elder was moving on and that he would be remaining available to the company for a 
period of time. 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove : After Dr Elder’s mediation meeting on 8 February 2013 
and after the exit package was signed off on 11 February 2013, did he, as Minister, 
inquire as to whether Dr Elder was to receive any additional remuneration—maybe 
without asking for the quantum—such as bein g paid to stay at home for 2 months; if 
not, why not? 
Hon TONY RYALL: Well, I think this is probably the third or fourth time I would 
have answered this question, a nd the advice that I received from Mr Ford is that Dr 
Elder received all the enti tlements he was entitled  to under his contractual 
arrangements. 
Hon Clayton Cosgrove : After battling with the board  of Solid Energy for over 18 
months, as has been alluded to by his Minister of Financ e, why did the Minister not 
invoke section 13 of the State-Owned Enterp rises Act where, via the statement of
